speechtext:
On occasion, it can be in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's interest to share facilities belonging to a private company rather than establishing its own facilities. When this is the case, the Corporation negotiates agreements to this end. This is in fact common practice in the broadcasting industry. Broadcasters often enter into agreements to use existing facilities, even those of competitors. In this respect, CBC has the following agreements with Radio-Nord Inc.
In Abitibi, where Radio-Nord has transmission equipment, CBC French radio and television services are available as a result of affiliation agreements with Radio-Nord Inc.

October 3, 1991
Routine Proceedings
In 1985, the Corporation concluded an agreement with Radio-Nord Inc. to use that company's transmission facilities in Rouyn to establish CBC English radio and television network services in Abitibi.
Also in 1985, in order to improve the quality of French television service in the Temiscaming region, the Corporation reached an agreement with Radio-Nord Inc. to improve its Fabre-Bearn transmitter. This transmitter feeds the CBC transmitter in Temiscaming.
In 1990, an agreement was concluded concerning the sharing of existing equipment in order to implement new FM radio services in Rouyn and Val d'Or. This agreement replaced a previous one dating from 1976.
With respect to the costs incurred (a) and (b), Parliament has not, as a matter of custom since the Corporation's creation in 1936, required CBC to supply, in answering Parliamentary questions, such details about its internal management and administration. Parliament has had two reasons for following this customs: first, the independence of the CBC as a Crown Corporation, established for the purpose of producing and broadcasting, independently of political or commercial interference, programs for a national program service; and, secondly, the competitive nature of many of CBC's activities. The appropriateness of the CBC providing certain categories of information has been considered on many occasions by various Parliamentary Committees and the CBC has suggested that such information should not be made a matter of public record, its views have been accepted. Names of staff members and their functions in relation to specific programs and the costs related to such assignments, as requested in Question No. 2295 answered May 20, 1975, are examples of details which it has not been customary to require the CBC to supply. It is open to Parliament to discuss the policies it and when the CBC have followed in this regard and it would be appropriate to review them when the CBC's estimates are before the House of Commons Committee on Communications and Culture.
The government makes available all information requested by members except where publication would be inconsistent with the mandate given to the Corporation by Parliament. This principle is well established and accepted with respect to information about government
agencies and Crown Corporations which are in competition with the private sector.

He said: Madam Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, I would like to point out that we in the Official Opposition will be sharing our time slots today with the exception of my own introductory remarks which will lay out the basis of this debate. My colleagues will be sharing their time slots and each will be speaking for 10 minutes.
I would also like to ask your assistance, Madam Speaker, in view of the crisis that has developed in the agricultural industry, in finding a way for us to table some petitions put together in good faith by over 5,000 members of various farm organizations at a meeting in Lucknow, Ontario, that are unfortunately in the wrong form. These petitions outline the seriousness of the economic situation in agriculture and were put together in good faith. They do not meet the requirements here. I just received them this morning. I was wondering if there was any way they could be tabled along with the remarks that I am about to make here today.

It is a critical situation out there, Madam Speaker. In my own riding, there have been four suicides within the last month. These people need to be heard, they want the government to realize their problems and to take action accordingly.
I cannot help but think at the onset of this debate that there are strange priorities in this country at the present time. They are strange priorities when it costs $150 a tonne to dispose of Toronto's garbage, yet we only pay the farmers $115 a tonne to produce the food that we eat. I am speaking here of wheat.
This government, as evidenced by its vote on Monday, September 23, does not agree there is a financial crisis in the grain sector in this country. If supply management is destroyed by the government negotiators at GATT, similar devastating prices will occur in the dairy and poultry sectors.
In contrast to the grain sector, the poultry and dairy industries are healthy industries. It would be sheer economic nonsense and madness to see those industries destroyed by the government failing to maintain and strengthen Article XI of the GATT. Let us be clear from the onset, the process of tariffication will utterly destroy these industries. A system of tariffication is not acceptable to the producers of Canada.
For the last 60 years, beginning prior to the Great Depression of the 1930s, there have been actions by various levels of government to bring a level of stability to Canadian agriculture as the Conservative government itself brought in the Canadian Wheat Board legislation in 1935.
In 1949 the Agricultural Products Marketing Act was implemented, and in 1972 the Liberal government of the day proclaimed the National Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act. Of course the Canadian Dairy Commission was proclaimed during that same timeframe.
The National Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act allows for the establishment of marketing agencies with the power to set prices based on the cost of production, to plan production to meet market needs and other measures that would lead to a more efficient industry.
These systems, as they matured, became the most sophisticated of any in the world. In the case of poultry and dairy, the producers achieved a level of stability
Supply
which allowed them a small profit and a return on labour and investment.
Some critics would lead us to believe that marketing boards lead to inefficiencies. When we examine the records of the dairy industries, we find that the productivity per cow in Canada increased by 73.5 per cent since 1971, compared to only 46 per cent in the U.S. and 3.5 per cent in western Europe.
Better feed conversion, better disease control and more eggs per bird have occurred in the poultry industry during the last 15 years under this marketing agency. This is in sharp contrast to the chicken operations in the U.S. where often low levels of antibiotics are fed to combat diseases. Indeed, the chief of the United States Department of Food Safety, Mr. Crawford, recently stated that "the American people are tired of seeing one story after another about dirty chickens" on their markets. Mr. Crawford was commenting on a USDA report that found 35 per cent of the chickens raised in the United States were infected with salmonella bacteria, and other reports according to Reuters News Agency have put the number much higher.
Starting the early 1950s and up to the present time, there has been a growing concentration of control in food after it leaves the processors, a concentration that forced narrower margins for the processors and diminishing returns to the poultry sector.
Since January 1, 1989 to June 1991, 70 food processing plants in Canada were forced out of business, 36 of these were in Ontario.
I recently completed a study which I called "Compare the Share". It shows a huge increase in the price of food over the last 10 years. These increases have occurred after the food has been sold by the farmer and has already left the processor.
In fact, processors are being forced to close their doors not because of high producer prices but because of the untenable situation vis-a-vis distribution, wholesale and retail operations. Anybody who wants a copy of this report can have one by simply writing to my office. I should point out that there will be a brochure available at the Royal Winter Fair giving this outline so that the consumers of Canada know who is ripping them off in their food basket purchases. It is certainly not the Canadian farmers, who are among the most efficient in the world.

This graphic comparison of the cost of various food items clearly indicates that during a 10-year period, from 1980 to 1990, farm gate prices increased very little, in fact in some cases they declined, while retail prices have increased dramatically. For example, a box of corn flakes increased by 94.5 per cent from 1980 to 1989; a box of soda biscuits increased by 235 per cent during the same period; and sweet cookies increased by 135 per cent. And get this; a box of whole wheat cereal increased by 194.2 per cent during this period when the price of wheat to the producer was declining.
By contrast, a product under marketing board control, namely eggs, developed much more acceptable price increases to consumers. Egg prices to the producer increased by 14.1 per cent during this period and by 18.3 per cent to the consumer. Likewise, the farm price of eviscerated weight turkeys to the producer increased by 12.8 per cent and the consumer price by 25.8 per cent. Since 1980 the retail price of chicken has increased by $2.20 per kilogram, while the farm price only increased by 28 cents per kilogram. This retail price increase from 1980 to 1990 was 785 per cent higher than the farm price increase over the same period.
Madam Speaker, that is not acceptable. These price comparisons clearly show the cost of production formula used by the poultry sector has provided a steady level of prices to the producer and a correspondingly fair price to the processor.
It is interesting to note that the total farm value of all chickens, turkey, eggs and milk produced in Canada in 1990 was $4.8 billion, 32 per cent less than the total sales of $7.1 billion of one large grocery chain. The price of a litre of milk in Ontario at the farm gate increased by 19 cents since 1980, on the store shelf the price of that litre of milk has increased by 73 cents, or 97 per cent.
I would like to stress this. The Consumers' Association of Canada in the September-October issue of their magazine blames the fact that milk in Canada costs more than in the United States solely on supply management. However, the Consumers' Association of Canada has not provided us with any research, as far as I can see from
the article, on the price of these products. Madam Speaker, this is pure hogwash. The Consumers' Association of Canada says that it found milk 30 per cent cheaper in the U.S. than in Canada, yet it makes no comment on the fact that the difference in the price of a litre of milk in 1990 between the farm gate and the store shelf is 91 cents, the store shelf price being 160 per cent higher than the farm gate price.
It should be noted that the increase in the retail price of a litre of milk between 1990 and 1989 outstripped the food marketing cost index by 1.5 per cent. It is also interesting to note that neither the Consumers' Association of Canada nor the government consider the increase in input costs versus that of the United States. Input costs for our Canadian producers are approximately 25 per cent higher than those in the United States starting with interest rates, diesel fuel costs and labour. I will say more about that in a few minutes.
I suggest that the Consumers' Association of Canada could do the consumers a better service by investigating the entire food pricing structure, including distribution and wholesale sectors as well as the retailers, rather than singling out supply management for unwarranted abuse.
Why don't they complain about the cost of soft drinks? A small bottle of soft drink costs more than a glass of milk. I respectfully suggest that $793,000 in funding given to the Canadian Consumers' Association last year would be much better spent if it were used to provide food for our food banks in some of our larger cities.
It amazes me that one food chain in western Canada sent $538,700,000 in dividends back to its parent company in the United States last year. Where was the Canadian Consumers' Association when this took place? We didn't hear a word. Obviously we have a double standard in society today. The same is true of cheese. Since 1980 the farm price of cheese increased by $1.53 per kilogram, while the retail price increased by $5.34 a kilogram to $11.52 a kilogram. In 1980 there was a $3.13 spread in price between the farmer and the processor and by 1988 that spread was $6.94.
October 3, 1991

The power exercised by these few buying groups requires a countervailing force in the marketplace. Canada's producer marketing systems provide that counterbalance.
When one examines the chaos existing in the U.S. dairy industry at the present time, the concentration of the U.S. poultry industry and red meat industry, and the impact that concentration will have on Canada as the borders are opened, we on this side of the House realize that it will destroy our marketing systems and our industry. Climatic differences alone give the U.S. a tremendous advantage.
Canadian consumers spend 11.5 per cent of their disposable income on food, the second lowest portion of income spent on food of any nation in the world. The producer desperately needs a fair share of that consumer food dollar.
I should also point out that due to this government's free trade agreement with the United States that marketing boards have again found themselves under attack.
The Conservative government at the time stated that it "defended the right to establish" marketing boards "in the past and will continue to do so in the future" that ice cream and yoghurt is "a GATT issue" and "not a free trade issue". This was a statement by the former Minister of Agriculture in this House on September 13, 1989.
However, a former Canadian trade negotiator at the Tokyo round of the GATT, and in the FTA states: "I have reviewed Mr. Mazankowski's statement and concluded that it is simply not true. The facts are the FTA will result in the elimination of marketing boards whose viability depends on sales to food processors; the FTA caused the ice cream and yoghurt problem; and the government had an opportunity in the FTA negotiations to protect marketing boards and did not".
As these food processors close down, where are our Canadian farmers going to sell their products?
This House passed legislation giving the producers of the nation the right to plan their production and set their own prices under government supervision. This resulted in bringing order out of chaos. Now this government is demolishing these institutions in secret negotiations behind closed doors.
The farmers of Canada do not know what the government negotiators are trading away at the GATT. Cana-

dian farmers at the end of the negotiations will be told what kind of deal was made. They have no final say in it. They will not even have the right to reject it. This is not acceptable.
In answering a question in the House on October 15, 1990, regarding the GATT negotiations, the Minister for International Trade stated:
Mr. Speaker, on October 1 we had to file at Geneva, together with other countries involved in these negotiations, an estimate of the cost of the various programs in effect in Canada to assist agriculture. The total was $8.8 billion. The Minister of Agriculture should be ashamed of the amount of assistance he is giving Canadian farmers. It is a huge amount of assistance.
However, the Minister for International Trade failed to convince the opposition members and the Canadian public of the legitimacy of these false and misleading figures as opposition members, including myself, made statements in the House outlining the true and correct figures.
I stated in this House on October 18, 1990: "That $8.8 billion is a fictitious figure. It is about 53 per cent higher than the actual figure". For example, papers filed in Geneva on October 1 showed that Canadian dairy farmers received $2.2 billion in subsidies, when in fact, as shown by our own estimates in the House on expenditures, Canadian dairy farmers received only a cash subsidy of $261 million last year, and this goes only to industrial milk producers.
The $2.2 billion is a concocted figure, most of it being the difference between what the U.S. farmers receive for milk versus Canadian farmers and then calling it a subsidy. Again this game of smoke and mirrors ignores the fact that Canadian farm inputs are much higher than those in the United States.
I have to ask, did our negotiators consider U.S. school lunches and food stamps as subsidies. Nearly 50 per cent of the USDA's expenditures go indirectly for social assistance, such as these programs I just mentioned. Were these items included in their costs or subsidies? I doubt it.
Where was the Minister of Agriculture when the Minister for International Trade made that statement last year in this House? Did he inform the Minister for International Trade of the facts? Did the Minister of Agriculture point out that $1 billion of that $4.2 billion was drought assistance? No, he did not.

October 3, 1991

He did not do it in this House. The Minister of Agriculture was strangely silent. A newspaper editorialist and writers unwittingly used these fictitious figures to attach supply management marketing boards.
Did the Minister of Agriculture write to the editors to point out the true level of support for agriculture in Canada? No. Again he was strangely silent.
I, as a member of this House and as a farmer, had to refute these misleading figures in those various newspapers that cany them. These are strange actions for a man who claims to support Article XI and supply management at the GATT.
If the Government of Canada supports marketing boards, why did the Department of Agriculture give the Canadian Consumers Association a $45,000 grant last year to bring in a study that attacks marketing boards, a study that is partly responsible for these concerted attacks in editorials and other media coverage that occurred, the attack to which the Minister of Agriculture failed to offer a single statement of defence of our marketing board system in Canada?
The study is based on the Minister for International Trade's figure of $8.8 billion of October 15, 1991. I respectfully suggest the Minister of Agriculture took money from the Farm Women for the Survival of Agriculture budget to fund this attack of the Canadian Consumers' Association, which is already getting $793,000 from the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
The Minister of Agriculture said on September 18: "What we have asked for and what the policy of this government is is that article XI should be further clarified and strengthened. This has not been changed and will not change until the government says it will change".
Does that give you a feeling of security? It certainly does not give it to me because he said that it will not change until the government says it will change.
Last week, my colleague from Gatineau-La Lievre was asking the government if it would assure that the cost of production formula, which is essential to the operation of these marketing agencies commissions, would be maintained. In reply, the Prime Minister
appeared to identify the question as relating to GATT and assured the Canadian dairy industry-these are his own words: "The Canadian government will try to find new markets for them".
I ask you, Madam Speaker, if the government supports article XI which allows countries to limit imports when they have a system of production designed to meet only domestic needs, why are they now concerned about finding new markets for our dairy farmers? The answer is simple.
I do not believe it intends to support article XI of GATT. Why else would the dairy farmers need the government to find them new markets? Did it in fact agree to trade article XI in exchange for the U.S. giving up article XXII which gives the U.S. the waiver it used for years on dairy products, peanuts and sugar?
These people should wake up to reality, because if you look at the cost-input differences and if it gives up that waiver in exchange for Article XI, that puts us in an untenable situation, a no-win situation. The reality is we only have to look at the difference in input costs between Canada and the United States.
In Canada, the interest rates are 25 per cent higher for operating costs in terms of interest rates and 39 per cent for maintenance accounts in interest rates.
Machinery repairs, plough points, are 123.9 per cent higher in Canada; penicillin for animal use, 201.5 per cent higher in Canada; gasoline, 129.6 per cent higher; diesel fuels, 71.4 per cent higher in Canada and farm wages are 48 per cent higher.
How do you compete against those costs. It is impossible. We are going to see this industry, the only sectors of the Canadian agricultural economy that are on stable footing, demolished if we trade away article XI at GATT.
Last Tuesday, the government tabled its new constitutional package and tabled shortly after a document entitled Canadian Federalism and the Economic Union. It is tabled by the Minister of Finance. I have a copy here: Partnership for Prosperity. I quote from page 19 of this document: "For example the range of impediments created by the government includes agriculture supply market boards that regulate production and prices of the various food products, including milk, poultry and eggs."
October 3, 1991

That tells us what is in store for Canadian agriculture in the dairy and poultry industry. The former Minister of Agriculture described marketing boards as trade impediments. Is this how he instructed Canada's GATT negotiators, that marketing boards are trade impediments?
What constitutional change is the government advocating in relation to this and other examples of what it calls internal trade barriers? What is the government doing, creating a constitutional fail-safe way of removing marketing boards from Canada, a way in which the government can have big business do its dirty work by challenging marketing boards on constitutional grounds? Did the government include this provision to appease the rank and file of the Progressive Conservative Party who at a policy meeting in Toronto this past summer defeated a resolution supporting supply management? Has the government examined the U.S. dairy industry that is in total chaos, an industry in which 40 per cent of the producers cannot pay their bills?
Has the government examined the concentration of the poultry industry in the United States where one company controls 14 million laying hens, twice the number that we have in all of Ontario, and where one of their largest chicken producing companies, totally integrated, controls one-third of the chicken production in all of the United States? How do we expect our Canadian farmers to compete against that sort of thing when input costs are so much lower?
The government should strengthen Article XI at GATT and ensure that it includes a provision to block imports from countries which are not practising sustainable agriculture. To block food imports from countries which are creating unfair competition with Canadian farmers by using chemicals and pesticides which are illegal for use in Canada is clearly needed desperately in this country.
In conclusion, I call on the government to support the poultry and dairy sector in this country; to stop using misleading figures relating to Canada's dairy and poultry producers; to support and strengthen Article XI, as it promised; to reply to those editorial attacks; to stop using
Supply
blatantly false and misleading figures that cast a cloud over our dairy industry; to insist that the United States stop its export enhancement subsidies which are in clear violation of the free trade agreement; and above all, stop trying to drive a wedge between the Canadian consumer and the dairy and poultry farmers of this country.
I am appalled that one year ago this month the Minister for International Trade not only tried to mislead this House, but obviously mislead some of the news media of this country and the people of Canada. I call on the minister here today to speak up and clear this record; to admit the $2.2 billion support for Canadian dairy farmers, as stated by the former Minister for International Trade about one year ago, is a concocted figure. I call upon him to apologize to the dairy farmers of this nation because the actual figure of those subsidies was $267 million.

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Gustafson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have just a short comment. The hon. member speaks with great platitudes about what his administration would do. On the farm there is a saying that is common among the farmers when they go to hire a man. They say: "Don't tell me what you're going to do, tell me what you've done".
I think that it would do well for the Canadian people to observe very carefully what the administration has done. We remember when the Trudeau Liberal government said: "Sell the wheat". We remember when the Liberal administration dealing with farmers, whether it was the chicken industry, the feather industry or the dairy industry could not get one seat west of Winnipeg to represent them. They had to send senators out there to represent them. That is how serious it was.
We saw a very good example of that in this House just yesterday in terms of the votes that took place in this House. Where did the Liberals and the NDP stand? They stood with the labour unions. Forty boats in the ports, 10 more boats coming in to load grain and they voted against with the labour unions.
On the positive side, what the Conservative government has done is we have stood at the GATT. We have stood there for the dairy producers and we will stand there. We have stood there for the feather industry and we will stand there.

Supply
The Prime Minister was the first Prime Minister of Canada to ever address the Federation of Agriculture, which he has done three times. Check the record. I was at the meeting in Vancouver when he called 50 farm groups together.
What is he going to do?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Watch us. What I am saying is look at our record. Look at our record and judge us on our record. If there is a government that has stood with the farmers and will stand with them, it will be this government. We have had a history of doing this.
In Saskatchewan today they are going into an election. It is either going to be the labour unions under Roy Romanow or a man like Grant Devine who stood with the farmers, not always right on all issues, but always standing with the people they represent. We are the group of farmers. We are the members who represent the farmers and we will stand with them.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member asks whether we know where the government stood. I want to point out to him that under article 701.4 of the free trade agreement, the United States must take into account the effects of its export subsidies on other nations, how they affect Canada, and must ensure that they do not prejudice our exports.
Under article 1804, provisions are there for the government to call for consultations if such incidents take place and to ask for compensation. They did not do that.
I raised this in the House on March 18, and I would ask everyone to look at the response I got to that request by the prairie pools and by the farmers in western Canada. In terms of a former Prime Minister saying "why should I sell your wheat", I should point out to my colleague across the way and to everyone what the total statement was. He said: "Why should I sell your wheat? I could not sell it if I wanted to. You already have two government organizations doing it for you". Please use the full statement in total context the next time.
That was a bit rough.

Madam Speaker, I was very impressed by the attempt to defend the government record by the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister. It was only three or four weeks ago when grain and oilseed producers from across this land met and they are still waiting for government support.
Last year the government slashed support programs by $1.3 billion at a time when the price of grains and
oilseeds in the world market was dropping by 30 per cent, from $135 a tonne to $95 a tonne. This member and his Tory colleagues voted unanimously with our caucus in an agriculture committee meeting to call on the government to provide emergency transitional assistance, as was asked for by the farm organizations right across the country. That is why we are having meetings all across the country today. There were 3,000 to 4,000 people meeting in Rosetown this week, 1,500 in Brandon and over 1,000 in Lucknow, Ontario, because the government welshed on that commitment. It made a commitment last winter to provide that assistance and it did not live up to it. It supported a unanimous resolution in the agriculture committee and two weeks later, here in the House when the motion was put, it voted against the same motion.
That is why we are concerned about what is going on at GATT today because we know that you have double-crossed us in the free trade deal with the United States and we are scared that you are going to destroy this entire industry in those negotiations this fall. If you do, you are not just destroying 30,000 or 40,000 farms; you are destroying rural Canada and that is unacceptable to Canadians.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before I give the floor back to the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex, let me say that it is very early in the day and it would be appreciated if hon. members who have the floor would address their remarks through the Chair. It might make things a lot easier later in the day.

Madam Speaker, I totally concur with what my colleague has said. There are veiy few farmers in this House of Commons who worked their lives to put together a family farm operation. It distresses me to see the despair and hardship out there across this country. I see my own son experiencing it.
I have to wonder, when I look at the graphic illustration of this book, why this government has not been going after the concentration of power in the food distribution sector, the wholesaling and retail sectors. Where was the Competition Bureau when all this was going on? It is unacceptable that the farmers of this nation should not have an income and the level of security that is available to the rest of society. We need an income that is commensurate with the rest of society. I for one am not going to stand here in this House and say nothing while the GATT article XI may well be neutered or done away with.
October 3, 1991

Madam Speaker, I hesitate to rise on a point of order. I admire the hon. member and the presentation he gave but he did make several comments relating to the Minister of Agriculture misleading Parliament. Maybe he would like to have an opportunity to rethink those statements.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I listened carefully to what the hon. member was saying and I do not think he said that the minister deliberately mislead either the House or anyone, which is why I did not stop the hon. member on that.
I think it would be wise for all of us to be a little more careful with our words. As I said a minute ago, it is going to be a long day. It is a very strong debate. I think we can debate without using words that could be construed as insults to one another or to any other people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a short question for the hon. member.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is one minute left. It has to be a very short question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
How does the hon. member opposite reply to the statement when our negotiators in Brussels say "we are continuing to operate under the instructions we took into the earlier talks in Brussels and those instructions reflected a negotiating principle, a position that was worked out with all of the segments of the industry"?
Those are their instructions. Those are what they are working under. Yet the member opposite and his cohorts continually say that we are dealing away article XI. The member knows full well the negotiating position of Canada and that position has not changed.
What does he tell his farmer friends about that?

Madam Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture said that that was their position, as you laid out, and it will not change until the government says it will change. Why did he not say that the government never intended to change it and will not change it? He did not say that.

I would also like to point out the words of the Prime Minister a few days later when he said that the government would try to help Quebec producers find alternative markets. That again throws a whole question mark over these whole proceedings.
Certainly I am worried about it. I am sure that farmers here today in the gallery are equally worried. These are facts that are contained in the Hansard of this House.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am veiy pleased to be able to rise today and speak on this very important motion.
Before I start into my remarks pertaining to that motion, I would like to make a comment or two. The Lucknow meeting has been referred to many times by my colleague from Middlesex and my other colleague from the northern part of Ontario. Lucknow, Ontario is in my riding. I have to say that at that meeting the farmers were there out of sheer concern. It crossed all political boundaries. I do not believe it was a partisan meeting in any way. They conducted themselves with great, earnest sincerity and I compliment them. I am very proud of the people who were at that meeting that night.
Since that time there have been many meetings held across the country. That was one of the first meetings held. We do recognize the seriousness of the problem. It was well recognized before those meetings, but when we see people gather in a non-partisan way to bring their concerns to all levels of government and all politicians we know how sincere they are.
As you have indicated before, Madam Speaker, it is early in the day. I guess I am the second speaker. I would hope that we are hon. members, ladies and gentlemen in this House of Commons, and that we can conduct ourselves with that same sincerity and feeling that was at that meeting in Lucknow that night. We must drop some of our partisanship feelings and try to reassure the farmers of Canada that we as politicians are working with them. We will do everything we can to support their positions at the GATT talks or in any sector of agriculture, internal, external, international trade, the Uruguay round or whatever it might be.

October 3, 1991

I ask members of the House of Commons to give this the serious consideration that is necessary for the debate that will take place today. It is early in the day and I think that we can be helpful to one another and give the reassurances that are necessary. I do not think it is the time for political muck raking of any political party, no matter which side of the House it might be on.
I would ask my colleagues on this side of the House to do their part as well in keeping the debate on the high road, for those very reasons.
We always do that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I would hope that continues for the day.
As I said before, the motion before the House today asks that the government provide assurances to Canadian producers operating under supply management systems that will seek to strengthen and clarify article XI of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade in the current round of multilateral trade negotiations.
Let me assure hon. members that this government stands solidly behind the supply and management industries and is fighting hard to protect the interests of all Canadian agricultural producers. We could expand on that slightly or as much as we wish and have a debate as well on those two particular industries and what we have initiated in the past few years. In about the last three years the two task forces have brought the poultry industries together, the dairy industries together, all sectors, all the stakeholders in both of those two very important industries to Canada.
I believe by bringing all those stakeholders together we will have a much more solid position, a greater understanding by all the stakeholders, including the consumer who is one of the major stakeholders. I believe they have to have input and we have to understand what their concerns and needs are as well.
Our commitment to the supply management sector is strong, as I said before. We stated our position clearly last year at the multilateral trade negotiations in Geneva. Canada's offer for agricultural trade reform has not changed. It has not changed.
Canada's offer calls for greater security for supply management through a strengthened and clarified article XI at GATT.
My colleague, the Minister of State for Agriculture, met with Canada's poultry and egg marketing agencies
just last week. He reaffirmed the government's position in the GATT negotiations on agriculture. I will just quote what he said: "We are firmly committed to negotiate an agreement which protects our supply management programs and as such we will do everything in our power to obtain a clarified and strengthened GATT article XI".
As recently as yesterday our caucus met with a number of the supply management groups from various parts, mostly Ontario. I hope our colleagues had an opportunity to meet with those people as well and discuss this very important subject.
There can be no doubt of the government's position regarding international trade reform. We have identified the problem and are moving aggressively to secure a successful resolution. In fact, my two colleagues in the agriculture portfolio, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for Agriculture, have both been in New York this week representing our farmers' interests.
The Minister of Agriculture met Wednesday with the European community's Commissioner for Agriculture and Rural Development and impressed upon Mr. McSharry Canada's resolve to have the talks ended and brought to a successful conclusion this year.
I was in Madrid last week at international meetings of ministers of agriculture and there were times last week when we had as many as 35 ministers of agriculture at the table taking part in the agriculture issues of the world. All have a desire to see a successful conclusion to this Uruguay round of talks.
In a statement following the meeting, my colleague was quite direct in voicing our position, and I quote: "Canada wants to see an end to the international subsidy war in fruit market access and the development of clear and fair GATT rules that apply to all countries, including the strenghthening and clarification of article XI".
This week the Minister of State for Agriculture is participating in several meetings concerning the GATT negotiations in Europe. His itinerary includes meetings in Geneva with the Director General of GATT. In all meetings my colleagues will stress the importance to Canada of international trade reform. He will stress the need to protect Canada's supply management sector and will detail the devastating effects these subsidy wars have had on Canadian agriculture. I do not think anyone will disagree with what the subsidy wars have done to our economy.
October 3, 1991

My colleagues who will speak today will talk in more detail about our position on supply management. I also want to take the opportunity to talk about the world trading environment and how it is affecting our farmers.
The international grain export subsidy war has devastated grain prices. Canadian Wheat Board initial payments, which are set in relation to current world markets, are at their lowest level in 15 years. The subsidy wars attacked without mercy an industry which is essential to our Canadian economy.
Canadian farmers are recognized as among the most efficient producers in the world. I do not think it matters what commodity they are producing. They are efficient. They have concern for high quality and I believe the consumers of Canada rest assured when they buy Canadian products that they have the highest quality product, nutritious and wholesome. That is what they expect and that is what they get.
We have done it without using massive subsidies or massive amounts of agricultural chemicals. In a fair trading environment Canada's grains and oilseeds industry would be healthy and competitive. There is nothing fair about what is going on.
This year the Europeans are expected to spend about $4.7 billion Canadian on export subsidies, about twice as much as five years ago. European export subsidies are the highest of any country on wheat and growing fast. Its export subsidies per tonne on wheat have more than quadrupled from $44 a tonne Canadian in July 1989 to $190 Canadian a tonne in February 1991. Already this crop year the European's feed export subsidies are higher than $120 a tonne.
The U.S. is expected to spend about $1.4 billion Canadian on its export enhancement program this year, and that is $1.4 billion more than it was seven years ago. In 1991 total EEC agriculture expenditures were about $42.5 billion Canadian. That is more than Canada's entire $30 billion deficit.
Recently the EEC sold wheat to China at about $85 Canadian a tonne, using subsidies approaching $200 Canadian. A recent wheat sale carried an export enhancement program subsidy of $70 Canadian a tonne. Selling prices have been as low as $75 Canadian a tonne.
Supply
A recent United States barley sale to Saudi Arabia carried subsidies of $47 a tonne, with a selling price of $88 a tonne.
These kinds of subsidy levels have pushed grain prices to Canadian farmers to drastically low levels. The agriculture policies of the European Community and the United States have been a brutal assault on Canadian grains and oilseeds producers. Their policies have attacked individual farmers in countries like Canada, Australia and Argentina which depend on the export market.
The export subsidy is also harming the environment. In order to increase yields, a producer in the United Kingdom uses on average three times more nitrogen fertilizer than a farmer on the Canadian prairies. In the Netherlands the rate of nitrogen fertilizer application is 30 times the rate in Canada.
It is time to put pressure on. European environmentalists have succeeded in demonstrating a way of life for our natives, the fur industry and our seal industry. Why are they not concerned about the environment in their own backyard?
The subsidy war is a crime against the developing world. Developing countries trying to compete with similar products are also hurt by low grain prices, and because agriculture is such a large part of a developing country's economy this hurts their entire population.
I was in Madrid last week at international conferences of IICA and IABA. Latin American and Caribbean countries were represented, and we certainly know that they have problems we do not have. We have very severe problems in our agricultural industry but they certainly have more problems. I am very concerned that if we do not get some resolve from the Uruguay round of talks we will see countries go into isolation to protect themselves and try to protect their own market, while they know that they have to have export for the development of their country. Many times in those poorer countries in Latin America and the Caribbean it is the women and the children who are suffering the most in those circumstances. I believe that the various nations of the world have to work together to bring a resolve to this devastating grain war.

October 3, 1991
Supply
One of the best ways to generate wealth internationally is through trade. We know that. The EEC's policies shut borders, restrict competition and deny opportunity. It is hypocritical for the EEC to encourage the new democracies of eastern Europe to develop a market oriented agricultural industry, while at the same time restricting access to the EEC markets.
There has to be an end to the export subsidy war and the solution lies in the GATT. The next few months are critical. There is no question about that. That is why we have to work together and take a solid position.
The options paper put on the table by European Agriculture Commissioner, Mr. McSharry, shows a willingness to start the reform process but it must move further. At least what he is proposing is a start.
This government has a major commitment of resources supporting Canada's negotiating strategy in the Uruguay round. The EEC and the United States have to know what we want, an end to this madness.
My two colleagues are in Europe this week delivering the message, and we will continue to bring our message to the capitals in Europe. We are prepared to take retaliatory action against the EEC as the Minister of Agriculture pointed out to Mr. McShany just yesterday. He is the agricultural commissioner for the European community. I quote what was said yesterday: "I did not put it forward as a threat. I put it forward as a fact". We will make sure the farmers of these countries hear our concerns too.
I can assure members of this House that this government remains 100 per cent behind its negotiating position at the GATT on behalf of the farmers of Canada. Once again, I ask all colleagues of the House of Commons to work together. Let us keep our position solid. We believe that the position we have taken is fair and balanced and we have not changed that position.
I believe there is support in other parts of the world for the position we are taking. I know that our farmers, producers and consumers are all depending on us getting a resolve to this Uruguay round. I hope that we do have that resolve early in the next year.

Madam Speaker, I was glad to hear the parliamentary secretary's comments today.
The parliamentary secretary has told some of our colleagues here in the House that at the inter-American meeting of ministers of agriculture on September 25, the matter of article XI was not even raised. I wonder if the parliamentary secretary could explain why he did not raise the matter, why he did not try to get the support of those several dozen ministers of agriculture to support our position on article XI.
After all, we do not dump massive amounts of dairy or poultry products on the international market. We control our production so that we are not massively interfering in the international trade. I wonder why the parliamentary secretary, who speaks for the government, did not raise the matter at those meetings.
I also would like to ask him if he agrees with the resolution before the House today, that this House supports the strengthening and clarification of article XI in the multilateral trade negotiations which are going on in Geneva and that it will not be party to any agreement that fails to achieve those objectives.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, to my colleague from Algoma, article XI was raised in many bilateral meetings last week with ministers of agriculture in a different format. At all levels of meetings the Uruguay round of GATT talks was very much up front.
When you talk about reform to agricultural policies, we thought that reform meant all aspects of agriculture and that does include article XI of GATT. That is our position.
Our position is well known among all of those countries of the world and not ail Latin American-Caribbean countries are at the table at the GATT talks. Last week's meetings were a great opportunity for them to put their positions forward and the problems that they are suffering because of this international war.
Also in respect to the motion, as I said before, our position has not changed. We are solidly behind article XI. We have asked for it to be strengthened and clarified, and that is what we intend to have happen in respect to article XI.
October 3, 1991

Madam Speaker, in his remarks the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture spent some time discussing the world wheat, grains and oilseed trade.
He said something like this, at least this is how I got it as a quote: "In a subsidy-free world Canadian grain and oilseed producers would be healthy and competitive".
Agriculture Canada, through a study by Whorley from the University of Guelph and I think McClatchy from the department looking at what a subsidy-free world would do to international grain prices, did not come up with a terribly optimistic view of what we could expect. I think it was something in the order of 5 per cent or 6 per cent of an increase from current prices.
A couple of economists from the United Kingdom have just completed a study concluding that the most we could expect would be a rise of up to 12 per cent.
Given that the world price is around $2 a bushel Canadian, does he honestly think that Canadian producers will be healthy and competitive at $2.24 or $2.25 a bushel for wheat? This makes no sense and it does not compute with any economic reality. Where does the minister get his dreams?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think we all dream at times but this is not a dream. I am a farmer as well and I certainly know-and I think everyone in this House knows it whether they are farmers or not-that a bushel of wheat weighs 60 pounds and at $2.241 have never seen such a bargain in my lifetime. It is not fair. A farmer cannot survive at $2.24 or $3.00 bushel. We have to be very honest and frank about that.
What we all love to see is the export subsidies discontinued in particular by the two major countries, the United States and the EEC. We believe that if the treasuries were withdrawn from those countries-
The Economist assumed that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I am not talking about The Economist. I am talking about my position. I do not believe there is a huge supply of world grains in the world.
I have not interrupted anyone in this comment at all. I believe and it makes common sense that there is no use of trying to find new markets and lowering the price

every day you find a new market. Why grow more wheat to sell it for less?
Let us try to work together. Let us get paid for the crops we are growing, whether it be wheat, corn, barley, soyabeans or whatever. We know that there is a market in the world, but let us get some common sense brought back to it.
We can do all the studies we wish and predictions we make, but it takes some reality before anything will happen. I believe the first step is to get some common trade rules that grain producing nations in the world agree to and abide by.
It is not going to be a quick fix. Any of us who have farmed any length of time have lost crops. We have lost major crops and have not been able to produce much more than our domestic requirements. We know that in Canada we do produce for an export market. We have all forgotten the fact that we might lose a crop some year. We could lose a crop in all of Canada. It might not just be eastern Canada or western Canada, but those things have happened before.
I am a positive person. I do not believe in gloom and doom, but we have to face reality and we have all witnessed crop failures throughout the world. None of that has been taken into account by any economist study that I am aware of. There are other elements that often take place that will change those things.

Madam Speaker, thank you very much for giving me the opportunity to ask a question through you of the member for Huron-Bruce.
There are many of us from urban ridings who are not as up to speed as those members from rural ridings. I have a great respect for the member for Huron-Bruce who has worked hard for his constituency. I have been with him travelling the world where he has represented all of Canada.
During his speech today he talked about the unfair environmental practices that are going on in the European countries. It would seem to me that it would be a useful exercise if the European community at large understood that its farming communities were doing this unfair environmental farming practice that the member talked about during his speech.

October 3, 1991
Supply
My question to him is quite specific. Has his government, he, his colleagues or the Minister of Agriculture ever considered communicating to European countries at large, whether through newspaper, radio or television, in order to attract more popular European support as to what is happening to the Canadian farmer here, this unfair trading practice advantage? In other words, let us take a page out of the book of Greenpeace when it tried to upset our seal practice in the Arctic. I would like to know what the member's view is on this particular approach.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have not been privy to any discussion about advertising ads, but maybe that is a good way of making sure our colleagues in other countries are fully aware of what our position is and the devastating effect it is having on our agriculture.
It is a good point and one worth taking note of. I thank the member for that. I am sure that the producers in that part of the world are as concerned and as aware of their future environmentally as we are in this country or in any other part of the world.
It is my understanding that laws are being passed by the European communities that by the year 2000 considerable reduction by almost 50 per cent in the use of pesticides and chemicals has to take place. That normal reduction of pesticides and chemicals will ultimately result in lower production.
We have concentrated livestock operations in some of those smaller countries, extremely concentrated. Before you can spread the waste from those huge animal locations, pigs or dairy or whatever, you have to have a permit. You have to test the soil and you have to have a permit before you can spread that waste on that soil.
A friend of mine visited Holland earlier this year. He got permission one day to spread that liquid waste. They went away to visit and go on a tour. Another farmer knew it was okay to spread in that field, so he spread his liquid waste on the field while my friend was gone. That is the situation some European farmers are facing.
I do not want to leave the impression that European farmers are having it easy. They have their difficulties as well and are going to have to respond to environmental concerns as much as we are or maybe more.

Madam Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate today which gravitates around the Canadian position in the GATT with regard to the supply managed industries and the question of whether article XI 2(c)(1) becomes strengthened in the new GATT negotiations.
I think the question of marketing boards and supply management is not fully understood even in Canada. We have a reality that exists in the production and distribution of agricultural products that has to a certain extent been recognized by producers in their decisions to establish marketing boards and the type of marketing board that will be put into place.
As a general rule, you will recognize that there are perishable products in agriculture which generally can be stored for a few days or a few weeks, certainly not more than a year, and there are other agricultural products that are almost non-perishable, like most of the grains and oilseeds that can be dried and stored almost indefinitely. Some kinds of wheat have been found in Egyptian tombs that were 5,000 and 6,000 years old and still would germinate.
The strategy that has been pursued by farmers and governments over the years has been somewhat different for each type of product. Marketing boards were established during the 1930s, based upon practices that were utilized and developed in New Zealand and Australia. The first marketing board was established to permit producers to co-operate and sell all of their products through a single seller, single desk selling as it is now referred to. This method is used by the Canadian Wheat Board. A whole host of products utilize the single desk selling technique at the provincial and national level.
An additional wrinkle occurred when marketing boards began to see that there were some problems in some of the more perishable products if there was no power to control supply. The first supply management board was established under the Canadian Dairy Commission by a special act of Parliament which gave the Canadian Dairy Commission the power to restrict the amount of production of dairy products to the amount that would be consumed in a year in Canada.
October 3, 1991

They have not been strictly hide bound about this. They have always permitted a little bit of product to come in from outside. This is to keep the wheels of world trade going, and the system has worked.
Using that as a basis, some of the so-called feather-boards were established on a national basis. They got the power from this Parliament to establish national agencies which could control supply. The Canadian Egg Marketing Agency was established as well as the Canadian Chicken Marketing Agency, the Canadian Turkey Marketing Agency and the Canadian Hatching Egg Agency.
This Parliament also granted power to tobacco people to form such an agency, but that has not come about. I would prefer that Parliament make the establishment of these kind of agencies an automatic thing at the behest of the producers so that the law itself was wide open because awaiting approval from this House often kills an initiative. That is what happened with the tobacco initiative a few years ago.
At any rate, we have established this system that works in this country. We permit imports under licence. Imports are controlled by the Government of Canada in all cases. For a while the Canadian Wheat Board could control imports but that is slipping away now that we have had the Canada-U.S. trade agreement.
Under the board system we are much more liberal in our trading policies than our neighbour to the south, the United States. It does not permit any imports of dairy products. It does not permit any imports of sugar products. It does not permit any imports of peanuts.
It has a GATT waiver which it negotiated a long time ago in the early stages of GATT, and it will not give up those rights except under certain conditions. I think there were a few tiny little cracks opened up for some baked goods as a result of the Canada-U.S. trade agreement.
It controls those products very thoroughly. As an example to show how ridiculous it has become, the U.S. moved under GATT to get access to the Canadian market for U.S. ice creams and yoghurts. We resisted that as is our right under the GATT, but had we acceded we would have been in the ridiculous situation of permitting U.S. yoghurts and ice creams to come into the country.

If I or one of my neighbours wanted to take a trip into the United States for a tour of one of its parks and perhaps wanted to take a trailer or a motor home with us and happened to have in the refrigerator U.S. made yoghurt or ice cream and were inspected at the border, we would not be permitted to take those into the United States even though they were made there. That is the way the rules are at the moment.
The question of article XI 2(c)(i) has become a cause celebre among those producers of products that are produced in Canada under supply management. It is a very large proportion of the production in some of the provinces, particularly in Atlantic Canada, Quebec and in parts of Ontario.
Also, it is very important in British Columbia and the prairies. A big chunk of our industry is being bargained with at the GATT table. These producers are feeling very uncertain about what the negotiators are doing to them in Brussels or Geneva.
They are getting conflicting signals from this government and from some of the people who are supposed to be engaged in the negotiations. We are being told, as we were by the parliamentary secretary today, that the government stands four square behind a strengthened article XI 2(c)(i).
On the other hand, we listen to the hon. Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds who has been on a violent anti-European rage for the last six months. He has been addressing farm meetings telling them "Don't buy European. If you are unhappy with the way agricultural policy is going, dump your wheat on the parking lot of a European auto dealer or a dealer of farm implements that has European content. Don't come to me. Blame it on the Europeans. Boycott the Europeans. Don't buy any of their goods".
The reality is that prior to this rant by the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds we were depending upon the European community and the Nordic group to be our allies in pushing the strengthened article XI at the GATT. We did not have very many other allies strong enough actually to make certain that we would get a strengthened article XI. They read the newspapers. They have embassies in our country. They know what the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds is telling people across the country. They begin to think that maybe this is the policy of the Canadian government.

October 3, 1991
Supply
We get rumours back from the GATT negotiators that Canada is beginning to be pushed into a situation where the only real ally it has for article XI is Japan. We should realize that the Japanese are very passive negotiators in these sorts of things. They do not stand up and take strong positions. They simply stand there knowing that they have a very strong fortress, Japan. They have a very strong economy. They are very strong traders, and they do not think they are going to have to give up anything. If article XI is not strengthened, they are big enough players on the world stage that they can go on internally getting the same results for their producers as a stronger article XI would have produced, and the rest of the world can just go by or lump it.
It is not a very strong position that we are left in, thanks to the duality that we have seen portrayed by members on the government side.
I confess to Europeans and to Americans that our position perhaps seems a little schizophrenic. When it comes to grain trade on non-perishable products we are right in there saying that we want open borders, we want access, and we do not want international subsidies used and export subsidies used. When we are looking at perishable products, Canadians have always taken the position that we should produce enough to provide for our own market.
Some of the Americans are telling us that this is a two-tongued or a forked-tongue approach and it is a schizophrenic approach. Perhaps it is but it is also extremely rational when you think about what food production is all about. It is absolutely necessary to be able to produce those perishable goods that you need when you live in a country like Canada. We are not in the middle of all of the world's trading routes. We are a huge peninsula, I suppose, on the northern end of the Americas. We only have one country that we can trade with easily, and that is the United States. We are a northern community, isolated by long distances by three oceans, one of which is barely passable most of the time. We are isolated.
Our companions at the bargaining table at the GATT do not have that problem. The big powers have other choices.
The United States of America can trade to the south. It can trade to the north. It has a choice. It has a multitude of choices. We have only one choice.
The Europeans are sitting in a position where they can trade with the Nordic group, they can trade with the east bloc and the Soviet Union. They can trade with the African countries. They have lots of choices. They are all right on their doorstep and are all consumers who are well-educated consumers and they know the products that they have. They do not have to introduce the products and sell them, because they have a commonality of interests and the commonality of demands.
The Europeans are not terribly interested in getting a GATT result because their economy will go on very well, thank you very much, whether there is a GATT solution or there is not a GATT solution.
The Japanese are in a very similar position in their niche in southeast Asia, a huge market which they know how to penetrate and they have been penetrating for most of this century, actually.
Canada has been trading a little bit with everybody. We are a very large trader. We are dependent on world trade, so our seat at the table is extremely important in the GATT talks. But when we come to resolving the agricultural issues, we are not making it terribly clear or accepting the reality of why countries have agriculture in the first place.
I think we should be going to those talks, recognizing the reality that countries' first imperative is to tiy to feed themselves and to accept that that is a legitimate kind of trading and economic proposal. It is an economic proposition that has to be accepted. That would permit the production of perishable products within your own country, close to the demand that exists within your own country. That is what Canada had traditionally been saying. Even the United States has been acting on that, though it is not saying that in this round. The Europeans have definitely been acting upon that, as have the Japanese, who have become self-sufficient in the production of rice, even though they have a very small acreage. That is their key food input and they are self-sufficient in rice. They could, if they had to, live on rice and the results of their harvesting of the seed.

It is a natural thing for human beings in nation states to want to be able to feed themselves. The proposals that the United States has put on the table, and which has now become the dominant theme at the GATT, does not pay any attention to that reality.
Canada has, as often as not, taken the position of the United States, with the exception of Article XI and because the article XI argument has been shifted, or is in dire consequence of being shifted aside due to the reasons I outlined before, namely, that we have made ourselves less popular with the Europeans who should have been our allies and the Nordic group, we are now being isolated along with the Japanese and in consequence are probably going to lose it unless we very strongly start changing our public position.
The hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister pointed out that he thought that people made their decisions about whom to hire and in whom to put their trust by asking the question: "Don't tell us what you can do, tell us what you have done." I think that is what is beginning to be reflected in the rallies that we are seeing in Miami, Manitoba, Brandon, Manitoba, Lucknow, Ontario and most recently in Rosetown, Saskatchewan.
They are starting to say: "We have had these guys for seven years. They have not listened to what we have been asking; they have not done what we have asked; we are rallying to point out that the government has not reacted to the actual situation". The reality for people on the land is that world prices and their incomes have never been lower in purchasing power. In the history of this country since statistics were kept, the price of a bushel of wheat has never been lower in terms of real buying power.
Those commodities that are traded because they are considered non-perishable on a world market have never traded lower. The solutions that this government is offering is do away with all of the subsidies, do away with the export subsidies, do away with the internal subsidies and to rely solely on a world price.
Those were the assumptions that the two economic studies, that I referred to in my question earlier, used when they analysed what would be the result of going to that kind of a world. They looked at the kind of world supply-demand structure that most of the world experts foresee. They concluded that there would be very little increase in price at the farm level, that that increase could be expected to be up to 12 per cent.

Farmers who are selling their grain this year, with wheat at $2, are not encouraged to know that they can look forward to the great day when we get to the dream of this government when they can get $2.25. Their costs are more than double that. They do not see this as the great saviour and they no longer see this government and its party as the great saviour. They no longer see the Conservative Party as the party that shares their dream for the future of agriculture and the future of their rural communities. They no longer support the government's policies and they are beginning to tell it so. They are giving it a chance to correct its ways and mend its ways, but there is not very much time.
The GATT positions will be laid down clearly. We will find out within two months whether Canada is going to join the United States and bring the Europeans along into tariffication of all of the border measures that are now in effect under article XI or whether they will in fact stand up and try to find some allies and correct the mistakes of the past six months and get us a stronger article XI(2)(c)(l) as has been proposed by the people who are producing in Canada under the supply management system.

Madam Speaker, I listened intently to the hon. member and was inspired to rise to my feet in particular reference to a statement that he made dealing with some of the statements that are being made by farmers at some of these major farm gatherings, sometimes referred to as protests.
As one who had the pleasure of being in the company of all Conservative members of Parliament from Saskatchewan at the Rosetown so-called protest, what I sensed that I heard was a protest against the price of grain. While yes admittedly there was the odd comment cast toward government, the majority of the comments were from a completely rational, fair and honest crowd who recognized that the problem was not this government inspired, but it was perhaps inspired by other governments, not the least of which was the European Economic Community and the United States.
I think you have heard over the past many members of the House of Commons in staunch criticism of the export enhancement procedures employed by both the European Economic Community and as well the United States.

Supply
I wanted to rise just to point out that there is another side to what one is capable of hearing at these events and to place on the record the fact that farmers, while despondent almost to the point of desperation realize where the problem is. They realize there will have to be some changes in agriculture in the future as well.
These changes include, as it has included everything in our lives, everything in the way in which we currently farm. Gone is the day when a producer can simply reply on a product that that particular farm has grown for 50 to 60 years. We find diversification becoming more and more the method of operation for farmers. However, we realize there are limitations in that regard as well. In reading about some of the problems that the European Economic Community is going through, 150,000 French farmers demonstrated, protested, saying: "Leave well enough alone. We rely on these export enchancements". That is the problem of the European Economic Community. Our problem, as we see it now, is one that we recognize, where the cash flow going to farmers, which in turn goes to support the small business sector, is one that we have to rely on.
I simply want to ask the hon. member, is my recall of events that occurred in Rosetown any different than what he heard?

Madam Speaker, yes, perhaps we do have selected hearing. I did not hear anyone in that crowd at Rosetown say that they were awaiting changes in agriculture, that they were unable to make changes or refusing to make changes. Farmers are very quick to adapt new techniques and to make changes in products.
I will go back to my notes to make certain this is right. I heard one person who stood up, and it was reiterated by several others, say: "The purpose of this meeting is not to damn the Europeans. What we would like is a similar commitment from our government".
Another person stood up and said: "We have been hearing a lot of talk about the problems that the Europeans are creating for us in world grain and oilseed trade. But let us not forget"-and they were reasonable people, I remind the hon. member-"the Europeans, after all,'only sell into about 20 per cent of the world market. Between Canada and the U.S., we control almost two thirds of the market". If we wanted to do something about a price, all it would take is the political
will to get together with them and offer products at a higher price, or stay off the market for the first month and a half until the Europeans have run out and then run the price up.
We have not had this kind of initiative. What we have had instead is a deliberate policy from south of the border, agreed to here, that the U.S. loan rate will continually go down and effectively becomes the world market price, because any grain trader can go to the U.S. Department of Agriculture and get his supplies, knowing it will be available at that loan rate.
That has overhung the market for the last six years since the new program went into effect. It was an intent expressed quite clearly by a former Secretary of Agriculture on the part of the United States to dominate the world grain trade and to engage in international warfare and use, in his words, food as a weapon. They have been veiy effective at that. We have not stood up to them. We have not done anything on a government to government basis.

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Gustafson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, just one brief comment. I too was at Rosetown. I think the one comment I heard rattling through the 4,000 people who were there was that when some of the politicians got up and tried to take advantage and turn it into a political thing, the murmur-ings came: "Keep politics out of it".
Truly, the farmers were there to try and show government, everybody involved, to Canada-you do not get
4,000	people together that often-that they have some very, veiy serious problems.
We as a government are listening. We have stood with them and we will continue to stand with them. The time has come when it is important that we make food a priority, that food becomes the number one right.
It is interesting that on the one hand there are surpluses and on the other hand there is a starving world. In defence of the government I am a part of, especially in the west or for Canada, I see two options. There is the NDP option which brings in a land bank and takes over the farm, which eastern Europe threw out. They threw that system out. It did not work. There were food lines. Seventy-five years of communist socialism proved to eastern Europe what they can do. Today they are coming to Canada and asking for food, and we are going to deliver it.
October 3, 1991

Number two on the other side is that I think we are in a critical situation. What does the Reform Party say? The Reformers say that all farmers should be cut 15 per cent right across the board. We could not live with that. My goodness, I am a farmer myself. I have three sons farming and I will tell you that it is difficult. This Conservative government put $22 billion into agriculture and even with all that assistance I say it is not enough. It is difficult, but we have been the government that has stood with the farmers.
I guess farmers have to ask themselves if they want radical approaches or one that recognizes the problems that exist. We are listening as a government. We understand. It is well time that international leaders at all levels make food a priority. Certainly it is a human right. If there is one right, one human right that people have, it is the right to eat. We as farmers do not apologize to anybody for being productive, for being hard working and for having produced food. Canadians buy food cheaper than any other people.
I stand with these farmers here today and the farmers across this country and say that we will produce food but we need a fair price.

Madam Speaker, I think the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister should be reminded that in addition to the items that were said at Rosetown to which I responded to my friend from Regina, we heard a persistent cry for a need for $30 per acre to bring farm revenue up to where the GRIP would have taken them in the 1991 crop year that was completed last August.
The parliamentary secretary makes a plea for not going to radical solutions. I think he has not studied history very well. His government is proposing to go along with the United States and to do away with any support by governments to food production and agriculture. That is a radical solution. It has never been used in the history of the world. It is a new and radical solution. When you look at it clearly and calmly as even right wing economists do, they conclude that the results will not be particularly useful to farmers.
We have had in the last eight years in Saskatchewan more than two farmers per day leaving the province
