under this so-called benevolent program we have been living under. What they are proposing is to move to a program that would do away with all government interference which, I repeat, has never been the policy of any national state or community in the history of civilization.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As we are resuming debate I understand that the hon. member for Algoma will be sharing time with one of his colleagues. The hon. member for Algoma has the floor.

Madam Speaker, I simply want to be closely associated with the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex who has proposed the motion as our associate trade critic today concerning the support of the Government of Canada, Canadians and this House of Commons for the retention, strengthening and the maintenance of article XI in the GATT negotiations which are taking place in Geneva this fall.
It goes on to say in this motion that the government will not be party to any agreement that fails to achieve these objectives. I believe this is one of the most important debates that we will have this fall. It is unfortunate there are not more members in the House today for this debate because of the magnitude of it. It is so terribly important. One of the basic underpinnings of a successful, rewarding and viable sector of our agriculture is the supply management sector. Those poultry and dairy sectors of our economy are the most stable and the most self-reliant in our industry. The fate of them will be decided over the next few weeks in the GATT negotiations.
I want to call attention to the spectators in the gallery this morning from the Dairy Farmers of Canada, the Canadian Marketing Agency, CMA, the Canadian Chicken Marketing Agency, the Canadian Turkey Marketing Agency and the Canadian Broiler Hatching Egg Marketing Agency including a group, I understand, from Quebec. It is these producers in the gallery today whose very livelihood, whose job, whose income, whose very ability to make a living is at question in these GATT negotiations. We welcome them to the gallery today for this historic debate.

October 3, 1991
Supply
It is an historic debate because at this very moment the whole grains and oilseeds sector is also completely undermined because the government has reduced its support programs by $1.3 billion last year. It has failed to provide transitional assistance to the new stabilization program last spring. I do not think there has ever been a time in our history when there has been so much uncertainty in the supply and management sector. Historically it has been the most stable and well underpinned. At the same time that uncertainty is combined with just a desperate uncertainty and cash flow crisis for the grains and oilseeds.
I was especially struck by the response of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture today. When he attended the meeting in Madrid of agriculture ministers from across the western hemisphere, he commented to our colleagues here in the House that the matter of the GATT was never even raised. It is unbelievable to me, knowing the incredible uncertainty in the farming sector this year, that he did not raise it. I mean, where else would he have the opportunity to twist the arms of so many influential people, the ministers of agriculture from the western hemisphere, to try to say to them: "Look, article XI is important to us. We are not destroying the world trade with surplus, low quality, low priced stuff. We are restraining our production. We are having a viable industry. Why did he not do it? That is the kind of thing that has our spectators in the gallery very concerned".
It is in the communique. The communique says: "Oh, yes, we want stable agriculture and good relations in the GATT negotiations and all the rest". But he did not raise it. He did not seek their support. If you look closely at his answer, he did not answer.
On the same topic I asked him if it is the policy of the Government of Canada to say yes to our resolution this morning. The resolution simply says that we want the Government of Canada to strengthen and clarify article XI of the General Agreement of Tariffs and Trade in the ongoing multilateral trade negotiations and that it will not be party to any agreement that fails to achieve these objectives. Surely the parliamentary secretary, who speaks on behalf of the government in the House of Commons and on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture,
should have said: "Yes, we agree with that motion. We will not be party to an agreement which fails to achieve these objectives".
That is the same kind of slippery answer that we have had from the Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture and the Deputy Prime Minister. They say: "Our position is to support article XI but if there is any change we will let you know". That simply is not good enough. That is almost exactly what the Minister of Agriculture said in response to a question from the hon. member from Haldimand-Norfolk here last week when he said: "Our position is to support article XI until we change it".
That simply is not good enough. This debate today and the whole question of the GATT negotiations is obviously very important to dairy producers, poultry producers, broiler producers, turkey producers and egg producers. There are about 40,000 of them but they employ another
40,000	or 50,000 people, perhaps another 100,000 people in those operations across the country.
They are the most stable, well organized producers in the country and they are self-reliant. They are not lined up at the door of the Parliament Buildings every fall demanding stabilization payments. They may be this fall, but they have not been in the past. If we let them down, you are going to see an exodus in rural Canada, especially Ontario, Quebec, Atlantic Canada, B.C. and many communities across the west including the prairies although they are not as dependent on the supply management sector. But certainly they are the most stable producers in that sector of the country.
We are going to see a withering of rural Canada. If we go the route of the United States-and often we think on this side of the House that is the ultimate plan of the Prime Minister-we will see these industries concentrated like they are in the United States where most of the eggs are produced in Georgia, Alabama and other southern states. You can go to states like Maine, which has roughly the same land mass as New Brunswick, and you will not see many eggs or dairy products produced there.
If we want to talk about regional development, supply management and these sectors have provided the greatest initiative for supply management that we see in this country.
October 3, 1991

This is a very important debate today. I am not getting your signals very clearly, Madam Speaker, as to just how much time I have.

I simply want to say to the government this morning that it is impossible to describe how important this issue is. We and the producers feel that we were sold out on the processing side of supply management commodities in the free trade deal. Madam Speaker, Canadian agriculture is in a state of crisis. The price of soy beans and wheat is 35 per cent below last year's level and 45 per cent below the fifteen-year average. In fact, losses in the province of Ontario total about $200 million this year. And now, supply management is threatened.

For the government to tell us that article XI of the GATT will not change until the government says it will change is hardly reassurance to the dairy farmers of Canada and the other producers of supply managed goods.
Let us remember that this is the same government that said that it was going to protect Canadian daiiy farmers in the issue of ice cream and yoghurt in the free trade agreement. Look what happened there.
It sold us out.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
That is right. It sold us out. [Translation]
Madam Speaker, the government has sent some alarming signals during the past few days. I have before me a document published under the title: "Canadian Federalism and Economic Union-Partnership for Prosperity", a document tabled in the House last week by this government. I would like to quote a few passages from page 19. Here, we see a list under the title: "Costs of Barriers". The following items are listed: agricultural supply marketing boards that regulate the production and prices of various food products including milk, poultry and eggs.

In its own document, the government refers to these measures as impediments to trade in Canada. How can the government tell us today that it wants to protect supply management, when in its own document tabled last week, it called the concept a nuisance?

I am worried. The dairy farmers, the poultry producers, the egg producers and others I represent in this House are worried as well. Dairy farming in Canada is a very important industry.

Let me give you a few facts. The electoral district of Perth-Wellington-Waterloo has 1,299 dairy producers. The one I represent, Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, comes second with 1,104 dairy producers. So you see how important this is for my riding! Lotbiniere, 1,089 dairy producers; Beauce, 990 and Bellechasse, 969. These are the five electoral districts in this country with the largest number of dairy producers, mine ranking second.
Madam Speaker, Quebec produces 47.4 per cent of Canada's dairy products and Ontario 31.1 per cent. So you see, this is a very important issue for both provinces, since 77.5 per cent of dairy production is carried on in those provinces, and 75 per cent of dairy producers are in the two provinces I just mentioned.

We are not talking here about a small issue. We are not talking about a major issue. We are talking about something which is fundamental for the survival of that industry, not only in our country, not only in the province I represent, but even more so for my constituents.
Dairy farmers of Canada produced a document for us and made it available to members of Parliament. It is entitled Update on GATT Negotiations, October 1991. They are very concerned about the all too prevalent rumours going on right now in the public domain. They are more than rumours and there is a reason for them. It is that the supply management system we have could be exchanged for other considerations at the GATT and, in turn, we would get a so-called tariffication system.
Supply

And if we had that system, Madam Speaker, Canadian farm producers would lose 20 per cent of their income right from the start, assuming that the system would work and would be in place permanently. I say this because it is quite possible that this government-although its chances of being around for much longer are not that good-might subsequently try to reduce the protective tariffs they introduced. Then, of course, any remaining tariffs would gradually disappear, thanks to free trade. Canadian farmers and dairy producers in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and elsewhere, would be left with nothing to protect them, and we would see a repeat of what we saw in the United States: a gradual concentration of dairy production and the production of many other farm products.

To those who say: "Well, that is free enterprise'', I say: "Nonsense". There is nothing free about countries battling each other with subsidies. I have no doubt that the dairy producer in my riding is as efficient as the one in New York State. That is not the issue. Why should a dairy producer in Glengarry, in Prescott or in Russell, compete with the Treasury of the United States of America? That is the issue, the long term issue, were we to lose our supply managed system.
Milk prices to farmers could decrease by some 20 per cent under the tariffication system. That could veiy well happen if the government lets go of our supply management system. Furthermore, this pro-free trade government could then lower the tariffs, and remove them completely over time. Canadian dairy, poultry and egg farmers need the protection of existing systems, supply management. We need to preserve that supply management.
The issue is not whether the Reform Party would do worse than the Conservatives. We are not competing for who can do worse. We already know what we have across the way is bad enough. Heaven forbid that we could get worse than this.
We want to make things better and at least keep what farmers have now, our supply management system.

October 3, 1991

Madam Speaker, the voters I represent in this House want to keep their supply management system. What we need is a government committed to maintaining and improving that system. I say to the parliamentary secretary that our experience of the past few years has shown us what the government's commitment or so-called commitment is worth. We saw it in the Canada-U.S. talks, and we saw it in the ice cream and yogurt dispute.
I remember a political debate in Saint-Isidore de Prescott, in my riding, where the Tory candidate sitting next to me, who incidentally received a whopping 19 per cent of the votes, tried to convince my constituents that ice cream and yogurt would be protected under the Free Trade Agreement. The farmers in my riding didn't believe him, and they were right not to, simply because it didn't happen.
In the past, I have seen how we lost out under this agreement, and my constituents and I are afraid of what might happen now at GATT I have confidence in the farmers in my riding and across Canada, but I certainly do not trust the government opposite to protect their rights. And members opposite will have to prove they mean what they say, because in the past, they have given the impression they want to terminate our supply management system.
Today, we will see whether the government opposite votes in favour of the motion.

That is what we need. We need to arm our negotiators with a clear resolution of this House, that we want to keep, retain, enhance and improve our supply management system for our country.

I want to thank my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. Last year I had the privilege of visiting Moscow and Riga, Latvia. When I was there I noticed that every morning on my way to this environmental symposium that I was attending that people would start lining up at the grocery stores at about seven o'clock, sometimes even earlier than seven o'clock, hopefully to get in there and hopefully get a little bit of bread or cheese. Very rarely did I see milk. Sometimes the meat that was there, I must confess I don't think we would have used that quality of beef on
our pets here in this country. It was the most shaking experience that I ever had when I was in Moscow for that period.
We have heard a lot today about supply management and we are addressing our remarks primarily to the farming community. As an urban member of Parliament I would like to ask my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell what effect this is going to have on security of food supply and also prices for people in our major urban centres. We need our urban community, the people in downtown Toronto and downtown Montreal, to understand what this debate is all about today. With respect to all rural members, I wish when you address your remarks today that you could put in your speeches what effect this is going to have on the consumers.
With all due respect to the farming community-and I care and I understand from my colleague from Lamb-ton-Middlesex who has done this fabulous document on Compare the Share-we need to communicate, not to the 300,000 farmers in this country who are suffering and who are in deep pain, but with the 25 million other consumers who are out there.
Madam Speaker, through you to my colleague, what effect will this have on my constituents who are not farmers?

First of all, I want to congratulate and thank my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood. It is important for all members, whether they be rural members like myself or urban members, to be interested in agriculture.
Every time we have a debate on agriculture in this House, some urban members are very, very interested, and the member for Broadview-Greenwood among the most interested, if not the most of all urban members, and I congratulate him for that. Of course, the people on the farms produce the food and the people in the city eat the food, and they have to remember that. The member for Broadview-Greenwood knows that.
In terms of the remarks of the hon. member for Souris-Moose Mountain who qualified me as an urban member, the village of Sarsfield where I live has 230 people living in it. That is urban Canada, Madam Speaker.
October 3, 1991

I was raised on a farm and I now live in that village of 230 people, that vast metropolis of Sarsfield.
What the member for Broadview-Greenwood said is very important. We have in Canada the highest quality of food in the world. We have a very reliable supply. When did we ever hear we had run out of milk in this country? We do not. We do not run out of supply managed commodities. The system is reliable, has worked for decades, is stable, and provides a reliable, though not fantastic, source of income for our producers.
Speaking of what this does for the producer, some people-and I hate to name the Consumers' Association of Canada, but I will anyway-say that supply management is costly.
I beg to differ with those people whom I hate to mention, the Consumers' Association of Canada, but I will do it anyway. They are wrong and they often are.
Let me tell you for instance that in 1980 the income going to farmers for a litre of milk at that time was 38 cents and it has jumped to the huge amount of 57 cents over 10 years.
But do you want to know something, Madam Speaker? The price to the consumer has gone from 75 cents to $1.48. In other words, it is not the farmer whose income is increasing. It is those elsewhere in the chain who distribute and sell the food to consumers. That is why the price is skyrocketing but the farmer is not getting his or her fair share.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Plourde (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since it came into power, the government has shown unwavering support of supply management. We believe it has been and should continue to remain a crucial element in Canada's agricultural policy. In this regard, we have been working with the provinces and the industry to ensure that supply management remains an up-to-date viable policy tool.
Thus, in the domestic agricultural policy review, we and the other stake holders in the supply management systems have been working hard to develop "second
Supply
generation" supply management. We all recognize that supply management is a dynamic concept which has to adjust to changes in the market place if it is to continue to serve producers, processors and consumers into the twenty first century.
Since 1947, the GATT has recognized that if governments effectively control supply, there should be a corresponding discipline on imports. Article XI,2(c)(1) of the GATT thus provides the international authority to apply import quotas in support of effective supply control systems.
Unfortunately, a number of recent GATT panels have recognized that the current GATT rules require clarification. In particular, there is a pressing need to clarify which processed products can be placed under import control. In the case of the dairy sector, milk is under production control, but it is dairy products which are traded internationally.
Madam Speaker, the industry, the provinces and the federal government have thus agreed that a key Canadian negotiating objective in the multilateral trade negotiations is the strengthening and clarification of article XI. We have pursued this objective vigorously throughout the negotiations and will continue to do so.
As you are aware, Madam Speaker, Canada's negotiating position on agriculture has been developed in close cooperation with the provinces and all segments of the industry. It represents a truly national consensus that all segments of Canadian agriculture stand to benefit from an international trading system which is based on effective rules which are equally applicable to all countries and all commodities.
All segments of the industry recognize that trade barriers and trade distorting subsidies must be progressively reduced. Madam Speaker, it is crystal clear that the current distortions and uncertainties in agricultural trade are just as disruptive to a Canadian dairy farmer as to a Canadian grain producer. The status quo is not acceptable to either.
Our export commodities need improved access to markets and a substantial reduction in all forms of trade distorting subsidies. Our supply management sectors need to know with certainty what the international rules are, so they can operate their systems accordingly. All of these interests are reflected in a balanced way in the Canadian agricultural negotiating position in the Uruguay round.

This government has forged a national agricultural consensus that the agricultural trade interests of all the regions and all of the commodities should be pursued aggressively in a way which does not prejudice the interests of one at the expense of the other.
Is the Opposition seriously suggesting that before we even know what is really negotiable, we should completely ignore the vital interests of all regions and commodities which will require a successful result? The Opposition may choose to do so, but we in this government will continue to pursue a balanced negotiating position which reflects the nation's agricultural interests. We will continue to consult closely with all segments of the industry and all provinces as we enter the last few months of the negotiations in Geneva.
Madam Speaker, the moment of truth is fast approaching. The Director general of the GATT has said that November will see the making or breaking of the negotiations. In order to set the stage for these crucial weeks, Mr. Dunkel, the GATT Director General, has indicated that he will put forward a comprehensive negotiating proposal on agricultural, as in other sectors, which he hopes will provide the basis for an agreement.
It is this government's intention to consult with the provinces and the industry once we have Mr. Dunkel's proposal.
The Minister of State for Agriculture is in Geneva, at this very moment, meeting with Mr. Dunkel, in order to strongly make known Canada's views on this important question. We will miss no opportunity of ensuring that Mr. Dunkel is aware of Canada's concerns, which he is drafting those proposals.
The Minister of State for Agriculture, the hon. Pierre Blais, issued a press release dated September 30th, in which he said: "We are firmly resolve to negotiate an agreement that will protect our supply management programs and, to this end, we will make every effort necessary to obtain a clarification and strengthening of article XI of the GATT". Mr. Blais reiterated that commitment to representatives of Canadian marketing boards during a meeting in Ottawa this morning.
Supply
When the negotiations in Geneva resumed, Mr. Blais met with officials of Canadian marketing boards for chicken, turkey, hatching eggs, chicken raised for meat, as well as the dairy farmers of Canada, in order to look at the evolution of the situation since last July.
Madam Speaker, Mr. Blais, who is going to Geneva, will have meetings regarding the GATT negotiations on agriculture and intellectual property. He will also meet the GATT Director General and the President of the negotiating group on agriculture, Mr. Arthur Dunkel.
The minister will then go to Paris where he will meet the president of I'Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec, Mr. Jacques Proulx, to look at the situation regarding the GATT negotiations.
In concluding, Madam Speaker, we intend to examine in detail the negotiating position of each country before deciding whether the emerging agricultural package is a deal which would be in the interest of Canadian agriculture. Madam Speaker, to do otherwise will be irresponsible. Canada's agricultural export interests and our supply management interests coincide in that both of them need a successful Uruguay round and both would be adversally affected by a failure.

Madam Speaker, just before I comment in support of the motion before the House today, I must point out to the government that it must guarantee to Canadian supply management sectors that the system as it is at the present time will stay in place.
I would like to point out to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, who has unfortunately had to leave the House for a moment, that he made some comments earlier this morning about the importance of people listening to someone. I want to remind him of a story, because I do not think the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister is getting the point of all of the groups of farmers who are coming to see him and his colleagues, the thousands of farmers who are coming out to meetings.
I will remind him of a story about the sheep farmer who was talking to a group of people and telling them that because the wolves were destroying his sheep, they should destroy the wolves. Someone in the crowd stood up and said that maybe what would be a better route would be to neuter the male wolves and therefore that would look after it. The shepherd's response was that that person did not understand the situation. The wolves were not molesting his sheep, they were eating them.
I would remind the hon. parliamentary secretary that the concern the supply managed dairy, egg and poultry producers have at the present time is that this present government is going to throw them to the wolves if they do not protect the system on their behalf for these producers. Further to that, I would like the parliamentary secretary or someone from the government to explain to Canadian producers and to this House and to those who are watching what their definition of supply management is. They do not seem to make that very clear.
In the last few weeks they have continually asked producers why they do not think a system of tariffication would work. If we look at the minutes of the Standing Committee on Agriculture from a week or so ago, when one of the chief negotiators going to GATT on our behalf was there, there was a fair bit of that type of comment made. Madam Speaker, if you listened to what the previous speaker said, he spent a fair bit of time talking about tariffication. Perhaps we are going to have to have a look at that type of thing. I agree that we have to look at different systems, but the point being made is that we cannot throw our system and our producers and what they have done for the Canadian economy and Canadian consumers to the wolves.
Without primary agriculture, which is the production of food and fibre, there is no question that many rural communities would disappear in Canada. Unfortunately, that has already happened to some extent.
The University of Guelph in a study and a report they put out in conjunction with some other groups over a year ago outlined that the agrifood industry, which the supply managed sector plays a role in, is a $42 billion to $43 billion industry in this country. We all know the discouraging situation that is faced by Canadian grains and oilseed producers at the present time when their returns in real terms are worse than they were in the 1930s.
Added to that concern of farmers and producers in this country are the concerns of our supply managed sector, our dairy, egg and poultry producers. They can very easily see the distinct possibility of the erosion of the system that they have for their production and for the production of the benefits that they have and they provide, not only to the consumer but to our society in general.
We must recognize, and I do not think any Canadian can complain, what this sector has been able to provide to everyone including the farmers, consumers and society in general. This system is one that allows a decent return on investment. I do not think anyone can object to that. It does not allow an exorbitant return on an investment. It allows the owners, the operators and the employees a decent living, not an exaggerated living. It provides Canada and Canadians with a steady source of nutritious, wholesome and the safest food in the world.
October 3, 1991

How better can we provide all of these things to Canadians than to have them produced in our own country under our own eyes, rules and regulations? This does this. It does not guarantee this for every producer in that sector but it provides that for the efficient producer. When we talk about efficiency, let us look at what these sectors have done for Canadian consumers.
The dairy industry for example, since 1971, has increased its efficiency 71 per cent; our American counterparts, 46 per cent. New Zealand dairy producers have only increased their efficiency somewhere in the low thirties and western Europe in the single digits.
The economic viability in these sectors of our agricultural community, because there has been some economic viability and a system in place that allows a decent return on investment and a decent labour, has provided this sector of our agricultural community the opportunity and ways and means to do all of those other things that our society wants today; that is, to carry on sound management practices that will put into place the proper control of the soil, crop rotation, water conservation, soil erosion and the proper care of the environment. Unfortunately, because of the disastrously low returns in some sectors of our agricultural community today, even though farmers know how to farm better, they cannot afford to do so.
In every case, who knows better what is best for the soil, for water, soil and wind erosion, than the producers. In the grains and oilseed production right now a bushel of wheat returns a western farmer $2 a bushel. They know how to farm better, but the returns are just not there in order to allow them to have the equipment and carry out the practices. Therefore, in some cases they do not do as good a job as they should and they do not do as good a job as they would like to.
I would say that this sector has not only provided a decent return to the producer, but it has also provided a proper and decent return to our society and to our consumers in general.
I stress, between the dairy, egg, poultry and meat sectors, there are 40,000 producers in this country, 40,000 businesses. We talk about the plight of the small business. Some of those businesses are relatively small and some are relatively large. But we are talking about the
Supply
economic viability, the economic future and the social concerns and the social effect that will have and the spin-off to the suppliers they buy from, to the people they sell to, to the processors they provide. We are talking about 40,000 Canadian businesses.
I ask this government what it has done in the recent past to tell Canadian consumers the benefits of the supply managed sector in this country.
I beg to question. I do not think it has done very much. I do not think, with the attitude it has of open free market, give it heck, way of doing business, that it cares that much. If it does, it has not not indicated it.
What has this government done to tell the other 100 countries involved in the GAIT" negotiations the benefits of the system that we have here in Canada and what it does for the producer, the consumer and the environment, the social fibre and fabric of our country and what it does for our whole society in general.
I stress to everyone that it does more than put food on the plate. The agricultural sector plays a major role. It is one of the four wealth creators in this country, the other three being fishing, mining and forestry. If the primary producer, the initial person in that chain, does get a reasonable return on their investment, labour and their management, how could they, as any business, stay in place?
Referring back to the comment at the beginning, this government does not seem to understand the importance of working and selling this on behalf of Canadian consumers and Canadian producers. It seems to be willing to very systematically consider throwing them to the wolves.
I do not think there is much more I can say. I only have one minute left, so I do not have to say much more. I hope I have made the point. This sector of the economy, agriculture production, is not asking for protection for the sake of being protected. As we have seen from documents prepared by colleagues, they are not getting a very large share of what the consumer pays. When we look at how much their share has increased in the last 10 years compared to what the consumer has paid, they are not getting an exorbitant increase. They are getting a fair share of the increase.

October 3, 1991
Supply
I call upon the government to explain to Canadians better than it has, and I am afraid, better than it cares to, the role this plays and how important this sector is, not only to the agricultural community, but to Canadians in general so that we can do what they have done for all of us in the future.

Madam Speaker, I have a comment in relation to what the previous member just stated.
The hon. member and I entered this House at the same time in November 1988. Since I have been here, I do not think there is anything that would indicate that we are about to dismantle supply management. I think every time the former Minister of Agriculture, the present Minister of Finance, has been on his feet in this House in the last three years he has indicated our support as a government for supply management.
During recent GATT negotiations and the breakdown of those negotiations, we have continually sought clarification and a strengthening of Article XI. We very strongly support Article XI, we support supply management and we have no intention of abandoning that.
How we can drive that message home any clearer than that I do not know, because the present Minister of Agriculture is in Brussels at this very moment and that is the message he will be carrying: We have no intention of dismantling supply management.
I come from a farming community. I was on the telephone to some of my own farmers yesterday and they are very coiicerned about that. Believe me, Madam Speaker, I have no intention of moving off of that target myself. The object is to maintain it, clarify it and to strength it because it is very, very important for me as a member of Parliament. That is a major part of my constituency, as with the member who has just spoken. It is a very important part of my constituency and an important part of his.
Agriculture is the backbone of rural Canada and I do not want in any way, shape or form to be a member of a government that is going to abandon that. It is very, very important that we continue, all of us on both sides of this House, to encourage the strengthening of our supply management system through article XI. Our present Minister of Agriculture is doing that at this very moment in Europe.

Madam Speaker, I do not question the fact that the present government has said that it is going to stick up for supply management, but what I will remind the remember of and what I asked someone in my speech for a definition, is what is the present government's definition of supply management. If it is the same as we have at the present time, why does it not say so? If it is going toward the United States suggested proposal of tarrification, let us fess up and let us tell the producers that that may very well likely be the case. But the government is not saying that.
The concern out there in the producer organizations and on the farm, and they keep asking the question, is why would tarrification not do the job that is being done now?
I remind this House that tarrification will not do what the present system does because tarrification opens the door, sticks the toe in and begins the ratcheting down of the system that is there at the present time.
Before I sit down, I want to remind the House that the speaker who just spoke said that he could not and would not be part of a system that did not protect supply management as we know it now. If that does not happen I would expect that the member would have to see fit to step down because he did not want to be part of that government.

Madam Speaker, today we are not just participating in another opposition day or discussing another opposition motion. Rather, we are discussing an issue that concerns all Canadians and all members of Parliament. It is a survival of our food production sector.
We have heard a lot about the desperate plight of farmers in the last year, but I believe that any clear-minded individual would agree that our agricultural sector is going through a serious crisis, the worst probably since the Depression. How bad is it? In July the Ontario Federation of Agriculture declared: "A plunge in grain and oilseeds prices, the rush by governments to get out of ad hoc programs, have left Ontario agriculture in a state of emergency". OFA president, Roger George went on to say: "Prices are down dramatically. Ministers McKnight and Buchanan had better start taking the situation of Ontario farmers seriously or there won't be any farmers left to make the transition from ad hoc payment to the new safety net programs".
October 3, 1991

I believe the agricultural industry is in dire straits. That is why I asked the House of Commons Standing Committee on Agriculture to be called back in August to deal with the crisis facing our farmers.
Representatives from prairie pools presented a submission to the committee which indicated: "Grains and oilseeds producers are in a desperate financial situation. Prices have been bad and they are getting worse. The younger guys are starting to say there is no future in it for us" unless they have other sources of income. The average grain producer will be living well below the poverty line. That is how bad it is.
These people are not crying wolf. I had an opportunity to spend some time in western Canada this summer and talked to many farmers. It was alarming to hear the prediction that unless something is done quickly, and I emphasize the word quickly, 40 per cent of all farmers will be forced off the land this year. If things do not improve, 30 per cent more will be forced off next year.
Farmers continue to provide a high quality food. Yet they receive less than the cost of production for their labour. Does that sound fair to anyone in this House?
Many areas in Ontario have the worst crops in recent memory and have nowhere to turn. But there are none of their members in this House today addressing this issue.
Farmers and agriculture are the cornerstone of our economy. We have heard that time and time again by probably all members of Parliament. In the past they have resolutely accepted the increasing losses of income with an external optimism only found in rural Canada.
However, this hope has all but been extinguished. Farmers are desperate. Farm families are dedicated to providing food for Canada and the world. They have given all they have. They have given their savings, their homes and their futures and they cannot give any more.
There is a feeling of desperation and despair in rural Canada. That stems from a feeling that no one cares, that this government does not care for them.
Rural Canada is suffering. When agriculture suffers, everyone suffers, the country suffers. Low commodity prices, poor crops and international subsidy wars will
Supply
mean the demise of many more farmers in this nation if we do not act now to save them.
Members opposite are saying: "Why get into this now? We thought we were discussing the GATT situation". We are talking about farmers in desperate need, the grains and oilseeds producers. But who are the farmers who have the most stability in our system who under normal circumstances can pay most of their bills, look their banker straight in the eye? It is the supply managed commodity farmers that can do this.
Is this a coincidence? I do not think so. These producers operate under marketing systems that assure Canadians adequate supplies of safe and nutritious food at fair prices while providing some sort of efficient income for these producers. These are the farmers that this motion is dealing with. These are the farmers that will be in an equally desperate situation as the grains and oilseeds producers, if we do not stand up for them now and defend them at the GATT.
We have heard the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds, the Minister of Finance and the Minister for International Trade and our negotiators all say that they support supply management and that they are committed to seeing the strengthening of Article XI of the general agreement.
The question is: Can they be believed? They have mouthed support for grains and oilseeds farmers. They said that they are going to protect them. They have admitted that there is a $1 billion shortfall this year for the 1990-91 crop year.
Have we seen anything? Have the farmers got anything in their pockets yet? No. One might legitimately ask: What is its ultimate objective?
I believe this government is hell bent for leather to destroy the department and the industry that we have built together over a long period of years.
Always remember, it takes longer to be a builder than it does to be a wrecker. We have had how many studies in the past three years? I would say about a dozen. What did it tell us? Anything new? It did not tell us a damn thing.

October 3, 1991
Supply
It basically tried to implant in people's minds that farmers were inefficient and must become more market oriented. All the facts and figures I intend to show will prove otherwise.
The agriculture producers of this land have become the most productive people in our society and have reaped the smallest reward for their efforts.
These highly efficient producers have been falsely attacked by both inside and outside this government. The former Minister for International Trade stated that the Minister of Agriculture should be ashamed of himself for his actions in subsidizing farmers to the tune of $8.8 billion.
It is an out and out falsehood. It is a direct lie. Never in previous history have moneys received from the marketplace been called a subsidy in an international GATT meeting.
It is a damn falsehood, and it is a lie. I believe that this is a purposely orchestrated attack to deter people's minds from the really costly culprits in our society.
Millions are spent and lost. Consumers are paying much more than they should per producer, in some instances increases in prices of over 150 per cent, and not a peep out of anyone in those benches. Why? Is this a special vendetta against a minority group of people? I think so, but why?
The highly subsidized professors and civil servants who pay for economists subsidized by the big food chains are dictating to them what they should write. I want to make it clear.
I see nothing wrong with criticism as long as it is accurate and honest, but half truths, supposition and lies I will not accept and neither should anyone in this House.
We have built an agricultural industry that is second to none in the world, one that allows farmers some say in the marketplace, one that is subject to public scrutiny like no other producing sector of our society. These are the farmers we are defending in this motion.
In many cases it took years to build these marketing structures such as the Canadian Wheat Board, the
Canadian Dairy Commission and the poultry marketing boards. These are all legal structures, allowed by our democratic provincial parliaments and our federal Parliament. These are not illegal entities. They are subject to more scrutiny than any monopolistic multinational that you can find.
My hon. friend from Lambton-Middlesex was speaking this morning. He suggested that the former minister for trade was directly misleading Canadians and totally misled this House in the facts that he presented to GATT and in this House last October 15. I think he was calling him a liar and I think that if the former Minister for International Trade did not withdraw those comments and did not correct those comments in the paper, he was lying and that the hon. member was right.
I know my time is up, but I want to finish by saying this. I thank the hon. member for his comments. I want to end by saying that the government has proposed that it is protecting our supply managed commodities.
I was at the GATT last summer, and I met with people from the European commission. They told me that they had not once heard from this government on article XI of GATT. That was well after the negotiations began, so who do you believe? Do you believe the members or the ministers of the Crown who get up and suggest that they are protecting supply management?
Do you really believe the European community which is negotiating this, which said directly that the minister did not, nor did anyone from this government, ever bring forward supply management as an issue?
I see my time is up, Mr. Speaker, and I thank you for your indulgence.

Mr. Speaker, I do not mind taking part in a debate and responding to anything in this House but there were many inaccuracies in the previous member's comments, particularly in relation to the GATT. He knows full well that our agricultural minister worked very hard on behalf of all farmers in Canada to ratify strengthening article XI, that which pertains to marketing boards, that which defines marketing boards in this country.
That is absolutely absurd.

He might have been to the GATT negotiations for an hour or two hours as an observer but he certainly was not there to watch what our minister did on our behalf as farmers of Canada.
I suggest that his remarks are totally off base and inaccurate and I suggest that he withdraw those remarks.
I was only relaying facts as I met with many members of the European commission over a period of a week that I was there.

Point of order, Mr. Speaker, what he is telling us is third party rhetoric or hearsay and if he is referring to it in that sense he should spell it out clearly because that is not what he said in his original comments. It is third party gossip that he is referring to.
That is not a point of order.

When I was over there last July I met with them and asked what the position of the Government of Canada had been on supply management. They said "silent". They had not met us, had not yet talked to us about that. I indicated surprise because our government has been saying back home all the time that it was standing up for supply management. They were somewhat shocked by the fact that all this rhetoric was going on but the government had not really put any major proposals to them on this.
I am just telling the member straight what the European community told me. It is not gossip. It is exactly what it told me. If he infers from that that his ministers are lying then that is up to him. I cannot say that directly. I can only tell you the facts on what these people told me.

Mr. Speaker, I think that we are going through an extremely difficult period in almost all sectors, but especially in our country's farming industry.
Today's debate could be worthwhile if together we sought ways to support our farmers instead of trying to insinuate all sorts of things that could lead the people to believe that the government is doing nothing to help farmers, which is absolutely false.
Supply
I find the arrogance shown by my colleague extremely unfortunate in that he seeks information in Europe and tells us that the government is doing nothing or doing a bad job when the whole policy and strategy and the proposals were developed in Canada with the farmers- that is the position our negotiators took and maintained from the beginning.
I find it insulting for our Canadian farmers to be told that the government is not defending them properly when we know very well that the government is maintaining and putting forward in Europe proposals that were worked on here in Canada. I think that my colleague should have become much better informed here in this county about the decisions and proposals instead of going to Europe to ask foreigners what our position should be or what position has been taken.

I say to my hon. friend that I am showing no more arrogance than the Minister for International Trade did to farmers when he told the Minister of Agriculture, in response to my question, that farmers were getting too much money. You tell me about arrogance. I would remind the hon. member, who represents an area with a number of dairy farmers, a number of supply managed commodities, that it has been this side of the House that has been running this issue for the last two years.
I ask the hon. member where he has been and where his colleagues have been on this issue.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join this debate today and state the government's position on negotiations under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade regarding article XI.
Canada is inescapably a part of the global economy as a country whose prosperity depends on the export of almost 30 per cent of what it produces, about 50 per cent for agriculture. It is essential to Canadians that the world trading system is fair and open. That is why this government has dedicated so much effort to the Uruguay round of multilateral trade negotiations under the GATT. We strongly believe that the best way to ensure long-lasting beneficial trade relations is through an open, stable and free trading world marketplace.

October 3, 1991
Supply
Canada has been actively participating in the Uruguay round negotiations for the past five years and has been pushing for a strengthened and balanced set of rules regarding agriculture. Canada will continue to do so.
A successful resolution of the MTN is one of Canada's highest trade priorities. It is founded on the simple principle that the fewer trade barriers there are between countries, the more prosperous these countries will be.
The current rounds of talks began in Uruguay in September 1986. We had high hopes that we would achieve breakthroughs in many fields, as for the first time agriculture was in the forefront of the discussions. It was this government that insisted that agriculture be at that forefront.
It was a long journey, both literally and figuratively from Punta del Este to Brussels where the round was supposed to conclude last December. Along the way those hopes were tempered, almost dashed, but the work continues and our goals remain the same.
Canada's goals were spelled out in our offer which was tabled in Geneva last October, almost a year ago. I would like to review them.
We as a government, as a country, are seeking substantial reductions in trade distorting subsidies, particularly export subsidies. We want improved, predictable and more secure access to export markets by a reduction in tariff and non-tariff barriers. We would be prepared to offer comparable access to our own markets as well.
We want clearer and fairer GATT rules that apply equally to all countries, including a strengthened and clarified article XI, the elimination of a country's specific exemptions and better disciplines on the use of countervailing duties. Finally, we want to see the development of a framework of rules to prevent the abuse of health and sanitary regulations as disguised barriers to trade.
We have developed a balanced and comprehensive offer which is consistent with our objectives of substantial trade liberalization, fairer and more predictable trade rules, and equal treatment among GATT countries.
Canada's offer and objectives in the MTN remain unchanged.
We continue to pursue those objectives because we are convinced that an agreement which achieves them will be beneficial for all Canadian agriculture.
The clarification and strengthening of article XI remains a key objective for Canada. Our proposal, tabled last year, includes specific proposals for clarifying a country's rights and obligations through rules on product coverage for processed products, the meeting of effective supply control, the establishing of import access and new disciplines on exports. This balanced proposal was developed in close consultation with all sectors of Canadian agriculture and enjoys the support of the entire agrifood industry.
Canada has vigorously pursued the proposal of article XI, working with other countries including the EEC, Japan, Austria, Switzerland, Norway, Finland and Korea, which support the retention and clarification of article XI. In fact most countries supporting the continuation of article XI have indicated that they believe the Canadian proposal should form the basis for negotiation.
If this kind of agreement is reached, governments will still be able to provide support to the agricultural sector. Our objective is to make sure this support is provided in ways that are less trade-distorting. However, a number of countries continue to be of the view that all non-tariff barriers should be converted to tariffs, including import controls under article XI.
An agreement along the lines of our over-all position would also carry other benefits including improved and more secure market access, clear enforceable GATT rules, improved market stability and improved GATT mechanisms for resolving disputes.
It is important to note, Mr. Speaker, that we are not alone in this struggle. Canada is one of the original members of the Cairns group of developing and developed countries. This group of medium-sized agricultural exporters is dedicated to promoting agricultural trade reform. The Cairns group played an important role in making agriculture a priority on the agenda at the GATT ministerial meeting in Uruguay in September 1986 and we are continuing to work closely with the other members to achieve our goals at the MTN.
The Uruguay round has tried to deal with some very contentious issues. Not surprisingly, the task has been difficult. The European community especially has not been able to reach internal agreement on how to revise its common agricultural policy. The United States in turn has been unwilling to stop wielding its big stick in the export enhancement program.
October 3, 1991

As a result, we have witnessed a long and very destructive trade war and Canadian farmers have been caught in the cross-fire. The U.S. and the EEC have been using massive export subsidies that hurt all exporters. Canadian farmers feel the impact of export subsidies directly because the prices they receive are based on world markets. The Canadian Wheat Board sets its initial payments on the basis of international prices. The low world grain prices this year are reflected in the Canadian Wheat Board initial payments for wheat of only $95 per tonne.
Yesterday, the Minister of Agriculture met with EEC agricultural commissioner Ray McSharry to press for an early completion to the current negotiations and to emphasize Canada's objectives with respect to the GATT. During that meeting, Mr. McSharry assured our Minister of Agriculture that the EEC continues to support Canada's position on article XI.
Our Minister of Agriculture underlined to Mr. McSharry that extreme difficulties were being experienced by Canadian grains and oilseed producers as a result of the destructive EC and U.S. export subsidies.
The minister similarly raised concerns about these damaging export subsidies and the need for clear and freer trade rules, including the strengthening and clarification of article XI when he met recently with U.S. Agriculture Secretary Ed Madigan.
Today the Minister of State for Agriculture is in Europe to reaffirm Canada's position at the GATT. Tomorrow he will meet with Arthur Dunkel, Director General of the GATT, to make our concerns clear.
Mr. Dunkel has been holding technical consultations with delegations since February. He has been working hard to facilitate the detailed negotiations that must occur this fall if talks are to conclude successfully.
As I mentioned before, Canada's position at the MTN was developed in consultation with all stakeholders in the agri-food sector. We are continuing to consult with both industry and the provincial governments as talks progress.
As negotiations proceed in the coming months, Canada and other countries supportive of article XI will need
Supply
to continue pressing the case for strengthening and clarification. This period will obviously be one of uncertainty about the outcome of negotiations. It is therefore important that all those having an interest in supply management, government and industry, work closely together to achieve our common objective.
It is in our interest and the interest of the international trading system that we achieve an international trading system based on rules that treat all players as equals. That is why we have worked as a government and continue to work so hard for a successful conclusion to the MTN.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the member who just spoke.
It has to do with the motion of the day. As we know it is an opposition day, but the opposition seems to be very much focused on our abandoning of supply management. The question to the member is simply this: Can he see any evidence where this government might be weakening its position with regard to supply management or any sign that this government may indeed want to abandon its position with regard to supply management?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the question.
There have been a lot of discussions in the past two or three weeks about supply management in Canada. I see no evidence that Canada is weakening its position.
As a matter of fact, I believe there was a meeting yesterday of all the supply management groups in Canada and at that meeting, as I understand it, those supply groups supported Canada's position.
They supported the fact that Canada is continuing to fight to protect supply management in Canada. We have done that from the beginning as a government. There has never been a government in Canada that protected supply management more than this government.
What government managed to have agriculture put in the forefront, on the front burner at the discussions at GATT? It was under a former Minister of Agriculture from my riding that those talks were put on the front burner, because of discussions by him and our present Prime Minister.

October 3, 1991
Supply
There is no evidence that this government is weakening its position. We are prepared to continue with our position of supply management for Canadians because we recognize the fact that it has been of tremendous benefit to Canadians, both producers and consumers. We will continue to do that.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if my hon. friend from a neighbouring riding is aware of the fact that Mr. Mel Clark, a former deputy negotiator for free trade and the GATT, spoke about a program where the former Minister of Agriculture talked about the government's position on supply management.
The former minister said: "The Conservative government has defended the right to establish marketing boards in the past and will continue to do so in the future, but ice cream and yoghurt is a GATT issue and not a free trade issue and the GATT waiver for certain U.S. agricultural products is most unfair".
Mr. Clark said he reviewed Mr. Mazankowski's statements. I am just reading from his remarks and he says that: "(a) and (b) are simply not true, (a) being that the Conservative government defended the right to establish marketing boards in the past and will continue to do so. And (c) is a part of an attempt to hide from Canadians the effect of the FTA on marketing boards".
I am wondering if my hon. colleague is aware of these comments and may I have his views on this.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend from the riding of Haldimand-Norfolk.
The hon. member has raised the issue of whether or not a former, very distinguished Minister of Agriculture for this country, supports supply management and free trade for Canada.
I think it has been stated on many, many occasions that this government has indicated that both are necessary for Canadians. We have indicated many times, in many speeches in this House that we wanted the GATT to be clarified. We felt there were many things that needed to be clarified for many countries so that we know exactly where we stand when we are exporting and talking about subsidies, whether it be export enhancement subsidies or domestic subsidies.
That has been our position all along and we will continue to support the farmers of Canada as we have done in the past.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been a long time since a Minister of Agriculture, the Hon. Eugene Whelan, used to tell Canadians that we do not have a food subsidy situation in Canada. What we have is a cheap food policy in Canada. I used to tell the people in British Columbia that we were not subsidizing farmers, we were subsidizing consumers.
I do not intend to say very much about our grain growing. That is something with which I have had no personal experience, other than to say this. With respect to grain, it is costing a lot of money to produce the grains we are exporting and, to some extent, using here. I believe 80 per cent of grains and oilseeds are produced for export, not because we want farmers to grow feed or oilseeds or grains as such, but rather because we need something to export. These commodities make up our second largest export class in Canada.
Last year alone, 1990, we paid some $27 billion in interest on the debts of all Canadian governments. It would be nice if we could print dollars with the pulp we grow here and ship those out, but nobody wants them. We have to either borrow from abroad to pay that $27 billion or we have to ship out some concrete goods.
It is very important to us to ship out that grain. If the cost of that in part is helping farmers get a price that will enable them to keep on producing those grains and oilseeds, well then it is in the interest of Canada to do it. It does not help the farmer so much, because they would quit producing if there was no sale. It certainly helps Canada as a whole to have that very important export commodity.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister I think was the one who said: "It's rather peculiar that the two opposition parties together have been supporting the government employees represented by the alliance and yet, at the same time, are now standing up and supporting the farmers".
October 3, 1991

Over the years it has certainly been in the interest, whether it is the Liberals or Conservatives that are in power, of both of those parties to keep a wedge between these two groups; between organized labour on one hand and farmers on the other and yet they are natural allies.
Farmers certainly want union workers, organized workers, all workers to get a decent income so that they can keep on buying Canadian food if nothing else, and certainly the workers have no objection to farmers getting a decent return for the work they are doing.
I can draw on my own experience to give an example of that. I became Minister of Agriculture in September 1972. Prior to that, ever since the milk board was established, whenever the milk board announced that because of formula calculations or whatever there was going to be a price increase in fluid milk, there was an immediate drop in consumption, utilization if you like. People bought less fluid milk. It would then gradually climb up again. This happened regularly every time there was a price increase.
When I became Minister of Agriculture and the time came for an increase in price to be announced I announced it. I went to the news media and I said: "We need an increase of one cent or two cents a quart on the milk that the consumers are buying here in B.C. because the farmers need that extra money to pay their increase in costs." Not once during the 39 months that I was Minister of Agriculture was there ever a dip in consumption. The consumers, organized labour and everybody else, as long as they were convinced that it was the farmers who were getting it, felt that there was a real need and they were willing to support that and kept on drinking steadily increasing amounts of milk.
We are natural allies, labour and farmers, and yet it is to some people's advantage to try to drive this wedge between, to separate.
I see people smiling. They were not listening to my argument I suppose or were not paying too much attention to it.
Union workers do not have it all that easy. Although they were not able to negotiate any kind of a contract between the alliance and Treasury Board, even if they had a negotiated contract, they would know, in signing

that contract, that in all likelihood inflation was going to keep on at the rate of some 6 per cent a year for the next three years. During part of that time they were to get no increase at all, part of that time there would be a 3 per cent increase, something like half the rate of the inflation increase, and in the third year the same thing. They are steadily losing ground.
As it is, they are probably going to be something like 14 per cent behind at the end of this period that was forced through the House by the government majority and there is nothing they can do about it. They know that in bargaining they do not know just how much it is going to cost them to live some one, two or three years down the road. They do not have it all that easy. They have to make their best estimates. They have to bargain for what they hope will be a contract that will enable them to keep their ground, to hold their position, although often they do not make it.
It is the same thing with organized workers in all fields. They are the only ones who say: "Yes, we are prepared to accept such and such a wage this year and next year and sometimes into the third year", without being assured by anyone that the cost of living is going to be controlled in any way at all, although the Governor of the Bank of Canada says he is trying to, as to how much of the increase they have negotiated is going to be eaten up simply by the increase in the cost of living.
There was a time when we did control it, Mr. Speaker, and I think you might remember this as well as some of the members in the House, simply by controlling the bank interest rates. Some of you will remember when it was fixed, when you knew exactly what it was going to cost you this year and 10 years down the road to borrow money from the bank. In those days there was very little, if any, inflation. It worked. We cannot do that now because of the banks and we do not want to do anything to the banks.
The unions do try to negotiate wage increases to hold their own. Once they have negotiated the unorganized people in all of those industries for all of those employers are given an increase which is always more than the organized workers get. They are getting a higher salary to start with and their percentage increases are usually higher again.

Professionals seem to manage too. We hear of farmers going bankrupt. We hear of individuals having troubles.
We do not very often hear of professionals who are doing their job properly having that kind of trouble whether it is engineers, accountants or medical practitioners. They form organizations. They do not always set their rate of return, their pay for what they are doing, but certainly in the medical profession they do because in Canada we do have a Canadian medical plan, and they negotiate with governments to get a certain return for their labour. They know what it is going to be. They have trouble some time in the same way that organized labour does. They all get together and try to achieve some sort of unified approach, some way of trying to get a reasonable return for their labour, what they consider to be reasonable. Sometimes we are inclined to think that an increase that somebody else gets is unreasonably high, whereas the increase we ourselves get is always unreasonably low.
Nevertheless, they manage. They form their associations. They form their organizations, whatever you call them. In the case of trade union workers, they form trade unions. They all work in the same way.
The one major group in society that does not seem to have been able to make as much headway in that way is the farmers. In some areas it is particularly difficult for the farmers to try to do it. How can they negotiate in the same way that an employee working for the government among 100,000, 200,000, or 300,000 members of the alliance could? One employee would be in no position to go to his employer and try to negotiate some change in working conditions or some increase in pay or whatever.
I believe I am still on the 20-minute time allowance.
Farmers, when they try to plan their return from their work, their investment, everything they get, have not to be concerned only about the price they are going to get above the market return. TTiey have to worry about whether they are going to have anything to sell at all. They have to worry about the weather. They have to worry about pests. With animals they have to worry about diseases. They have to worry about whether they are going to be able to sell their products and, if so, if the price brings back a reasonable return.
It is much more complicated for farmers to run their business than it is for most other groups in society or
even most businesses. There are many more problems to be considered and many more things that are just totally unknown from one day to the next. They do not know when there will be an influx of grasshoppers to wipe out their crop. They would know a day ahead but not much more than that. Disease might strike as has happened when I was in the poultry business.
I keep layers for a period of some 20 years. For a short time during that 20 years they kept me, but most of the time I was keeping them. That was before marketing boards.
I can recall in 1951 getting a wholesale price of 87 cents a dozen for eggs. The price today is about 20 per cent more than that. I bought feed grain at $34 a ton 40 years ago. The price today has increased almost eightfold. The difference has been that the farmer has learned to become more productive: Technology.
When I went to university in 1949 I was told that the average egg producer in British Columbia, trying to make a living with a flock of less than 1,000 hens, was obviously not going to make it. He had to have 1,000 layers. That is 40 years ago. Today the figure would be at least 20 times that, probably more by now since I am out of touch.
It is just that difficult. The egg producers have learned to use technology, have learned to take advantage of the improvements in breeding as well, and they are able to do it. Although they are paying eight times as much for all of their input costs they are still able to get a reasonable return. The marketing board has made that possible. I said that 40 years ago the price I got for eggs was 87 cents a dozen. Six months later it was down to half of that. There was no ma rketing board. How could you plan under those circumstances? You could not. The marketing board has made it possible, and the resolution talks about supply management.
Someone asked what supply management means? It is very simple. It is knowing l ow much you want to produce in advance, whether you are going to produce it for your own people only in your own province, your own country or even in your own municipality, knowing how much is required in reasonable limits. Are you going to have any to export? Should there be my exports? Should there be some that would be manufactured into other products?
October 3, 1991

It is adding all those quantities together and determining how much is going to be produced of eggs, for example, and then dividing that in some rational system among the egg producers. It works.
Society does not pay the cost of that. Consumers are paying but they are paying less than they would be without that kind of a system in effect, and the farmers are getting a decent break. That is supply management.
We cannot use it for grain but even with grain, as I said earlier, we are producing it for export because we need those export dollars. Canada as a whole needs them, not the farmer. The farmer does not get export dollars. He or she gets Canadian dollars, but Canada as a whole needs those export dollars, so we have to produce everything we can for export.
It pays, in part, the $27 interest charge annually. It is important that we do win this fight at Geneva. It is extremely important to our system of supply management. It works at the resolution stage for the dairy producers. It works for the feathered groups, the birds, and it could work for other products. There is no reason at all that we could not extend it.
I am sure if it is protected and saved it will be extended to other animal crops as well. I was talking about the hog producers who have an association in B.C. There is not a full marketing board set up, but at least they work together to try to improve the lot of everyone in the industry.
The cattle producers in B.C. have tried to arrive at some kind of a system. So far they have just fallen short of being able to come up with anything that is reasonable.
In not being able to accomplish this, as I said earlier, the farmers are behind every other group in society. Every other group organizes and no one criticizes them for organizing. Some people such as those at the Fraser Institute will say that marketing boards are costing consumers a lot of money.
That is not the case. They are paying a fair price for the product. The prices of eggs to consumers and fluid milk to consumers are not being subsidized at all. They are reasonable prices. Farmers are getting their return. The consumers are paying a fair price, although some want to take advantage of cross-border shopping. I appreciate that. Some want to earn their high incomes in
Supply
Canada and then go across the border and buy cheaper products that are being produced at the cost of the people who are producing them. They are not getting a fair return.
In Canada we have been able to achieve a fair return without cost to society as a whole, without cost to the government. The cost is only to the people who are consuming the products. It is the one instance where we are not running a cheap food policy.
As Mr. Whelan and I used to say, we are running a reasonable policy. We are planning our production to suit the needs of the people in our community, and it is being paid for within the community.
We have to salvage this at GATT, and I wish I could feel confident that we will do so.
