speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had that assurance from the Prime Minister. I would remind you that Prime Minister is the same person who said, when he was running for the leadership of the Tory party, that getting into a free trade deal with the United States would be the worst thing that Canada could do or words to that effect.
I can recall that the Minister for International Trade was another person who, when running I believe for leader or at least some time around that date, gave us exactly the same reassurance that Canada could not afford to get into a free trade deal with the Americans. The Prime Minister and the current international trade minister were right then. When it suited their purposes, they very soon changed their minds totally and got us into this free trade deal with the Americans which has been so costly to us.
With that kind of a reputation and that kind of a record, can we believe those ministers when they say that they are going to do the best they can to salvage article XI?

Mr. Speaker, today we look very seriously at the GATT agreement, particularly the area that is affecting supply management, article XI of that agreement.
Many people are showing a great deal of concern for livelihood as Canadian producers if that clause is not strengthen'ed. We know that supply management in this country affects very strongly the dairy, poultry, egg and feather industry. I have to stop and think and ask myself
the question: Why is the business of agriculture not treated and looked upon in the same light as every other business?
It seems that we have heard supply management as a word to avoid. Many consumer groups have suggested supply management is not the best way to go. I have read editorials in major newspapers across this country which condemn somewhat supply management.
They don't understand it.

My colleague is very correct. I think they do not understand it clearly.
When I start to ask myself what supply management is, I relate back to the manufacturing industry. I relate to the auto industry or the clothing industry and I think to myself, these industries operate under very controlled supply management systems.
They market a product. They do research on sales. They produce products to match that market and match those sales.
When we start to look at it, what does that really achieve for an auto company? It knows how many cars it is going to produce in any one year. It knows how many workers it employs. It knows the cost of the raw materials going into the product. It knows what its energy costs are going to be to produce that product. It then hopes that it will anticipate proper sales. If those sales are not achieved we are in what we call a recession. That basically is the situation for almost every manufactured product in this country.
Let us take that scenario from the manufacturing industry and bring it into what we would call the agro-industry. When we stop and think about it farmers who are in supply management systems have done exactly what people in manufacturing areas have done. They have tried to define a market, done research on quantity of sales, set up production quotas to match that sale projection, and set up quotas so that they can be extremely efficient. Efficiency is the goal. Reasonable supply is the goal. When we stop and think about it, they really are doing what should be done in any business or any industry. They are looking at optimum values out of inputs, optimum value out of what is being put into that industry.
October 3, 1991

How is the consumer then affected by what they are doing? First of all I have to say that any consumer who realizes part of an industry is being developed to the point where it can control what goes in and what comes out, is sure to say we are going to have a very safe supply of food. We are not going to be in situations like my colleague referred to a while back this morning in which many countries of this world do not know where the next amount of food to the family is going.
We have to somewhat control our own destiny in agriculture in this country and supply management may be one of the better ways to do it, reliable supply of food.
Second, we have rules and regulations about safety in our country. By making sure that we have a very safe, adequate food supply, we do another service for that Canadian consumer. We make certain that safety and health are maintained at the highest level possible.
I hear stories about chicken barns in southern United States that are not cleaned for six months. Every chicken barn in the supply management system in Ontario, every time it goes through a series of production, is cleaned and changed. Antibiotics are not given to the chickens to prevent disease as much as they have to be in other climates and in other sections of the United States where safety is not the same concern.
I believe that quality control has come about because we have a reasonable marketing system in this country.
We heard the government side suggest this morning that there are a great deal of environmental concerns. It stated several countries of the world that overfertilize, that create all kinds of problems on the land by overfertilizing, overusing pesticides and herbicides which in the long run are going to destroy much of the agricultural land they are using.
With supply management systems we have found that Canadians are becoming most effective. They are becoming very environmentally sound and in our country today we use far less fertilizers than many regions of the world. We have become efficient to the optimum level. We have been able to look at those problems, do the proper research, and ensure efficiencies in the industry.
Because the farm community is operating in marketable systems and management systems that are produc-
Supply
ing a very solid agro-industry in Canada, probably the most stable part of Canadian agricultural industry, as consumers we should be quite ready to support it, realizing that it is to our benefit.
The previous speaker from the NDP suggested that Mr. Whelan, a colleague, a very good friend of mine who comes from southwestern Ontario and who was a former agriculture minister, stated that the strength of agriculture is really the strength of our country. We must realize that when we support the agro-industry, when we support the food industry, we are supporting the consumer in this country. We are supporting safety and all the good things we can think of within self-production.
We must remember that second to the manufacturing area, in particular the auto industry, agriculture is one of the largest industries in this country.
If I go on and start looking at who is operating management boards, I would see Canadians who are serving Canadians, Canadians who are buying products from other Canadians who produce food, Canadians who are buying pesticides, herbicides, using Canadian energy, paying Canadian taxes, paying financial institutions in this country, buying at every commercial enterprise in this country. They are Canadians who support Canadians. They are Canadians who pay taxes. They are Canadians who do what this country needs to survive, and that is generate and produce a tremendous amount of business in Canada.
I look on it from the government's point of view, this House's point of view, that if we do not protect the farm industry this country loses a tremendous amount of business which cannot be reclaimed.
When I look at article XI, at the protections we need, I realize that we must make certain that our programs are maintained very strongly.
I ask myself: Why is the United States not interested in defending our supply management system? I know that Canada is not going to have a major impact on people in the United States. Our supply management systems have been designed to serve the Canadian public. They have been designed to make certain that we as Canadians receive the benefits.

Many statements have been made today, but the most important part is that we must make certain agriculture survives.

I want to take this opportunity to express my appreciation for the excellent work done by one of the artisans of this attempt to save our country, a man I admire because he respects Quebec, the Right Hon. Joe Clark. I am happy to announce that on October 10, I will have the honour and the privilege of receiving the Right Hon. Joe Clark in Laval at a dinner organized in co-operation with the Laval Chamber of Commerce. At this dinner, Mr. Clark will speak on the Canadian Constitution and have an opportunity to dissipate any fears-

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance.
The government keeps saying that we are out of the recession, but on every front the economy is reeling: grain farmers, fishermen, Imperial Oil, Consumers Glass, small business and now 4,900 jobs at risk at de Havilland.
By tomorrow night American threats to our forest industry which employs almost one million Canadians could be felt throughout the nation.
Does the Prime Minister have a promise from the President that the United States will not take action again Canadian softwood lumber producers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:

We have served notice in the appropriate fashion as is our right under the provisions of the MOU. Obviously the U.S. will be contemplating whatever action it may or may not wish to take.

I would suspect that we will have an indication as to whether or not it will take any action with regard to this later on this afternoon, at which time we can respond in an appropriate fashion.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister. This government's economic policies have already crushed Montreal's economy. Now the Canadian forest industry is being crushed by high interest rates. Softwood exporters are being crushed and the workers have the right to know whether or not the Prime Minister has obtained a formal guarantee from the President of the United States that there will be no punitive tariff on softwood exports. Did the Prime Minister obtain a commitment from the President of the United States on that or not?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated to the hon. member the process which is contemplated and is followed under the provisions of the MOU. Whatever action is taken or contemplated would obviously have to be consistent with international trade law and we will have to wait and see if in fact there is any action contemplated by the United States administration. If action is taken, the Government of Canada will respond as necessary and appropriate.
In regard to her allegation on interest rates, Mr. Speaker, interest rates have declined by 560 basis points, that is 5.6 per cent since the high of May last year. I am sure the hon. member would find it pleasing to note that the bank rate dropped another 13 basis points today.
Mr. Speaker, that is obviously too little, too late, for more than a million Canadians who are trying to find work.
Hear, hear.

Six years ago the Prime Minister said this in the House about the great deal on de Havilland:
We want to make the best deal for the Canadian taxpayer, secure
those jobs and that technology in Toronto and that is what we have
done.
I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister what he has to say today to those 4,900 workers who have been
Oral Questions
sold out by the policies and the trade actions of this government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is really unfortunate that the hon. member cannot stand good news. We have had four consecutive months of growth in the economy after a recession that was more severe than we expected. I remind the hon. member that Canada is not the only country that has experienced a setback in economic growth.
Canada is emerging from a recession, recovery is on the way, we have had a growth rate of 4.9 per cent in the second quarter, we expect growth to continue in a moderate way, we want that growth to be sustainable, and we want it to be achieved with price stability.
That is our goal, Mr. Speaker, and we are on the right track.

Mr. Speaker, I too have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday, the Minister for International Trade told this House, about the lift of the surtax on softwood lumber, and I quote:
It is our judgement that there will not be a 301.
We heard that the Americans are threatening to retaliate today or tomorrow. Here is my question: what contingency plan does the government have in place to prevent yet another disaster from crippling the Canadian lumber industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member has evidence that the United States is going to take action under 301 perhaps he would like to produce that evidence for the House.

Mr. Speaker, I was asking the Deputy Prime Minister if the government had a contingency plan in order to counter what the Americans may to do tomorrow afternoon.
During the free trade debate this government told Canadians time and time again that we would get secure access to the U.S. market. The memorandum of understanding on softwood lumber violates the spirit of the free trade agreement.

October 3, 1991
Oral Questions
Again my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Did the Prime Minister get a guarantee from President Bush that his administration would respect the spirit of the free trade agreement and would not take punitive action so as to not totally destroy the Canadian lumber industry.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member asks a hypothetical question. His first question asked what the government would do now that the United States imposed an action under 301. I asked him if the United States was imposing an action under 301 to give us the evidence. Hon. members on that side of the House want the United States to engage in imposing a countervail or a 301. We chose not to.
I should also remind the hon. member that under the free trade agreement we do have secure access, and furthermore we have a binational dispute solving mechanism that puts Canada on a fair and equal footing with its largest trading partner.

Mr. Speaker, a final supplementary. I am perfectly prepared to table these documents today. What this government does not seem-

Today the Canadian Federation of Independent Business released a survey which showed that more than one-third of small businesses in Ontario will be considering moving their operations to the United States, putting at risk more than 500,000 jobs.

Oral Questions

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I can help the hon. member in correcting his interpretation of the news release I have in my hand which says that: "Startling results from a current survey reveal that more than one-third of the small business sector in Ontario, 36 per cent, report that they are considering moving all or part of their operations out of the province, thereby putting at risk, 500,000 jobs". speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
When the softwood lumber tariff memorandum of understanding was brought in by this government in December 1986 the Social Credit government and the Prime Minister said the deal was great for Canada and B.C.
Their enthusiasm for this sell-out of our forest industry cost thousands of jobs, particularly in B.C., Quebec and northern Ontario. speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is aware that the MOU was not considered to be a permanent fixture. It was put in place to ensure that appropriate offsetting measures could be instituted and most important, so that any countervail or duty would remain in Canada.
I think it was a logical move and a logical step in the right direction. We now sense that conditions are normal, that trading patterns should be resumed on a normal trading process and we think the time for the MOU to expire has come.
We believe we are on solid ground, and whatever action the United States may or may not take, we can respond in an appropriate fashion based upon international trade laws.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley Valley):

October 3, 1991

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext:

October 3, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):

speechtext: Now the facts. Of course bonuses are a complex issue and I am not surprised-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Revenue and it pertains to the matter of cross-border shopping.
In the past when the minister has been asked in this House about the effect of the GST on cross-border
shopping, he has stuck to the increase in the number of trips that Canadians have been making across the border, which have increased in and of themselves, but has never gone to the heart of the matter which is how much more Canadians are spending when they make those trips.
Statistics Canada collects that kind of information. The information we have is that those figures show there has been a dramatic increase in the actual spending by Canadians, something in the neighbourhood of 57 per cent.
I want to ask the minister if he has seen those figures and, if so, why does he continue to talk only about trips and not tell Canadians the whole story about how the GST has affected cross-border shopping.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am surprised at that question coming from an hon. member who knows better. Statistics Canada hands out all the facts, all the statistics and we on this side of the House, as opposed to some members on the opposite side, support those statistics 100 per cent and talk about them.
The last time this issue came up in the House, Statistics Canada made it very clear that the introduction of the GST played a minor role, a very minor role, in the increase of cross-border shopping, both in terms of trips as well as in terms of dollars.
We consider cross-border shopping as a very serious problem. That is why we are working with the provinces, with the private sector, with labour, with the Retail Council of Canada, to move in the right direction that would make Canadians more competitive and allow Canadians to shop in Canada rather than south of the border.

Mr. Speaker, if the minister is so confident in the Statistics Canada data, would he undertake to instruct Statistics Canada, or to have the appropriate minister do so, to publish all the figures so that we can compare oranges and oranges, and apples and apples, first quarter with first quarter, last quarter with last quarter, spending with spending, trips with trips, and all the things we need to know in order to make a true measure of what the GST is doing to cross-border shopping instead of having the minister get up and selectively cite statistics with respect to trips and not with respect to over-all spending.
October 3, 1991

Is it the government's intention also to provide the provinces with additional taxing powers or alternatively additional federal funding in order to allow them to continue on the national housing programs within their own jurisdictions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member will know, the proposals for constitutional reform have as one of their main themes the rationalization of the operations of different levels of government to ensure that services are provided by those levels of government closest to those being served and at the present time most of the housing services themselves are being provided by provincial and local governments.

speakerposition: subtopic
Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Communications. In the
Oral Questions
past, the minister vehemently denounced federal propaganda practices in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Yet today he is in power, and we are witnessing the CBC recycling old directives from 1978 with respect to the constitutional debate. They are now asking journalists and media people to apply a double standard, that is, on one hand, to emphasize the benefits of the status quo, and on the other, to denounce the costs and consequences of constitutional reform.
For the sake of freedom of information and so, the real Canada can show through, is the minister prepared to immediately withdraw that directive reminiscent of the witch hunts of the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the CBC has one responsibility and it is to ensure that its reports are completely accurate and that its comments made are fair and impartial. That is their mandate and that is what they do.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. If the minister has bothered to read the Corporation's directives, he will know that they are applying a double standard: on the one hand, the reports must emphasize the advantages of federalism and, on the other, they talk about the costs and drawbacks of constitutional reform. Can the minister, who should have a sense of fairness, not see that there is a double standard, that it is not right, and that it is not in accordance with the criteria that he just defined himself? Should he ask the CBC to do away with this procedure that is totally unacceptable in the 1990s?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the responsibility of the CBC, whether the French language arm or the English language arm, is to ensure fair and accurate coverage of the news and of public affairs. That is its duty. It is one it discharges with distinction. Throughout the whole of the constitutional debate that is the direction in which it will be going. It is obligated under the Broadcasting Act to do precisely that.

October 3, 1991
Point of Order

speakerposition: subtopic
Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, will the government House leader share with members of the House if there is any movement with regard to the subject matter of conflict of interest in terms of what the government intends to do in terms of an all-party committee which may be struck in order to further examine ways in which this particular institution, as well as the Upper House, may be monitored pursuant to the conflict of interest guidelines?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have put proposals to the opposition parties as well as to the other place for the establishment of a joint committee of this House that would take the subject matter of a conflict of interest bill that was before the House in the previous session, as well as taking it upon itself to examine how this issue was handled in other jurisdictions such as the United Kingdom and other nations with political systems similar to ours.

It would be my hope that this committee could look at that and come back with recommendations that would be tantamount to a bill that we could put before the House and deal with this matter, hopefully with some degree of finality.
The government does not come to it with a fixed position in mind other than recognition that we are all members of Parliament and members of the other place in a situation in which we must satisfy our publics that we recognize the requirement that conflict of interest be dealt with and in a formal, legal fashion. Beyond that we would await the advice of that committee and except for keeping the natural obligation of having the Department of Justice examine and write the bill so that it stands up to the legal requirements of our system, it would be my hope that in essence the House of Commons and the other place in committee would provide the fundamentals of a conflict of interest position that we could all agree to.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, would the government House leader just perhaps elaborate. I am not asking for a fixed commitment, but in the discussions of this particular subject matter, assuming that a bill would be tabled by the committee itself on the subject matter, would he explore the real prospects of perhaps having on that particular piece of legislation an opportunity for members to exercise their rights and remove the party lines in terms of our whips and have a free vote on the subject matter on the floor of the House?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, clearly the question of party lines only comes to play when you are talking about an initiative from the government and very specifically this initiative would be from Parliament. This question of how it is handled is something I certainly will look at in discussion and I do not come to it from a perspective of assuming that it is going to be a government bill, quite the opposite.
This issue affects all of us equally on both sides of the House as members of Parliament and we have to, somewhere between the two extremes, assure that there is absolutely never a conflict of interest nor apparent
Point of Order
conflict of interest, and somebody has even suggested nowadays the standard is a possible apparent conflict of interest or, on the other hand, a situation in which it is recognized that conflicts of interest are a part of life, but that they should be open and obvious so that people can make their judgments as to whether that conflict of interest has caused the member to act in an inappropriate fashion.
Between those two extremes perhaps we can find some accommodation that will meet the standards of Canadian citizens and enable this House both to operate and to ensure that we can attract in future quality men and women who are needed to ensure a successful Parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have one final question for the government House leader. I wish to thank him for his intervention. I wish to offer to him that we would be favourably disposed in terms of the way in which he has outlined a process in terms of the conflict of interest. My colleagues from Ottawa-Vanier, Kingston and the Islands and our critic from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell would certainly want to be very involved in that particular process.
I am wondering, since I have got the government House leader's attention, if he has given any thought to the prospects of the committee which will review the subject matter including members who are Independent members. I know that he cannot include them all. We would have members from the three main parties, but there are also Independent members in this House.
I think to be fair to Independent members, wherever they come from, whatever region of the country they come from, we might want to try to involve them in the process as well so that there will be a complete legitimacy of Parliament working on a subject matter which has profound consequential effects on each and every member in this House, and likewise in the other House.
Would the government House leader entertain that possibility?

October 3, 1991
Point of Order

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have no difficulty with that suggestion whatsoever. If this is going to be successful, it will provide for input from everyone who has an interest in the subject in this House.
My only qualifier is as one balances off representation and so on one gets to a size of committee which becomes unworkable. As Parkinson said, once a committee passes 20 it effectively goes into the control of the executive of the committee. To make sure it is a group that can work I would like to have the committee small enough so that it can be effective and that everyone who has an interest in it has an opportunity to participate. I am sure we can work out the modalities of that.

Madam Speaker, the questions from the House leader of the Official Opposition are welcome on this topic. I enter the debate only to say that I seemed to hear the House leader saying that in order for something to be considered as the object of a free vote, it would have to be seen as not being part of the government's agenda but coming from Parliament.
If I recall correctly, the conflict of interest legislation and the proposal to do something about the lingering problem of conflict of interest was in the throne speech and was therefore part of the government's agenda and part of the platform on which the government seeks to curry support among the Canadian people.
I ask the government House leader to consider, because I know he has commissioned a paper in this regard with respect to free votes, that it is not only those things which are seen as coming from Parliament, somehow independent of the government, but also maybe some things which come from the government that may be subject to a free vote of the government's own members. That, it seems to me, is the direction in which the debate about free votes is going.
It is not just a question of private members or things that do not originate with the government but about giving government backbenchers some freedom with respect to a wider range of government proposals, which up until now at least conflict of interest legislation has been.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is an interesting subject and perhaps we should set aside a day some time to explore it further.
My interest in this regard in the comments I made to the House leader of the Liberal Party was to reflect merely the fact that for conflict of interest legislation to be effective, if that is what results on the recommendations of the committee, it should reflect the views of the House and not the views of the cabinet.
The problem we have dealing with the notion that the hon. member talks about is our adversarial system. Any time a government proposes something, the opposition feels obliged constitutionally to oppose. May I humbly suggest I welcome the day when the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party participate and take responsibility for some of the positive actions that occur and not simply be in the position of opposing everything.
For example, the hon. member's party and others have been suggesting we should be providing help to farmers, fishermen, and those in need. I agree and I look forward to the day when they stand up in the House and say they agree to raising taxes to fund these activities.
That will be the kind of co-operation from both sides of the House that will make this institution work in a way that the public of Canada would appreciate.
A point of order, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will recognize the hon. member in a second. I would just suggest to members that we are getting into a debate which is not on orders of the day.
I am the servant of the House, but I wanted to remind members of the time and that some members have asked for the floor to render a tribute to a departed parliamentarian.

Madam Speaker, I am sorry that what could have been a useful preliminary discussion about free votes was turned into a sort of partisan opportunity by the House leader.
The fact is, and he knows this well because he has been here longer than I, that there have been occasions in which governments, opposition and third parties have agreed on things. He knows also that this discussion about free votes is one that we want to have precisely so that we can get out of the adversarial system which he laments and yet which he just employed in order to avoid answering the question I put to him.
October 3, 1991

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
With due respect, I did not avoid answering the question at all. The hon. member talked about why I think it is appropriate to proceed in this manner for conflict of interest and why I think a free vote situation is appropriate.
I am trying to suggest that if the government sat down, wrote up a conflict of interest bill and brought it to the House constitutionally the opposition becomes opposed to it. That is the way we operate. That does not mean at the end of the day that it is not supported.
The role of the opposition is to criticize, point out weaknesses, et cetera. I am saying that on this issue in particular perhaps we could work together since we are all in it together and at the end of the day we could vote in that fashion.
You are right. I have a paper coming on free votes. We are committed to proceeding in that direction as a government and more will be happening in that regard.
I also have to say that free votes is not at the root of excesses in our adversarial system. There are other things and we need to look at those as well.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a last comment. I believe my colleague from the New Democratic Party has said it well. I have attempted to say as well as to the government House leader that there is a disposition now, as we viewed from the comments of my colleague from the New Democratic Party, to sit down and discuss the process, the intricacies of this particular matter, in terms of conflict of interest for members of Parliament.
I think it would be a good beginning. I want to thank hon. members to my left, as well as the government House leader, for entertaining some of the suggestions that we have made. We look forward to further discussions later this week, perhaps, and early next week so that we can consummate something on the subject matter before too long.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: THE LATE SENATOR HAZEN ROBERT ARGUE

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Gustafson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: THE LATE SENATOR HAZEN ROBERT ARGUE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to rise and pay respects to the late Senator Hazen Argue.
Tributes
Senator Argue served the area that I served as a member of Parliament and I remember with a great deal of appreciation, especially his kindness to me as a new member of Parliament.
Senator Argue served his country for 43 years. That is a long time. He was always a defender of the farmers. If I may add a personal note, I recall being chairman of the task force on drought and shaking in my boots facing 1,500 farmers.
Senator Argue rose and he really broke the ice. I will never forget what he said. He said: "The experts told you farmers to buy more land. The experts told you to buy more machinery. The government told you this and it was my government that did it". The farmers just broke up.
He was always very kind to me as a new member of Parliament. He served the people well. He defended his constituency, and to Jean and the family we send our sympathy and the respect of the government for his long years of service to Canada.

subtopic: THE LATE SENATOR HAZEN ROBERT ARGUE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada, I rise to join in the tribute to the late Senator Hazen Argue and extend, on behalf of my colleagues and myself, our deepest sympathies to his wife Jean and members of the Argue family.
It is true, as the hon. member just said, that Senator Argue had a remarkable sense of humour and a very warm welcome for anyone he met. He served bravely and courageously the people of his province and Canada and helped promote a better understanding of the legitimate aspirations of Western Canada among people from various regions of the country.
I had the privilege of serving with him in Cabinet under the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau. On several occasions I had the opportunity to hear and appreciate the strong stand Senator Argue took in Cabinet on behalf of Western farmers and the people of Western Canada in general.

October 3, 1991
Tributes
Just recently, with Senator Fairbairn I had the pleasure of paying him a last visit in hospital while travelling in Saskatchewan. I will treasure the memory of this visit because, even on his hospital bed, his death bed, he kept showing his love of life, a remarkable joie de vivre. He had remained very clear-headed, in fact I noticed that he was still monitoring what was going on here, on Parliament Hill.
That is why, I am sure that, had Senator Argue been here today when the hon. member for Lambton- Middlesex put a motion concerning Canadian farmers, he would have risen with those of us who beg the government to do something to rescue the Canadian agriculture and protect Canadian farmers in the GATT negotiations in Geneva.
I think, Madam Speaker, that we are not about to forget Senator Argue and his contribution to Canadian life and politics.

subtopic: THE LATE SENATOR HAZEN ROBERT ARGUE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on behalf of the New Democratic Party to speak in remembrance of Hazen Robert Argue, a man who was born, raised and educated in Saskatchewan.
He was a graduate of the University of Saskatchewan in agriculture and farmed at Ormiston. He was first elected in 1945 at age 24 to represent the CCF in the riding of Wood Mountain which later became Assiniboia. At the time he was the youngest MP ever elected.
I first met Minister Argue, known as "Blazin Hazen" to his constituents, at a district meeting of the Farmers' Union in southern Saskatchewan in the late 1950s. I was there with Roy Atkinson, a young vice-president of the union who later became president of the NFU.
That part of Saskatchewan was suffering from a drought and infestation of grasshoppers. Those topics dominated the meeting and one of the people who came and spoke very eloquently was Hazen Argue, the local member of Parliament.
Mr. Atkinson and I were joined at lunch by Mr. Argue. Conversation turned to agricultural policy and the future of agriculture, not the dismal immediate future but the
long-term hope for farming and farmers and things that could be done.
A long time later, in the summer of 1984, I remembered again my first conversation with Mr. Argue. My last long conversation was in the summer of 1984 when the same three people met by chance in the airport in Toronto. We were all awaiting flights out to the west and we got talking. Mr. Argue had just been let go from cabinet. Our conversation again turned to the shortterm dismal future of agriculture. It was a drought year again in southern Saskatchewan. The same long-term hope and unreasonable optimism that pervades Saskatchewan farmers' conversations came out. I remember just before he got on the plane, the last thing he said was: "Well, I hate to be kicked out of cabinet, I hate to lose the job, but it gives me a chance to go home and watch the grandkids grow". It is to those grandkids and their fathers and mothers, the two daughters and the son and their spouses, and especially to Jean that our thoughts go today.

subtopic: THE LATE SENATOR HAZEN ROBERT ARGUE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too would like to add my personal sympathy to Jean Argue and her immediate family and her extended family.
When I first came to Ottawa in 1979, whether it was in caucus or in other meetings, Senator Hazen Argue was one of the first people to come, extend his hand and welcome the new members, and I will never forget that.
I saw the greatness of the man when we were passing the western transportation bill, known as the Crow bill. We spent a lot of time in Saskatchewan. I see my colleague nodding his head across the aisle here. We travelled through the small towns and talked to individual farmers and big agricultural organizations. Everyone knew Hazen Argue and everyone had something positive to say about Hazen Argue.
I know that he will go down in history as making his mark on the growth of this country. My personal contact with him remained even though I was defeated. Senator Hazen Argue still kept in touch. He still had a special interest in members who were newly elected here and he was always there to offer a guiding hand.
October 3, 1991

Again I extend my sympathy to Jean and her immediate and extended family. He will be missed and he certainly made his mark on this country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: THE LATE SENATOR HAZEN ROBERT ARGUE
speechtext: I wish to thank hon. members who took part in this tribute, and I would also like to offer, on my own behalf and on behalf of all members, our sincere condolences to the bereaved family.

stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Ferguson (p. 3200).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will recognize the hon. member, but I had to check whether the member who had the floor at 2 p.m. was still in the House.
Resuming debate, for ten minutes. The hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel.

Madam Speaker, in the 1970s it was Liberal governments who created marketing boards to protect Canadian farmers and, at the same time, ensure that Canadian consumers would have access to an abundant supply of high quality farm products at competitive prices.
It is important to recall that one of the greatest achievements of the Liberal government was the creation in 1975 of the Canadian Dairy Commission. Some
16,000	Quebec farmers annually receive a guaranteed income under this program.
Over the years, the program was refined and improved, and it became so popular among farmers that the Tories decided to renew the program for five years. Unfortunately, the program's continued existence may be at risk as a result of the current GATT talks. The government has not only failed to defend the interests of Canadian farmers, it is also, as was explained this
Supply
morning by the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex, trying to hide the truth.
The Prime Minister and his Minister of Agriculture are looking the other way, while the Minister for International Trade is selling out Canadian and Quebec farmers in Geneva.
Quebec farmers who put their trust in the Prime Minister must realize he could not care less what happens to them. I think this is quite clear if we consider the question put by my colleague, the hon. member for Gatineau-la Lievre, on September 24. The hon. member asked the Prime Minister, and I quote:
Given that the survival of agriculture, especially for joint plants in Quebec such as the one for the dairy industry, is based on the principle that production costs will be taken into account and farmers will have a reasonable income, can the minister or the Prime Minister assure farmers that this essential criterion will always be maintained for our farmers?
The Prime Minister's answer was, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend wants to know whether there is anything in the proposals tabled this morning to -
He stopped, and then went on.
If the question is whether we will maintain our previous programs in spite of the document tabled this morning, the answer is yes.
The Prime Minister was referring to the tabling of the document on constitutional reform. I realize the Prime Minister may be totally absorbed by the constitutional question, but that is hardly a reason for assuming the hon. member for Gatineau-La Lievre was talking about the constitutional proposals, not the GATT talks, and answering that the constitutional proposals had no connection with the problems of Quebec's dairy farmers.
To help the Prime Minister, I prompted: "It isn't about this morning's document, it's about the GATT talks". Then he made a quick recovery and said, at page 2633 of Hansard and I quote:
My hon. friend from Papineau, who is also an expert on agriculture -
-those were the Prime Minister's very words-
- tells me that this issue is mainly up to GATT That being so, I would be pleased to answer a supplementary.
So my colleague from Gatineau-La Lievre did ask a supplementary question:
The Quebec farmers' union, the UPA, is very concerned about their future because the Minister of Agriculture is always talking about productivity without considering production costs. That concerns them and they would like to have an answer about it.

October 3, 1991
Supply
Here is the Prime Minister's answer:
Mr. Speaker, productivity applies to everyone. But mentioning productivity in no way undermines the ability of the UPA or its members to meet the competition that they face now. Nothing was said or done to keep farmers in Quebec or elsewhere from maintaining their production.
The Canadian government-
-this is the gem-
-will try to find new markets for them.
Very clearly, the Prime Minister did not know what he was talking about then. Very clearly, he misled the hon. member for Gatineau-La Lievre, although unintentionally, I think, by telling him about something completely unrelated to the GATT negotiations because, as my colleague from Lambton-Middlesex said this morning:

"If the government supports Article XI, which allows countries to limit imports when they have a system of production designed to meet only domestic needs, why are they now concerned with finding new markets for dairy farmers? The answer is simple". And I quote my colleague: "I do not believe they intend to support article XI at the GATT. Why else would the dairy farmers need the government to find them new markets?"

Obviously, as my colleague rightly says, the government has absolutely no intention of protecting farmers and supporting Article XI; otherwise, the Prime Minister would not make an issue of finding new markets for milk producers. And come to think of it, where will we sell the wheat, butter and all the dairy products that are already in such oversupply? One of my colleagues said, "Eastern Europe". They already produce those things over there; they do not need our Canadian production. Europe has a massive surplus of these products. I will remind the hon. member that we already imported dairy products from Poland. So we cannot send them over there; they can send us some here. We must product the markets that we have in this country.
What is serious-and I conclude with this-is not just that dairy farmers are threatened by the GATT negotiations in Geneva, but also everyone at the egg, chicken
and turkey marketing boards. If the government does not fulfil its responsibilities and does not properly defend the interests of its farmers in Canada and Quebec, the whole future of agriculture is in danger. That is why I am pleased to speak in this debate and to support the motion of my colleague from Lambton-Middlesex.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I missed the beginning of the speech of the hon. member for Papi-neau-Saint-Michel who, on top of being an expert on agriculture, as the Prime Minister mentioned, is the Liberal critic for External Affairs.
Could the hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel tell me how he perceives the European countries which, as regards the GATT, are more inclined to support an American proposal on tariffication? Tariffication, is a new buzz word in the GATT negotiations.
Also, is the hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel aware that Canada, as a member of the GATT, finds himself in a rather lonely position in his fight with the farmers, with the agriculture ministers, and with the president of the UPA, who is presently in Europe? We reassured him. We want to keep the supply management system for milk, eggs, poultry and other products. However, as a central state and a member of the GATT, we must obviously also think of the grain producers and other goods that are not subject to quotas.
Is the hon. member aware of that? What would he do, today, if he was taking the place of the Minister of Agriculture in Geneva, at the GATT, as regards this concept of tariffication? Would he be rather in agreement or in total disagreement with the European countries who want to support the American position concerning tariffication rather than article XI of the GATT?

Mr. Speaker, obviously once again the US government is dictating its will to the government of Canada. This time, they would want us to believe that, while the European countries might be prepared to make some concessions, they will do so at the expense of their own national farming industry. I can assure the hon. member that the French, German and Italian farmers will have their governments stand up for them.
October 3, 1991

The question right now is who is defending who? The government of Canada, instead of always obeying the orders of the US government and be its puppet, should stand up at the GATT negotiations in Geneva and protect the interests of Quebec farmers and all Canadian farmers.
In response to the question of the hon. member, this tariff approach could work in Europe, but not at all for the Quebec dairy producers. Once the Quebec farming industry will have gone belly up, it will be too late. The hon. member and her Prime Minister will have failed to fulfil their responsibilities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel, is a smart politician indeed and very good at dodging the question. I will ask him again. The Canadian government is facing problems with the GATT, we must live up to our commitments regarding contingency but, at the same time, it is our duty, as a government, to protect non-contingency production. In that context, when we seek to strengthen Article XI of the GATT agreement, we come up against new difficulties relating to the export of non-contingency products.
We have made it clear, Mr. Speaker -and I might add that our jobs are at stake, as someone mentioned earlier-that we will protect the Canadian farming industry. There is no doubt about that! But would the hon. member tell me how he can reconcile the two when the European countries would prefer instituting a tariff policy rather than strengthening Article XI of the GATT, which is our choice as a country?

Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that at the current GATT talks the Canadian delegation is now on the sidelines.
The talks took the turn they did because today, interests other than the interests of Canadian farmers have prevailed. I want to repeat to the hon. member that even if she proceeded to name all the reasons the Europeans have given, this would do nothing to advance the cause or the interests of Canadian farmers.
I would prefer to see her over there, explaining what has to be done to protect Canadian and Quebec farmers, than listen to her here in the House, trying to convince us that the Europeans are right about their new tarifica-tion. Go tell them Quebec farmers won't buy it!

Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe my ears!
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in the debate today on the opposition motion that the government "must immediately provide Canadian producers, operating within these supply management sectors, firm assurances that it is seeking and will continue to seek the strengthening and clarification of article XI of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade".
First of all, I feel I must comment on what was said by the hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel. I was not impressed when he told us that the interests of Quebecers were not safe with the Prime Minister, especially when we consider how safe they were when the hon. member's party was in power.
We won't get into that today, but just the same, the record was not impressive.
Mr. Speaker, what my hon. friend opposite fails to understand and may not realize, is that the whole strategy and the proposals tabled at the GATT talks were developed by the agricultural sector and the government. The proposals were approved and the offer made to GATT, on that basis. I think it is wrong to say that the interests of our farmers and producers are not being defended as they should be, since our producers were involved in preparing these proposals.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps it would be useful to comment on what the government has done in the past few years to cope with current and future challenges.
I agree, Canadian agriculture is facing unprecedented demands, but it is also being offered a wealth of new opportunities. Never before has there been such tremendous pressure for change and adjustment. In response to these pressures, in 1989 the federal government, in co-operation with the provinces and the private sector, launched the most exhaustive study of agro-food policies and programs ever undertaken in the history of Canadian agriculture. We have worked very hard on clarifying and revising the rules of international trade under GATT.
Canadian agriculture must maintain its position at the forefront of this sector, both nationally and internationally. The changing tastes of consumers, advancing technology, the globalization of markets and environmental concerns made this review necessary.

October 3, 1991
Supply
We did all we could to avoid a dialogue of the deaf and set up a vast nationwide consultation process to include governments, farmers, everyone involved in the food chain, and of course consumers and other interest groups in setting the framework for a national agricultural policy. We therefore asked all participants to put their ideas on the table, to put their differences on hold, to say what they thought and to listen to what the others had to say. They were then asked to see the process through with us. And I wish to assure you that we have no intention of going back on our commitments.
Thus the federal and provincial agriculture ministers agreed in July on a series of decisive measures for the future of the agri-food sector at their annual meeting in Kananaskis, Alberta. These changes, from second-generation supply management systems to increased industry participation in agriculture policy development, will begin the next stage of the Canadian agri-food policy review.
The systems now in place are viable and can be effective, but they will have to change to improve. They must be more market-sensitive, more independent and more responsive to regional diversity. Supply-managed sectors should design and operate their system while respecting the environment. Supply management policies must help and not hinder the development over time of a more competitive sector.
Canada's international trade policies must continue to allow us to operate our supply management systems effectively. With this in mind, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government took concrete action by tabling a proposal in Geneva in March 1990 to strengthen and clarify article XI of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, GATT.
We wanted, among other things, to define precisely what effective government control of supplies meant, to determine the products eligible for import quotas on the basis of their manufacture, in whole or in part, from a fresh product whose domestic supply is controlled, to clarify the administration of import quotas and to impose export limits on products subject to supply management when import quotas apply to the same products.
Last October, after consultation and receiving support from the industry and provincial governments, the Canadian negotiators tabled legal wording to be included in our GATT proposal.
Well, Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of State for Agriculture, Mr. Blais, told the press a few days ago, Canada has not changed its position on article XI of GATT one iota. The government has promised to defend vigorously the Canadian supply management systems and we remain just as determined to do so.
In fact, Mr. Blais is presently in Geneva. Earlier, our colleague was blaming us for discussing this motion in the House instead of being in Geneva to negotiate. Well, we have our negotiators and our Minister of State, Mr. Blais, is presently in Geneva where he will meet, among others, the GATT Director General and Chairman responsible for negotiations on agriculture, Mr. Dunkel, to discuss those negotiations.
The minister will then go to Paris where he will meet Mr. Jacques Proulx, the president of the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec, to discuss the state of the GATT negotiations.
Also, the Minister of Agriculture, Mr. McKnight, met yesterday with the European Community commissioner for agriculture and rural development, Mr. Ray Mac-Sharry. They discussed the multilateral trade negotiations, including the desastrous effects of the subsidy war on the Canadian agri-food industry. The minister also stated Canada's firm intention to seek re-enforcement and clarification of article XI of the GATT, as well as ensuring a fair implementation of the GATT rules on agricultural exchanges.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, this government does not intend to leave anything to chance, nor does it sit on its laurels or rely on others to protect the interests of Canadians abroad.
In the document on Canadian federalism and economic union that was made public last week, the Government of Canada proposes that article 121 be updated in order to facilitate the mobility of people, of capital money, of services and of goods within Canada, by prohibiting the federal government and the provinces from passing legislation or implementing programs or practices that would create obstacles or restrict such a mobility.

Some think that the marketing boards are threatened by such proposals, since those boards would be a barrier restricting the circulation of goods and services. I want to emphasize here that the marketing boards serve other purposes regarding the foreign markets. Any amendment to the clause dealing with the common market must not be detrimental to the equalization programs or regional development, nor to any program classified as an exception by Parliament in the national interest. In short, we are saying that the national interest will prevail and that we are intent on using that clause in the case of marketing boards. It is also in that perspective that the Castonguay-Dobbie Committee was set up by the government. This committee will study every aspect of the Canadian economy so as to ensure that, after adequate consultations, the decisions made will be based on the national interest.
To demonstrate its support for marketing boards, the government intends to give second reading to Bill C-16, which seeks to amend the Agricultural Products Marketing Act. These amendments would give provincial marketing boards and other agencies additional powers to enable them to have a more concerted approach and thus improve the marketing of their products on interprovincial and international markets.
We know how important the supply management system is to the dairy co-ops in Canada. Its implementation enabled us to stabilize the economy of that sector and to ensure an adequate supply of high quality dairy products to Canadian consumers, at affordable and stable prices.
I am almost finished, Mr. Speaker. As regards the Canadian dairy policy, this government took, in 1985, the necessary measures and will keep working in the same fashion.
I am convinced that, through consultations, we will find ways of making more competitive those sectors where the supply is regulated. There is a vast consensus on the need to change the system. Working groups on the dairy and poultry policies, as well as independent studies made by consultants, have all come to that conclusion.
So, Mr. Speaker, allow me, in the few minutes that I have left, to simply reassure the Canadian producers and in particular the producers in my riding of Joliette, about the firm intention of my government to continue in the direction that it has been following for at least two years,
Supply
to cooperate with the agricultural industry and all the stake holders in order to set policies and strengthen our external policies-the proposal is being examined today at the GATT-, and to ensure that our producers will be adequately protected within our contry, while at the same time having access to external markets.
It is very important to protect them-we know that, we see it and we know what the Western producers are presently going through because of the war between the United States and the Europeans, in particular the French-and it is precisely in order to improve their fate that we are working, at the GATT, to create a much more lucrative and appealing market.We must put an end to this impossible and very harmful price war throughout the world, while at the same time protect our marketing boards and our producers.
Even though we hear all kinds of comments to the contrary here, I believe that our producers-in fact we had the opportunity this week to meet several of them- are aware of the initiatives taken by Canada and they support these initiatives. There is no doubt that we will continue to work towards that goal, and we hope to get our position accepted in this country and at the GATT. Our position is very well balanced and would guarantee brighter days to our agricultural producers.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment my colleague. Since his time ran out or so he thought, I would like this House, the Canadian people watching us and above all the farm producers in our ridings to hear him again.
The member for Joliette comes from a most prosperous farm area where tobacco growers have experienced certain problems in recent years. However, I am sure that the vitality of the growers will see them through these hard times. Could the hon. member tell us how producers, at the local farm board level, are reacting to this new threat regarding GATT tariffs? What Canada wants instead, what we want as a nation, Mr. Speaker, is the strengthening and clarification of article XI of the GATT agreement to prevent dumping of foodstuffs in Canada. We want to put and end to the unstable economy of our producers who have worked so hard to build a system for themselves these last few years. They work very hard, but at least they are guaranteed an income at the end of the year.

October 3, 1991
Supply
I would like the hon. member to tell us what we have been done these last two years to try and convince the European producers, the Americans, in fact all GATT members, that Canada has interesting policies which they should take as models and establish marketing boards in their countries and strengthen article XI of the GATT agreement.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for her very interesting question. I think that we are going through a period of major changes, and our farmers' concern is quite legitimate. We have long felt the threat to our marketing boards. We recall the last election campaign when our farmers told us that they were very worried. Free trade with the Americans was the issue, but in fact the real threat was related to article XI of GATT
Since then, we have worked and they know our position very well. We intend to spare no effort to protect a system that has served us well and should continue to do so. As I said not so long ago, we developed our whole strategy together, to make them more confident and especially to inform them of everything we intended to do. Together we developed the strategy to work out a proposal which, as I said, is very well balanced and should reassure them to some extent.
Of course, we are negotiating as one country among hundreds; we cannot expect our whole policy to be accepted and we are very well aware of the war now going on between the Europeans and the United States. We know that it is not easy. We spared no effort, we worked together. It was just mentioned that Mr. Blais was to meet Mr. Proulx in France tomorrow, I believe. We are working together. I think that in this way our farmers should be reassured and that we will see it through together. And I find it somewhat regrettable today that it has become a partisan debate in which it is suggested that the government is not doing everything required to protect farmers properly.
I think that instead of getting into a partisan debate, we should-I think that this is not the time for division. This would be the time for all parties to join with farmers and everyone concerned in agriculture to defend our interests. It is not a war between farmers and the government; it is an extremely important process for the future of our agriculture with foreign countries. I think
that if all parliamentarians and the farming community join together, we will be in an even stronger position to have our position adopted. It is very well balanced and could ensure prosperity for Canadian agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, this is an extremely timely and important debate. This motion is necessary because agricultural producers are losing confidence in this government.
What does the motion seek? What it seeks is very important. It seeks assurances from this government that it will do everything possible to support article XI of the GATT, that it will seek clarification of that article, and that it will seek strengthening of that article.
The motion seeks those things from the government because the very livelihood and the very future of supply management, the very future of dairy and poultry producers in this country, depend on the outcome of the GATT negotiations.
Let the record make it absolutely clear that if Canada caves in on article XI we will lose our dairy producers. We will lose our poultry producers. We will lose our egg producers. It is as simple as that. It will be the beginning of the end of an absolutely thriving and very successful industry in this country, an industry that will measure up against any other industry anywhere else in the entire world.
But the people who are in these industries are worried. They are sick of the possible prospect of the government caving in. That is why they are so worried and they have every reason in the world to be worried. Because, after all, we have to remember who we have over there in government. We have a Tory ideology that really does not believe in supply and management, a Tory ideology at the very base of all this that does not believe in orderly marketing.
I remind you, Mr. Speaker, and you will know this very well, that there was a resolution before the Progressive Conservative convention in the city of Toronto just this past summer. It was a resolution seeking support from supply and management and it went down to defeat. It went down to defeat. Little wonder the poultry producers and the dairy producers in this country are worried sick.

I do not have to remind you of how this government sold out Canada in the trade negotiations with the United States, the famous free trade negotiations. It sold us out. It sold us out. There is a lot of reason to believe that it will cave in again.
Oh, I know government members have given us assurances. They have given us assurances they are going to do their best. They are going to work hard and do everything to defend and strengthen article XI. But can we believe them? The Americans want to get their hands on article XI and want to destroy article XI. They want our market. Unfortunately, ever since we had this Prime Minister going back to 1984, every time the White House says "jump", the Prime Minister asks: "How high?" Whatever George wants, George gets.
How did we get the GST? How did the GST get its name, the GST? George said to, George said to. That is how the goods and services tax got its name.
We have a supply management system that is working extremely well. But if we were to cut out article XI and go for this tariffication system proposed by the Americans, the fact of the matter is our producers could not compete. There is no way they could compete.
Our producers have input costs that are much higher than those of their counterparts across the line in the United States. I just have to mention things like fuel, labour and things like that. The input costs are much higher on this side of the border.
Let there be no mistake about it. We have to preserve the industry. We have to preserve it. It is rather ironic that we are expressing concern for the industry at this particular time, because dairy and poultry are the most successful segments of our entire agricultural industry. They are. They are the most productive. They are the most stable.
Here we have on the other side of agriculture, grains and oilseeds in a lot of trouble, in a lot of trouble. We are trying to get help for them. Yet on this side we have dairy and poultry doing very well, thank you, and it is possible that the government may cave in and give the industry away. Does that make sense? I do not think it does.
This industry is extremely productive. My colleague from Lambton-Middlesex, who probably has as much
Supply
expertise on this subject as anyone in the country, was pointing out this morning-and I want to point out again-that since 1971 the productivity in the dairy industry per cow has gone up 73 per cent compared to only 46 per cent in the United States and 3.5 per cent in the European community.
You can say the same thing for poultry. There is better egg production and they certainly have a better handle on disease control than their counterparts in the United States, a lot better. This is a productive and efficient industry. It is an industry that gives consumers quality, quality.
My colleague from Broadview-Greenwood was asking this morning in some of his remarks, and rightly so, what is in this for the consumer. He has a riding in Toronto full of consumers. I have a riding in Winnipeg full of consumers and I can understand a consumer's point of view when they say: "Well, what about this industry? Are we not already paying a lot in the way of food?"
Let me point out that when it comes to our disposable income, we spend about 11.5 per cent on food. We are probably about the second best country in the entire world when it comes to spending a portion of our disposable income, 11.5 per cent, on quality food.
Let me go on, because I know there are consumers who wonder about certain prices. Let me point out some prices to you. During the 1980s the cost of a box of corn flakes went up almost 100 per cent, about 94.5 per cent. The cost of a box of soda biscuits went up by 235 per cent, sweet cookies went up 135 per cent and cereals went up 194 per cent. As my hon. colleague points out, when those prices were going up, skyrocketing like that and the consumers were feeling it, what was happening to grain prices? They were going down. Farmers today are living with grain prices that their grandparents lived with back in the 1930s.
When the consumer looks at prices on the store shelf and expresses concern, and understandably so, do not blame the farmer. Do not blame supply and management. Those prices skyrocket after leaving the food processor. Those prices skyrocket after leaving the farm gate.

Supply
I just want to mention a couple of other points. The price of a litre of milk, for example, in the province of Ontario at the farm gate since 1980 has gone up 19 cents per litre. On the store shelf the price of a litre of milk has increased by 73 cents a litre or 97 per cent. I could go on and on and on comparing the prices that farmers and producers get with the prices that consumers have to pay, and over and over again the proof is there, that you cannot blame those consumer prices on the farmer. If there are unreasonable price increases, look at the people in the middle. That is where you should point your finger of blame.
I think I am running out of time. I just want to say over again that it is absolutely paramount for the future of supply management and the producers who work under supply management that we hold on to article XI. We remind the government that it must go to the wall on this article XI. It cannot be a party to any agreement that will cut out article XI.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are saying-and I know the member is fully aware of it-that they are tired of highly partisan debates on subjects like this very important one.
Maybe if this House was made up of 50 per cent women those highly partisan debates would not take place. We would discuss strictly what is going on.
The member is suggesting that the majority of the members on this side of House who represent rural ridings in Canada are not supporting farmers.
This is a nonsense debate. I have to say this, Mr. Speaker. The Government of Canada is trying to strengthen article XI against the world. We have certain countries, but the Uruguay round now has its mind directed to new ideas of tariffication. We are opposed to this. We want to strengthen this and we need the Liberal Party behind us to support our farmers, not to say out of the blue that we are not supporting farmers of this country. The facts are there and I want the member to recognize that.
We are not perfect people, but we are there. We are trying to help. We need the members of the Liberal Party and the NDP to say to the world that article XI is needed. We deserve it and we want it to protect the farmers of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. parliamentary secretary for the question.
I find it passing strange that at the very time when this government's agricultural policies are failing and agricultural producers in the country are losing confidence in the government, the parliamentary secretary pleads for understanding. She pleads for a non-partisan debate. Give me a break.
Here is a government that has been asked for months to provide emergency aid. Here is a government that promised farmers that it would tide them over when they moved from the old ad hoc system of payments to GRIP and NISA. Government members made a pledge and made a promise to farmers that they would fill the gap. They have not honoured that pledge and they have not honoured that promise. Why should we have any confidence in this government? The other thing is that the government reached an agreement with the United States in the FTA. There is an article in there which in effect says that each country would not raid each other's grain markets. The Americans have done it with their Export Enhancement Program. They have done it over and over again. What does this government do? Absolutely zero, zilch, nothing. It pretends the Americans do not exist or it pretends that the Americans are not doing anything. So why should we have any confidence in this government? The polls tell us that the Canadian people do not.

Mr. Speaker, I must thank the member for Broadview-Greenwood for letting me go ahead of him. The reason is that I have a wife and four children I promised to meet in 15 minutes. He has been very kind to let me go ahead.
We are debating my party's opposition day motion to the effect that article XI of the GATT in regard to supply marketing systems should be strengthened and clarified during the current Uruguay round of GATT negotiations.
Let me, perhaps foolishly, attempt to state briefly the essence of this issue to the supply managed sectors of Canadian agriculture: industrial milk, eggs, chickens and turkeys. It is true, speaking as a westerner, that many of our producers in the supply managed sectors live in central Canada. But in 1989, the year for which I could obtain the figures, western Canadians had the following national market shares of our supply managed sectors: chicken, 24 per cent; turkey, approximately 28 per cent; eggs, approximately 34 per cent; and milk, 20 per cent.
October 3, 1991

There are, for example, about 5.6 million broilers in Alberta and 5.2 million broilers in B.C. Manitoba, the home of the member who just spoke, has about 2.5 million laying hens and B.C. has 2.8 million of the same.
In short, the supply managed sectors of our four western provinces provide a decent and stable living and reasonable consumer prices to thousands upon thousands of western Canadians.
In essence, article XI2 allows for the existence of farm marketing boards in a country without violating the provisions of the GATT.
My understanding from the most knowledgeable Canadian expert on trade matters, a former GATT negotiator on the Tokyo and Kennedy round negotiations, is that the current Uruguay round of GATT negotiations will in all probability soon result in the removal of article XI from the GATT. If so, in consequence our provincial and national supply management boards will soon fold for violating the current GATT.
The trade expert friend to whom I referred a moment ago assures me that in reality, the long-term viability of most of these various boards, provincial and federal, has already been dealt a fatal blow by the particular wording of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. Canadian food processors are increasingly relocating to the U.S. where most food products can, for a variety of reasons which were mentioned by the member who just spoke, be bought more cheaply than here and then exported back to consumers in Canada through retail food outlets.
If however GATT removes the article XI exemption, the present cabinet in Canada can attempt to blame the GATT member nations for the demise of our marketing boards, which will be a veiy misleading conclusion to draw.
Why, one might ask, are the GATT member governments, approximately 100 of them, now likely to approve the removal of article XI?
