In essence, it appears that both the current U.S. administration and the European community member nations have no further interest in keeping it on the books, so to speak.
The U.S. government dislikes supply management on ideological principle grounds. My trade friend believes
Supply
that the European community member governments have simply and finally-one might say it sure took a long time-had enough of seeing 75 per cent of the European community budget go each year to the Common Agricultural Policy, CAP.
A constellation of other interest groups in Europe, environmentalists, workers needing retraining and poorer European community members like Portugal and Greece have recently carried the day. Wealthy farmers on the Paris plains and others have simply lost the campaign to maintain the European community's megasubsidies on agricultural production.
The good news for the world, really, is that a very large GATT agricultural deal is in the works. It will be the biggest agricultural deal since 1957. It is likely to be announced shortly, thereby saving the current Uruguay round which, as everyone knows, has become beached on the agricultural rock.
My trade expert friend believes that a 35 per cent cut in the European community support prices for cereals which will bind the GATT and an over-all drop of about 35 per cent on export subsidies for agricultural exports are coming very soon, within a matter of weeks.
A new and better arrangement on GATT dispute settlements is also likely to emerge. There might also be a framework agreement on services. I remind you, Sir, that about 64 per cent of Canadians work in the service sector, so that would be a very good thing.
In short, it will be a minor or a major GATT miracle with good results for all but our supply managed and much abused farm communities.
I would answer with this. Today in Canada each farm family across the nation feeds approximately 65 nonfarm families. That is in the parliamentary secretary's riding. It is in virtually every riding in the country which has farmers.
For virtually all of our farm families across Canada outside the supply managed sector, one or more of the spouses are required to work off their farm to feed their own families. Is that not disgraceful?

October 3, 1991
Supply
Somebody put it very well recently. "Our farm fields of dreams", she said, "have become acres of despair". Those opposite, if they run true to form with respect to article XI will see our remaining healthy sectors under supply management reduced to the squalor that affects so many other sectors.
Shame on those opposite who represent in this place the views of a few thousand wealthy residents primarily of Toronto and Montreal.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the now Liberal member who used to be a PC member in this caucus knows very well that the Progressive Conservative government of Canada supports farmers, is there to help farmers, and that the actual third level of revenue systems is on its way to being dealt with.
It takes a certain amount of time I know, and I am fully behind the farmers in western Canada. I remember when I sat on the agriculture standing committee that one day farmers from around Regina said to me that because of the despair and the low revenue of the farmers, family violence was emerging from among the agricultural sector which was not there before.
I was very concerned about this, given the fact that the farmers of this country are family oriented people. The emergence of family violence is a damaging factor.
I want to ask the member this. He is speaking about non-contingency agriculture that absolutely needs to export. On the other hand, Canada is faced with the reality of a supply management market which deserves to be kept in place because it helps. We know the difference.
He pointed out very well that if you are in agriculture in a contingency situation, you work as hard as the others but you are in a better situation than if you are not. This is one of the realities and I want to ask the member what should we be doing now to have both realities of farming in this country.

Mr. Speaker, with all due respect for the hon. member opposite, I think that she seriously misunderstood what I said.
I said that there is presently a crisis in the non-contingency sector across the country. I wish she had come along, just a few days, when I campaigned for the Liberals in Saskatchewan. She would have seen the
poverty, the hardship and the distrust of the farmers of this province which is so important to us.
Since the hon. member is from Quebec, I would like to quote some figures regarding her province, if I may, Mr. Speaker. Of the 300,000 farmers across Canada, there are 41,000 in Quebec. They represent 26.4 per cent of our farm population, but own 40 per cent of the Canadian dairy industry, with their 500,000 plus dairy cows.
In Quebec, as she certainly knows, there are 3.8 million chickens and 15 million broilers. So, how can she be telling her constituents, from the riding of Oka I believe, that if my friend and myself are right, she will give these farmers another chance at a decent income and having a decent standard of living?
I know that she just loves the Canada-United States trade deal. I used to be a member of her caucus. Is she under the impression that farm products regulatory boards are better than FPAs? That life is getting easier for these farmers and her constituents? I think that, in all honesty, she will have to say no, Mr. Speaker. She must tell her constituents and that this trade deal has been a disaster for thousands and thousands of farmers in Quebec.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, listening to opposition members makes me think that they must surely pray to the Lord every night to sit on the opposition benches when the time comes to make difficult decisions. They must surely be glad to be on the other side and always contradicting what the government does.
I asked the hon. member what he would do if he were sitting at GATT in place of the ministers who have to protect two agricultural sectors, one subject to quotas and the other not, in a world that exports, that buys and sells. Could he give me in writing his vision of what the minister could defend at GATT?

Briefly, Mr. Speaker, I would tell her to read the motion we are debating today.
I think the reality, Mr. Speaker, is that those groups, as I said, who represent the opinions of the wealthy in Montreal and Toronto, must understand one thing: they are eliminating the protection as such for farmers in Quebec and the rest of Canada, first, because of the trade agreement with the United States, and second, with its position on GATT now-which is not stated publicly, of course-but because of its position in GATT now in the Uruguay Round.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of participating in this debate. In my riding of Broadview-Greenwood there are very few people who really understand what supply management is all about. I will take the words of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services when she said earlier in this House today that she felt uncomfortable that we seemed to be taking a partisan approach in this debate.
I have been listening to the debate since my colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex started earlier today and quite frankly I did not detect that tone of partisanship that she referred to. I have not detected anything in this House today that would suggest that we on this side of the House do not share the commitment that I hear from the government side today that it wants to keep the current supply management system in place.
In fact, earlier in the day I rose and addressed the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, the member for Huron-Bruce. I complimented him on the hard work he has done not only in his riding but throughout the world. I have been with this man when he has travelled and worked on behalf of Canada and I think he has done a terrific job.
What we have here in this country today is a genuine crisis of confidence. Also, there is a feeling out there that politicians in general are not trusted, not just politicians on the government side, politicians on this side.
As my hon. colleague mentioned this morning, this round of GATT we are heading into is an historic round. It is going to be a very complex round. We are in the middle of one of the most vicious trade wars that has ever happened in the history of the world.
When we have farm rallies coast to coast, the likes of which we have not seen in many years, it would be absolutely irresponsible for us on this side of the House not to put forward the views of all of those constituents who are concerned about the resolve of the government, concerned about whether or not it is going to take a firm stand. They are concerned about that because there have been incidents in the past where the trust that the government has been given has been shaken.
Supply
I am not saying that trust given to Liberals in the past has also been shaken, but we are not talking about the past right now, we are talking about the present, and we are talking about a very important up and coming meeting.
Our responsibility on this side of the House is to make sure that the French, Germans, Italians, and everyone who is present at that round understand that it is not only the position of the Government of Canada but it is also the position of the opposition that we want the current supply management system to be in place and we are in fact united on that point.
The other point that we have to raise in this House is the fact that this is not just an issue for those people who actually live and work on the farms. In my riding there are over 300 restaurants. The restaurants in my riding are the primary employer. They employ not only on a full-time basis, they employ on a part-time basis, and we depend on quality food, security of supply, and on stable prices. Make no mistake about it, Mr. Speaker-
I'm hungry.

The hon. member for Laval-Est just mentioned that he is hungry. Whenever you are in Toronto, you are welcome in the riding of Broadview-Greenwood, Queen Street, the Danforth Drive. Please come. You are welcome.
Whenever I get a chance to speak here today on national television, I am not too shy about promoting my riding and the great restaurants that we have. You are all welcome.
The bottom line, Mr. Speaker, is this is not just a rural issue. This is an issue for those people who live in urban areas. As I mentioned earlier, last January when I had the opportunity to speak at the Soviet-U.S. citizen summit on the environment, and I was there for a few days, I had some spare time to walk around Moscow and visit some of the grocery stores. We in this country cannot imagine the desperate state that the people are in in terms of food supply in a place like Moscow. They start lining up for their food supplies at seven o'clock in the morning.

Supply
It was embarrassing for me to see senior citizens with their brown sacks lining up for food. What was more embarrassing was to go into these stores and see the quality. Never mind the fact that the supply was virtually limited, it was the quality.
We in this country are blessed with not only quality food, we are blessed with security of supply. We are also blessed with the second best food prices in the world. That is something that we take for granted.
We take for granted the life of someone who lives on a farm. How many people have ever thought about what it is really like to live on a farm? In Toronto the only real reminder that you have about what a farmer's life is all about is if you get up early in the morning, and some mornings I get up early, and turn on radio station CFRB, which is one of our larger stations. At five o'clock in the morning you hear the news for the first five minutes and after that, for the next 10 minutes, you hear the farm report.
That is the last you hear of it. Why? Because a farmer gets up at five o'clock in the morning. He works until six o'clock at night. He works seven days a week. Very rarely do they get a day off. Then they have problems like lack of rain and, therefore, the crops are in trouble. Too much rain and they have got a problem. Try and find people today who want to work on a farm.
We in this country have, I believe, one of the finest farm systems that exists anywhere in the world. One of the reasons why we have that farm system is because our farmers have had a system that has allowed them to produce quality food with stable prices. We as Canadians have benefited from that from all walks of life, from all regions of the country from coast to coast, to coast.
I cannot believe that anyone in this House or anyone in this country does not believe that we as a country must have an image, must have a strength to show that we are a nation that measures our strength by the mouths we feed, not only here but all over the world, a nation that measures our strength at the same time by the environment we protect.
I want, and I have less than a minute left, to try and give one constructive piece of advice to the Government of Canada. It said earlier today that it is going to the GATT round committed to keep the supply management system in place. I mentioned this last week to the Minister for Grains and Oilseeds.
It is no good to communicate our problem just to those officials and just to those politicians who attend that meeting. Go over the heads of those officials and go over the heads of those ministers of agriculture and go right to the people of Europe. Take some of that money out of the envelope that is promoting Canada's 125th birthday and put it into communicating some of the concerns that we in this country have and some of the necessary things that we have to do in terms of protecting our environment with farmers, not only in Europe but here, so that we can get through this crisis together.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood for his excellent remarks. As an urban member, he has taken a very deep interest in agriculture. We really appreciate that because this debate has taken on a new tone of interest in both urban and rural Canada, and that is precisely the way the issue should be.
My hon. colleague talked about his restaurants and the quality of their food and of course the production of food within Canada generally. He realizes that in order to keep up this quality and quantity of product, we are going to require great negotiating skills as well as negotiating tools in the present GATT rounds. Therefore, some things become very important.
In terms of skills, I have not heard too many compliments in the House today about the way this issue is being handled. Second, with regard to negotiating tools, the Minister for International Trade, as was so aptly put forward this morning by the hon. member for Lamb-ton-Middlesex, stated that each nation participating in the GATT round had to submit the amount of money that was being spent on programs to support agriculture in the various countries, and $8.8 billion was submitted as the figure going into agriculture and government programs here in Canada, a totally inflated figure, and then $2.2 billion going into the dairy industry of Canada. That is another totally inflated figure.
I want to ask the hon. member who has just spoken: if we are going to win this debate, why are we giving away tools such as that? Why are we inflating those figures? Surely we are providing an argument for the other countries to use against us. Has the government not shot itself in its own foot on behalf of the agricultural community of Canada?
October 3, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I wish I had an absolutely sure reason why the government seems to from time to time play gymnastics with its figures. I really do not have the answer to that.
It seems to me that part of the reason why we have this tension in the country today is that if we play gymnastics with figures too often, the trust factor breaks down. That is probably the greatest reason why we have a crisis today, not in terms of just the agricultural community, but in every other sector. There is not a sector of our economy today that does not feel the lack of trust. Trust is the central issue now in public life. Nothing else really matters.
I believe that because of the intensity of this debate today, we are saying to the government that we trust you so that when you go to these GATT rounds in the next short period of time, you will live up to the commitment you made in this House today, and you better not come back with an empty basket.
I repeat, I believe that if we can send a signal to people that we want to be a nation that measures our strength by the mouths we feed not only here and abroad, but also that we are a nation that is concerned about our environment, I believe that if we put that message into the GATT negotiations, we can maybe put pressure on some of those European countries which are ignoring some of those environmental regulations.
Maybe we can get them on focus, and that will put a more balanced approach to this agricultural problem.

I have received written notice from the hon. member for Trinity-Spadi-na that he is unable to move his motion during private members' hour on Friday, October 4, 1991.
It has not been possible to arrange an exchange of positions in order of precedence pursuant to Standing Order 94(2)(a). Accordingly, I am directing the table officer to drop that item of business to the bottom of the order of precedence.
Pursuant to Standing Order 94(2)(b), private members' hour will thus be suspended, and the House will continue with the business before it prior to private members' hour.

Mr. Speaker, I am very
Supply
pleased to rise in the House today and speak in full and complete support of the motion put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex.
The member and I go back many years in both politics and agriculture, more years than I would like to admit to, and I am proud to support the motion of the member whose riding borders on mine in southwestern Ontario.
This morning the hon. member from Elgin-Norfolk in debate and in answering questions-I did not have the opportunity to question him-stated that he had replaced the Hon. John Wise who was then Minister of Agriculture. He referred to the hon. minister as the finest agriculture minister the Progressive Conservative Party ever had. He was a gentleman, and I support those views 100 per cent. In the riding of Kent we always held the Hon. John Wise in the highest esteem. I remember the hon. minister making a statement that if the marketing boards were ever to weaken he would resign. In September 1988 the Hon. John Wise resigned.
Later today I hope to get the opportunity to ask the hon. member for Elgin-Norfolk that question. This time, I am speaking on article XI of the GATT.
As everyone involved in agriculture is aware, the current GATT talks will in large measure determine the future of farming and marketing boards and supply management as we have known it in Canada. The director general, Arthur Dunkel, has fixed a wheat deadline to produce a final framework. A complete GATT package should be reached in early November.
The vast number of subsidies for agriculture by the European Economic Community is the main stumbling block. The EEC proposes to cut internal support by 30 per cent over a 10-year period while considering to increase markets by only 3 per cent.
The EEC countries will not accept a complete elimination of support or even a 70 per cent or 90 per cent reduction for which the United States is calling. Canada wants 100 per cent elimination of all existing export subsidies over a 10-year period.

Supply
The real issue on all these complex negotiations is our government support of supply management. Is it firm? As my colleague for Lambton-Middlesex has outlined, he believes that a deal has been reached that would include the tariffication of article XI of the GATT.
This would have serious negative effects on supply management in Canada. We have the best marketing systems in the world and nothing should jeopardize Canadian agriculture.
Supply management is based on three fundamental pillars: import restrictions, adequate price and production control. Our supply management system must be maintained and improved by the GATT talks.
Our system has brought stability for both producers and consumers. Canada's egg, poultry and dairy producers firmly believe that any final agreement not meeting that bottom line should be rejected.
Given that the government says it is committed to its supply management system in Canada, does the government recognize that to be viable and effective border protection is needed to ensure that imported products do not undermine our own production or returns?
As well, we must have firm border protection while allowing us to export. The inspection side of Port Huron, Michigan is staffed 100 per cent by full-time inspectors. What is the situation on the Canadian side in Sarnia?
A neighbour of mine and of the hon. Speaker was turned back at the border by Dr. Brown from the department of agriculture who was a vet for the U.S. government. This returned load cost the farmer $3,000 in losses. It was strictly a sham, in my view. I was talking to the doctor and I asked him if Carla was giving him a little trouble over the free trade agreement and GATT. He said: "No. The law has been there since 1907 and I am just upholding it". It is things like this that we are running into at the border.
I am meeting with some farmers in my riding this weekend to discuss the GATT. They want a chance to compete fairly with the support of the federal government. One is the chairman of the Kent Dairy Association and his group.
The issue of tariffication is one of the major stumbling blocks to a settlement. The proposed tariff equivalents would not offset the price advantage of American products. Tariffication would not limit the import of supply managed products. With no specific limit on the level of imports, it is impossible to run a supply management system at either the federal or provincial level. Tariffication for supply managed commodities would damage the entire Canadian economy.
As the agricultural industry goes, so goes the whole Canadian economy. Production would decline in most, if not all, regions in Canada as family farms are forced out of business. Our industry must be protected since the cost of an operation in Ontario is much more than a similar operation in Michigan.
I know that in my operation, in corn alone, it has a net of $90 to work with that that I do not have. I am not competing on a level field. Another example is the difference in interest rates on a 10-year mortgage, $14,690, a difference in favour of the U.S. farmer of 22.4 per cent.
U.S. gasoline is $1.35 plus a 10 per cent annual rebate for using gas that is 10 per cent ethanol as an environmental measure. Farm delivered gasoline in Canada was 54.9 cents a litre. The difference is 61 per cent higher in Ontario.
Fertilizers are 20 per cent a tonne higher in Canada. Dairy feed supplements with 40 per cent protein cost 73 per cent more in Ontario.
What about machinery parts? A package of six Case International French bottom plough points cost $115 in Emmett, Michigan. In Exeter, Ontario, the same points cost $143.70, a difference of 24 per cent. I am the same distance from Emmett, Michigan as I am from Exeter.
Our agricultural industry is vitally important to our nation. Too often people go to the grocery store or eat in a restaurant and think the food is magically produced. Our farmers are the bedrock of Canada and they are not getting a fair return for their efforts. A box of corn flakes is nearly 100 per cent corn, and yet the farmer gets only 14 per cent. That price last evening in an Ottawa store was $4.89.
October 3, 1991

A box of wheat crackers has increased in price at the retail level by 235 per cent between 1980 and 1989, but the value of the wheat in those same crackers is down 43 per cent.
If supply management is damaged by the GATT negotiations, Canada's dairy farmers could face a direct loss of $143 million in internal support plus $75 million in import protection for a total of about $218 million.
Farmers right now are being faced with Mother Nature and historic low prices. A Chrysler bought in 1949 when wheat was $2.85 a bushel was $2,800 and change. Today with the price of wheat 1,000 bushels will not put the tires and wheels on that car.
The farmers in my riding certainly know of the government's lack of support. On the Kent-Essex drought situation, the feds should join with the provincial government in transition funding until the next crop year.
Our poultry, egg and dairy industries must not be pawns in the GATT talks. The government has talked a good line and has said it supports the strengthening and clarification of article XI. We hope that it will not back down. Canadian farmers are worried about their future with GATT and with the free trade deal as double whammies hitting the agricultural industry.
All of us in this House support an end to the subsidy war. I am sure members from all parties hope for a successful resolution to the article XI question. The farmers of this nation deserve a fair share of the Canadian food dollar, an income that will allow them to survive and continue producing the highest quality food, not only for the people of Canada but for the opening markets of the world.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was pleased by the tone of the speech of the previous speaker, the member for Broadview-Greenwood. I hope he will listen to my comments.
I want to urge the hon. member for Broadview- Greenwood, whom I know is a very successful businessman, to join the Standing Committee on Agriculture because it is important for other sectors of the economy to participate in the debates relating to agriculture. He noted, in a good manner, that the business people in this
Supply
country need to keep alive the supply management concept that this country is part of.
I want to say to the member who just spoke that this is a reality for the caucus members as well. I know, Madam Speaker, that you are a member of a very successful agricultural community. You will be inclined with me to say that never will any member of this caucus, the government that I represent, support any suggestion or attempt to withdraw, dismantle or do anything that will hurt or affect the supply management system in this country which protects the revenues and the lives of thousands and thousands of Canadians. We simply will not support that, Madam Speaker, and I am sure you will agree with me.
I want to ask the member if he is aware of this new tariffication system that the rest of the world is trying to put in place during those GATT negotiations and, if so, does he agree with it?

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for her question.
I am as aware of the tariffication in other parts of the country as I am aware of free trade in other parts of the country and as I am aware of the GST in other parts of the country, which have all been the downfall of those areas. We as Canadians look to other countries for guidance. I do not know why we always pick the worst part of every country's programs. Here we are with tariffication and we are going to let other commodities come into Canada and completely decimate our crops.
I have been impressed by the questions of the hon. member this afternoon and of the different members here in the House. I was hoping that in future she would join us over here. She seems to be a real fighter. I certainly would appreciate having her on our side.
I am aware of the question. The answer is that it would be the start and ruination of article XI. It would eat away at it within five or ten years. It would completely wipe out our marketing boards.

Madam Speaker, I just could not let this pass by, and I don't know how I am going to finesse this question through you back to my colleague. I could not let that compliment go by from the member for Argenteuil-Papineau. Through you to that hon. member I would just like to let her know that she was so generous there today that she has an outstanding invitation from me to come to my

Supply
riding and I would be happy to take her to dinner on the Danforth.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before we resume debate I would like the House to allow me to thank the hon. member for Elgin-Norfolk who was kind enough in his position as a member of the panel of committee chairman to preside over the debate this afternoon for an hour while I was attending other duties. I know everyone has been quite kind to him and I thank you all very much and I thank the hon. member very much.

Thank you, Madam Speaker and colleagues of the House of Commons. It is indeed a pleasure for me to engage in debate and discussion on what is no doubt a very, very important situation facing Canadians. Let us be honest, when it comes to agriculture, other traders in agricultural commodities, even our neighbours to the south of us I think find the subsidy war a problem. A war is really what it has become with regard to agricultural products.
Let me make some comment on the proposal put forward as an opposition day for discussion. In my view, it is healthy that it was brought forward in such a manner because it does allow all sides of the House to discuss this matter and put our positions on it. If I read what I have heard so far correctly, there are not a lot of differences of opinion on this matter before us today. The argument, I suppose, is should one of these other parties be in power today they would do a far better job, or the fringe parties that would like to govern this country, whether they are in Quebec or in the west, would be able to do a far better job of dealing with this serious situation we are confronted with.
Can you imagine Preston Manning, for example, going out and solving a problem on a policy which he adopted directly from the Conservative platform? Read what was said in this House just last week by the member for Beaver River, who chooses not often in the country to debate the agricultural policy. As I read it, when examining the policy of GATT and the problems with agricultural subsidies, that group states: "The Reform Party recognizes that there is a need for transitional support to protect agricultural producers". With the dilemma we face right now with $2 wheat, you would think that the Reform Party would be at every one of those western
rallies of farmers who are demanding some action by the government. In reality, the Reform Party does not go as far as this party does in terms of finding solutions to those problems, which we have demonstrated in the past.
I find it quite amazing that the Reform Party seems to have a solution but in fact it has none. They use these funny little platitudes such as "well, when the price of these commodities come down in this country and that country, we will get out of our problem". That is not solving a problem, that is sitting back waiting for something to happen.
I am going to jump around a little bit and I am going to go back to May 1986. In 1986 our Prime Minister was in Tokyo. While some splinter parties were dreaming up ways of electing members to the House of Commons, our Prime Minister was dealing with one thing and it is probably the first time in a long time that under the G-7 our Prime Minister of Canada convinced others that agriculture and its concerns of trade are very important and should be dealt with. In an interview he said: "In an interview we decided, as you know, how important it was to raise agriculture and for the first time as a group,"-this is the G-7-" the heads of government focused on the paradox of preaching freer trade while pumping billions of dollars into subsidies for agriculture.
This topic dominated our discussions yesterday afternoon and today on the economic side.
Protectionism is damaging to everyone and especially to the poor countries which depend on agriculture almost entirely for their livelihood. Canada has been obliged to take some actions but to try and even match others, as I indicated to our colleagues at the summit, for Canada to even attempt to match the magnitude of subsidies elsewhere would savage the government's deficit reduction efforts".
I think we could even probably go further and I think we could say that in this House of Commons on those in the House elected, and not those who would like to be from some of these fringe parties, there is no way that the government could match the subsidies on agricultural products that have been put forth by Europeans mostly and subsequently by the Americans trying to beat them out on some of the trade they once had.
October 3, 1991

I think there is probably a consensus in this House that that is the fact. From time to time opposition members have stood up in this House criticizing this government for too little too late. I can recall in 1986 and 1987, $1.2 billion, $800 million, those kinds of figures of money were put at the agricultural problem, we were saying too little too late.
Whether it is $1 billion this year, or another billion next year, it seems like we have not addressed the problem and the argument put forward is that we would be stronger at GATT.
We want you to stiffen up your back.

Okay, I heard from the hon. member that we want to stiffen up our back. Listen to what was said here yesterday. Canada threatens retaliation over EC's farm subsidies. Is that not stiffening up your back?
Let me just quote this: "London. Agricultural minister, William McKnight, warmed his European counterpart yesterday that Canada will retaliate if there is still no resolution in sight to the trans-Atlantic grain subsidy war by the end of the year". It goes on to say: "I didn't put it forward as a threat. I put it forward as a fact".
I would think all members in this House would applaud the strength that this government has put into changing the GATT. This is it. This is the kind of thing that they thought this government never had the guts to do but it is doing it. Let us just go back, not because of this resolution, just a few days ago to September 30. Here is another news release. "The federal government", and you have all talked about it, you have all admitted it is there, you could not reaffirm it from your side any more than we could on our side, "is firmly committed to negotiate an agreement which protects our supply management programs".
Nobody has denied that, except a fringe party that would like to rule this country, the Reform Party. It does not even want supply management programs.
The issue is trust. I suspect there is an element of people that think this government is going to sell it away. There has never been any evidence given to date that we intended-
Not sell it, give it away.

Give it away. There has never been any evidence, Madam Speaker, that this government intends
Supply
to give that very fundamental part of the agricultural scene away to anyone. In fact, minister after minister and, year after year, our Prime Minister said that very thing in this House.
Let us go back to another news release. This is not so long ago, the hon. Minister of Agriculture: "I want to underline to Mr. McSharry the disastrous effects the subsidy war is having on the Canadian agrifood industry". He points as straight a point as anybody else could make it. One would argue that if you looked at the New Democratic Party.
Would for example the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca have been able to make a stronger case than our Bill McKnight did? I doubt it.
How about the Leader of the New Democratic Party? Is she not, that wonderful charming lady, a forceful individual? I rather doubt that it would have happened any better than under this government with the importance this government places on this very issue.
Here we have a government that defends the right of marketing boards supply management and at the same time attempts to find some sanity in the trade war. It is a trade war.
It was that party resolution that caused the problems.

Somebody mentioned it was a party resolution that caused this event. Do we realize how many times we would need to have days in the House to discuss party resolutions if we looked at the resolutions of the New Democratic Party? Would they fly in the face of this House? The same is true of resolutions of the last Liberal convention. Would it even think of introducing them as a party in this House? Likely not. Those are realities that from time to time a party does put before its general membership and asks for an opinion.
They don't mean anything.

They do mean something. I know the member is baiting me. Do they mean anything? I suppose they mean as much to the Conservatives as they do to the New Democrats or as they do to the Liberal Party. It does not get a real airing. They do not not get a debate, some of these resolutions that we have. They do not get the same debate as they clearly do in the House of Commons. You have given it a whole day.

October 3, 1991
Supply
The point is, the debate is healthy because it draws attention internationally to the concerns we collectively have as a people in our farming community of the total damage this does to our agricultural sector. The European common market, which we all sometimes admire as a collective organization, is not without its problems internally with respect to this very subject. I suspect lately if any members have had the opportunity in this House or you, Madam Speaker, as I know from time to time you meet international bodies and delegations, to talk to the Europeans and ask them about the French farmers within the EEC and whether they are prepared to play on the same playing field as they are with their member countries, you would find that there might be a little war brewing over in Europe on this veiy subject hoping that they can still maintain their trade balanced within each other's respective communities.
There are no simple solutions. There is a desire to get the international community to really look seriously upon us as by far the fairest traders in agricultural commodities. I can also say to my colleagues in the House that we demand fair trade among European countries with our products, yet we do not even have free trade within our provincial boundaries.
That has got to be part of our whole constitutional change as was proposed by this government. Maybe it needs to be altered, but I am saying if we want to say to the Europeans that we are totally free traders, then we should eliminate the trade barriers that exist between the provinces. They distort natural market productions and market forces which would make our products even that much more competitive on the international scene.
I would wonder if the New Democratic Party has a position on the interprovincial trade barriers. I would be interested to know its comments on it. As a way of unifying our country I think that is a major step we have to make.
While this debate is important, I think it is pretty fair to say that the policies taken by this administration in this particular area need very little criticism. It may be up to some criticism. I think if we look at the amount of moneys that the government over the years, as long as I
have been elected to this House, has applied to agriculture, it has not been insignificant.
At the same time, it has not solved that international problem. The Reform Party quite flippantly says: "Oh, we will just have to get them to all reduce little by little and we will all be wonderful children at this big, international family. We will be a very happy group of farmers and agricultural exporters, and our economy will boom and grow."
Where is Preston Manning when we are having a dilemma with farm demonstrations? Where is he? He is in Atlantic Canada on a little fishing boat floating around. He never dared show his face at an agricultural meeting. That group wants to quickly reduce any funding going directly to farmers because they have this funny, secret little formula.
The member for Beaver River does not show up at a farm rally to find out how she can help the grassroots. The new Reform Party for those of you who do not know wants to represent grassroots.
My friend from Winnipeg knows very well that you have to be within the ridings to understand what people are saying, especially if you have little agricultural background. You cannot go around looking at wheat fields and saying: "Isn't this terrible?"
When there is a demand to do something, you have to come up with a policy. I admire the member for Winnipeg St. James for attending farm rallies. He may not have always said the right thing, but you have to listen to what farmers are saying. You have got to be there to form an opinion and his opinion may not be the same as mine in terms of finding a solution, but for goodness sakes, he goes to the meetings.
We have a new party in Quebec that is going to solve all the problems of Quebec. I have never heard one of them talk about concerns they had for the farmers in the province. There is no imagination, there are no ideas. By listening too much to the splinter groups deciding what the future of the country will be will fracture any concrete decisions that the government has to take.

While this is a very important consideration that is put forward as a proposal, it is not so much a proposal but a reassurance that those supply management boards will stay. I believe we made our case to the Europeans; that it is not on the table. I as a former farmer-
As a former alderman.

My principal business now is politics.
As a former farmer, I am very well satisfied that in fact those situations as have evolved in Canada and were set up by Canada-earlier I heard a speech of a member who said that they were there when they initiated the Egg Marketing Agency which was in a mess at one time-served Canada well, and I believe they reflect not at all on our ability to trade as a free trader.
I think I can conclude-I do not know how much time there is-by saying that the debate is important. Agriculture is important. I think there have been enough illustrations and demonstrations that our combined Ministers of Agriculture and our Prime Minister have constantly put agriculture at the head of their agenda items every year since I have been elected.
It has been a long time since a Prime Minister has given the consideration to agriculture as our Prime Minister has. You may criticize him, but you cannot say he has avoided such an important issue. Nobody can say that in this place, because there is just too much evidence the other way.

Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by saying that, as always, the member for Portage-Interlake has been interesting to listen to, if not always informative in the sense that I do not agree with everything he has to say.
I do agree with him though that the Reform Party is not levelling with a lot of the people it is courting for support. It is not levelling with those people with respect to its agricultural policies, it is not levelling with those people with respect to policies on medicare, it is not levelling with those people with respect to its policies about the GST and a host of other policies.
It is hoping that somehow its position with respect to Quebec will cause people not to take seriously all their other policies and vote for them in that respect alone. I think it would be a tragedy if people in the west or
Supply
Ontario or anywhere else were simply to support the Reform Party on the basis of their perceived position in the constitutional debate. It is a position that is largely irresponsible, in the sense that it does not have to take what happens to the country into account in its constitutional posturing.
I did not get up to talk about the Reform Party. I got up to talk about this motion. I think I will respond to a few of the things that the member from Portage-Interlake said first and then, if I have any time left, I will try and speak directly to the motion.
The member mentioned the European community. What he did not mention and what was significant by its absence is the fact that the European community and its economic integration, its single market that is coming into effect in 1992, is a single market that is accompanied by a social charter. One of the conditions for the single market in 1992 in Europe is the social charter. Yet the proposition brought forward by the New Democrats, the leader of the NDP, the premier of Ontario and others that there be a social charter as part of the constitutional package is not taken seriously by the government. At the same time the member, on behalf of that same government, wants us to take seriously the European Economic Community and the way in which it is arranged for the free flow of goods and capital services, et cetera, within the 12 European countries.
You cannot have it both ways. If you want to cite the European community experience then you also have to take seriously the fact that it has brought forward a social charter. I would invite the member to think about that inconsistency and not cite the European community unless he is willing at least to admit the objective fact of the matter, that a social charter in Europe has accompanied the things which he wants us somehow to imitate or take seriously here in the Canadian context.
The member for Argenteuil-Papineau and others spoke about the government's commitment to the preservation of supply management. I am glad to hear those words, but I think they are grounds for anxiety. These motions do not just originate out of nothing. They originate out of a legitimate anxiety on the part of many people in the agricultural community and in the political community, but this government is not as committed to supply management as it may seem.

Supply
Let me cite a number of reasons why I think that anxiety is legitimate beginning with the free trade agreement. The free trade agreement in the North American context, never mind the global context, has created economic conditions for the kind of pressure that could eventually erode marketing boards here in Canada, with or without an agreement at GATT to do so.
I do not want to re-live the entire FTA debate, but the fact of the matter is that regardless of whether or not the text of the FTA agreement itself said that supply management systems would be disposed of, the fact is that the FTA created an economic context in which the pressure on supply management will eventually be irresistible because of the increased degree of free trade in food processing. Our food processors, having to compete with imports or whatever you want to call them that come from the United States in a non-supply managed context, are eventually going to be in a situation where something has to give. Either the food processors will give and go to the United States, or our supply managed system will have to go. These are the kinds of pressures which have been set up by the free trade agreement supported, promoted and passed by this government. People who know that, know that the commitment of this government to supply management is certainly not 100 per cent.
People also know that this is a government which has tried to make light of the whole phenomenon of crossborder shopping. It is another phenomenon which is not unrelated to this whole question of supply management. What are a lot of people doing when they cross-border shop, particularly in places where they can go every day? In many cases they are going across to buy milk, cheese and other dairy products, things which some people would argue are cheaper in the United States because they have a completely market oriented way of dealing with these particular products.
The government does not want to admit that. It wants to play down the cross-border shopping phenomenon. We saw that even today, when I asked a question of the Minister of National Revenue and he refused once again to acknowledge the full extent of the problem that figures show, when you take into account just how much
Canadians are spending in the United States and not just how many trips they are making.
With respect to the whole question of supply management, people with any sort of political memory know other things about this government. They know that some people on the other side made their political careers out of and cut their political teeth on struggles against marketing boards. I could name some of them on that side who made their political careers initially by opposing marketing boards within the agricultural community in their respective provinces. Some of them have become ministers.
One fellow in particular, whom I otherwise quite respect, except that we disagree on this fundamental economic point, was the one responsible for taking oats out of the mandate of the Canadian Wheat Board when he was minister. This is another form of orderly marketing.
It is quite unreasonable for the government to say to members of the opposition and members of the public at large that we should relax, that we should trust this government when it comes to supply management. We know that as individuals many of them have a history of being against supply management. We know that as a government it has a history of supporting agreements, in this case the free trade agreement that has created a context which has put pressure on our supply management system. The lack of trust that exists there is not something that has just been created by opposition politicians for political purposes. It is a well grounded anxiety.
The situation that so many of our farmers find themselves in, particularly our grain farmers, has also been a subject of much debate today. I hope I will be forgiven if I use a bit of humour to describe the situation that so many of our farmers find themselves in.
I am reminded of the story about a fellow who comes into the hardware store and buys a hammer for $10. He goes out and sells it on the street. He buys it for $10 and just in front of the store he sells it for $5.
The next day he comes in and buys two hammers for $10 each. He goes out on to the street and sells them to the people on the street for $5. The next day he comes in and buys three hammers for $10 each and goes out on to the street and sells them for $5. This continues: four hammers, five hammers, ten hammers.
October 3, 1991

Finally the guy in the hardware store is having a hard time keeping up with all of this so he asked: "What on earth are you doing? You are buying these hammers for $10 and selling them on the street for $5. How on earth can you make a living?" The guy said: "It is not great, but it beats farming".
This is the situation that so many of our farmers find themselves in. What it costs them to produce the product is far and away more than what they are able to get in this tremendous international marketplace that has created this incredible tragedy. People on one side of the world are crying, literally, because land that belonged to their family for generation after generation is being lost to the banks as a result of wheat at prices that would have been acceptable in the 1930s. On the other side of the world people are crying, weeping, suffering and dying because they cannot lay their hands on that product. Is this not a wonderful achievement of human civilization? What a wonderful global order we live in that sees these two sets of teary-eyed faces; one because they are losing their livelihood and their family way of life and the land they have lived on for generations, and the other where people are starving because we cannot somehow get these two things together.
We do not have a system that depends on supply and need. We have a system that depends on supply and demand. Demand is defined by the ability to pay and demand is defined by the ability of certain companies and countries, in this case in the United States, to manipulate that international marketplace so that they can have the upper hand.
This government has been afraid, as have so many other governments over the years, to say what is really going on here. What is really going on here is evil. It is evil that we should have this kind of system where people are starving to death and, on the other hand, the grain is piling up on the ground for lack of the ability to sell it at a reasonable price.
The problem with the government, it seems to me, with respect to the so-called trade war between the Europeans and the United States is that given its sort of economic ideology it cannot really understand what the Europeans are doing. Because the government wants to
Supply
understand the world completely in market terms, it thinks that the Europeans are just sort of being bad guys, that they are just cheating. In a world in which obviously we all accept, according to the Conservatives, that the market is the thing that rules, then people who distort the market by having the common agricultural policy or various things like this, these are bad people; these are people who do not understand reality.
What the government does not understand is that the Europeans have not made just an economic policy or an economic decision. They have made a social decision. They have made a social policy decision that they want to preserve their farmers and their farms and the way of life associated with farmers. This is completely above and beyond the capacity of this government and the Americans to understand.
Instead of making that same decision and saying "do we want to make a similar decision", do we want to say: "We will support our farmers and our farms and that particular way of life because that is a social decision, not an economic decision"? Instead, they are trying to do it on the cheek, so to speak. They are trying year by year, protest by protest, program by program, to make this problem go away by just giving them a little more. They are never willing to go the whole way, to make the full commitment, to say-and I think this would help with respect to the Americans and the Europeans to give a clear signal-"You are not going to win this war with us. You are not going to let your particular economic strategy wipe out the Canadian agricultural community". We have not given that kind of signal. We have also looked like we are saying: "Oh, gee, do we have to put another dollar on the table? Okay, well if there is enough pressure, and maybe there is an election in Saskatchewan or some other contingent factor, we will come up with some more money".
Instead, we should be making it absolutely clear to the people what we are up against in this and that we value our farm community as much as they value theirs. So far that is not the signal that this government has put out, in spite of the fact that it has spent, and I acknowledge this, incredible amounts of money. But all of the money that has been spent is for naught if in the next little while you

October 3, 1991
Supply
allow all those farmers that you have been supporting over the last little while to go under.
They will not be there. Farming is not something that comes back in the Same way as other economic activities. People leave and they lose their farms to the bank. It is not easy to just pick up and start over again. It is not like walking back into the factory, or whatever the case may be, although even that is getting to be more difficult. If it is not farmers losing their land, it is plants and factories shutting down and moving to the United States, which is an entirely different problem.
I think we need to make that kind of commitment to our farmers. I am sure that there are individuals on the other side who would like to see that kind of commitment made. I am sure that even individuals who are not willing to make that commitment understand and feel the dilemma that so many Canadian farmers find themselves in.
I do not know how so many of them do it, how they can tolerate this drop in their income, this incredible drop in their income, and carry on. It is only because farmers are the last vestige of what we call vocation. They are the last vestige of the people who have vocation.
We have taught people in our society for decades now that life is chasing after the buck. It really does not matter what you do, as long as you get paid well to do it. Farmers are some of the few people around still who say: "It matters what I do. If I get paid less and less and less to do this, I am so attached to this way of life and this way of earning a living that I am going to hang on till the vety last moment".
I think people who have that sense of vocation, whether it comes out of an attachment to the land or an attachment to the idea of providing food for the world, should be supported. I think we should find ways to support them, ways that give support in particular to smaller farmers, but I think we should find ways to make sure that we do not end up with a return to what I would call an agrifeudalism, in which the land is owned by a very small handful of people, the way the rest of the economy is owned by a handful of people.
The one thing that you could at least take some comfort in as the rest of the economy comes to be owned by 20 prominent families in the country is that at least
the land is owned by thousands and tens of thousands of families. Even that is disappearing.
We went through centuries of economic and social development to get to a point where one person, one institution, one power or one authority did not own everything and did not own the land. That was the promise of the new world of Canada. It was not exactly much of a promise to the aboriginal people, but let us leave that aside for a minute.
We are returning now to a situation in which fewer and fewer people own more and more of the land. Corporate farming, agri-business is the wrong way to go. The fact of the matter is that this government is not committed to fighting that over-all trend. Its friendships, its connections, its networks are all with the wrong people in this respect, with the multinational grain companies and the vertically integrated Royal Dutch Shells and others who want to control everything from the ground up, the patented seed, the fertilizer, the herbicides, elevators and the transportation system. You name it.
They have not got everything into place yet, but just about everything. What they need really now is to find a way to own the railroads, which they have in a surrogate form through the CPR for years anyway, and then find a way to own the land.
That will not bother anyone over there. There will still be the hon. member for Assiniboia talking about the NDP land bank and how we want to have massive collectivization of farms. He is worrying about something that was never in the cards here. Nobody ever wanted it. It does not concern him a bit that all the land may someday be owned by a few multinational corporations or by the banks. It does not bother him.
I say this is wrong and I say this is the blind spot in the approach which this government takes to agricultural policy.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, finally, finally, the very influential NDP member said he praised the government for 650 per cent augmentation of intervention in farming. The farmers are very proud people. They do not want subsidies. They want fair trade. They do not like to receive their income from the government. They need it but they do not like it. Nobody likes to have subsidies or a welfare cheque. When you need it, it is necessaiy, but farmers are proud people. I know that because they have told me that, at least my constituents,

and I know the member's constituents feel the same thing.
I posed a couple of difficult question to Liberal members and maybe they were not in a position to respond, but I will ask the NDP member if he agrees with the position of the federal government which is now working on this, that what we ask for at the Uruguay round negotiations is substantial reductions in trade distorting subsidies, particularly export subsidies; increased access to export markets; clearer and fairer GATT rules including the clarification and strengthening of article XI; and a framework of rules to prevent the abuse of health and sanitary regulations as barriers to trade.
Does the member agree with the position of the government under the auspices of the GATT? Just a simple response, thank you.

Mr. Speaker, the member tries to simplify the matter in this respect: over a hundred countries agree with that particular statement. The problem is trying to figure out what that means.
What is a trade distorting subsidy? That is the debate, is it not? Everybody can say: "We are against trade distorting subsidies", but what does that mean? Some people believe that any involvement of government in the economy is a trade distorting subsidy. Other people may not believe that. That is what is at issue.
What is at issue here is whether this government, the government of which you are a part, actually believes that things like supply and management are not trade distorting subsidies or whether it believes in the dark recesses of its mind, and sometimes in the not so dark recesses of it mind given the things that it has said and done in the past, that actually supply and management is trade distorting. It cannot possibly admit that just like it couldn't possibly admit that in the free trade agreement, so it had to go through the whole agreement saying: "We believe in supply and management, we believe in supply and management, we believe in supply and management".
Show us in the agreement where it says supply and management is not being threatened. Everyone who knew anything, anyone who had two brain cells to rub
Supply
together, knew that the free trade agreement threatened supply and management.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
I want to ask the opposition member about the particularity of Canada as an exporting country. Maybe all farmers, maybe all producers in this country should be under a marketing agency. For instance, look at the pork producers, potato producers, oilseeds, you name it, that not actually under a supply management organization.
Maybe at the end of this, because we are now discussing it on a world basis, because GATT is all countries together, the member will ask whether it is fair. Let us look at a pessimistic situation. At the end of the day when it is all over the world will say: "No. Article XI, we do not want to strengthen it. We do not want to do anything to it, but we want to go to tariffication by the Americans", I suppose.
Given the facts and taking into consideration that production in this country is not all under supply management, what will the member do if we have the obligation to do something as a government? If you were the government what would you do?

I am not sure I entirely understand the question. I think the member is hypothesising everything breaking down or the United States getting its way. Is that what you are saying? Supply management was seen to be a trade distorting practice. Is that what the hon. member is saying? That is a situation that any government of the day would have to deal with.
I think that an NDP government, for instance, would regard that as much more regrettable than I think a lot of your own people would regard it. Without questioning the integrity of the hon. member who just spoke, there are a lot of people on your side who are critics of orderly marketing and of supply management.
If the GATT breaks down it would be a dilemma. You want to have an international trading system that works and one for which there are generally accepted rules. On the other hand, you do not want to have a system which prevents countries from defending their legitimate interests and which simply imposes upon the global marketplace the kind of "survival of the fittest" that we have had in other contexts.

October 3, 1991
Supply
I think a lot of people in the Third World, for instance, are particularly concerned about that. At the same time as they want liberalized trade, they want trade that is fair and that respects their ability to look after their own interests.
If the worst case scenario that the hon. member points out were to happen, that would happen in a particular context. I think it would be very difficult for me or anyone else, including the hon. member, to speculate on just what the response of the Canadian government might be at that time.

Madam Speaker, this debate that we are having in this House today is one of the most important debates that could take place in this country. It is also a very historical debate because the industry that we are discussing today, agriculture, is as old as the first pioneer in this country. The first pioneer normally had a cow and a few chickens. This debate is on supply management. He certainly knew what his demands were in that day. He had to raise enough food to live, to start off.
Those early pioneers who came to this country and built up the agricultural industry, those pioneers who built all those stone fences and stone piles and cleared the land and built the farms, had really built the very basis of this nation. Today those farmers who are carrying on in that tradition deserve the help and every inch of effort that we can give them to win their case for them on supply management, because that is the lifeline of the farm community in those areas today.
To give the extent of the industry we are talking about today, Canada has 300,000 farmers. Quebec has 41,000, the fourth largest farm population of all the provinces. Ontario has 72,000 farmers, which is the largest farm population in Canada. In the dairy business, Canada has 35,600 dairy farmers, 16,000 located in the province of Quebec and 11,000 in the province of Ontario.
Ontario has 475,000 dairy cows, a farm average of 34 cows. In Quebec the average is 33 cows per farm, with a total cow population in the province of Quebec of 578,000. Dairy farming in Canada produces cash receipts of $3 billion a year. Basically, that is the industry we are talking about here in this House of Commons today.
The way this ends up at the GATT is going to tell us how successful that industry is going to be in continuing in this country.
I heard the hon. member for Joliette say that it was too bad that we are having a partisan debate on this issue in the House today. I am sure that every Canadian watching this debate today will fully understand our feeling about that when they see the kinds of answers we get on agriculture from this government in the House of Commons. Is it a love-in when it gives its answers? It gives answers that are so wishy-washy, it does not come to the point. When it does, it is certainly not gentle about it in the terms the hon. member for Joliette would like to see.
He said it was too bad for people the government was not doing anything. Normally, when governments are doing something, people recognize it, but they have to see the evidence of it. That is another thing this debate is about today. We want to see the evidence.
Would it ever occur to the hon. member for Joliette, for example, that the last thing we would ever want to happen to us in this House is to be identified with the image and policies of this government?
The Liberal Party of Canada brought in the National Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act, and we want to see it rescued. We want to see it continued and working effectively for Canadian farmers. The agencies that came in under this act have served Canada extremely well.
I did not speak about Hazen Argue today in a eulogy to him because I know that Hazen Argue is out there tonight, delighted that there is a debate on agriculture in this House of Commons. He lived for agriculture and he was a very dedicated figure in that field.
The National Farm Products Market Agencies Act was proclaimed in January 1972. I remember, I was here when that was proclaimed and I was here in this House with a number of other members between Christmas and New Years of 1971 because we had come back purposely to pass the farm marketing bill. It was proclaimed the following January.
No other Canadian knew we were here because they were celebrating the festive season and they would have thought we were a little off our rockers if they knew we
October 3, 1991

were sitting here in session in the House of Commons between Christmas and New Years.
As I stand here today to speak on the GATT negotiations and the possible destruction of our supply management system because of the lack of muscle that is being displayed by the Federal Government of Canada at the GATT negotiations, I find this whole international process very depressing indeed.
The most dangerous development I see at these GATT negotiations is the common ground thinking and the common ground linking that is going on between the United States and the European Economic Community. Over the years of our history, whenever the United States teamed up with any nation in Europe, such as Britain or with the European Community against Canada, Canada has lost, historically. We lost the Alaskan boundary dispute in 1903 because the United States and Great Britain lined up against us. We lost the State of Maine in the province of New Brunswick boundary decision because they lined up against us.
We Canadians have to stand solidly on rational arguments and never give up trying to win this case on supply management.
We can never cave in, and the government has to develop a strong muscle. The view is out there that the government is a bit spineless when it comes to defending Canada's agricultural trade. The feeling is out there that the government is rather spineless when it comes to defending Canada's interests even in the free trade agreement, and now we are into the GATT discussions.
We see the United States which is supposed to be our trading friend lining up with the European Economic Community against Canada. Where is the international justice in a system like that? The government cannot afford to sit back and be anything but absolutely aggressive toward this united action on its part.
A lot has been said in comments today about the Consumers' Association of Canada. I simply want to say that it is not fair to make statements about food costs and food production in Canada unless you know the plight of the Canadian farmer first hand and unless you really know what is going on out there.
I grew up on a farm, and I have some knowledge of this subject. When you drive past a farm today, very few
Private Members' Business
people realize the tremendous investment that exists on that farm. They look upon it as a family home.
It is only fair that the farmers get a fair return on their investment because if they do not, they will not be in business and Canada will have lost that productivity. The farming pioneers of this country must be looking down on us in this House today and wondering what has happened.
I think that in negotiating tools, I cannot forgive the government for submitting $8.8 billion as a figure that the Government of Canada is giving to farm organizations in Canada by way of subsidies and help. That has destroyed a lot of its argument to begin with. It has taken away a punch, and even by saying $2.2 billion for the dairy industry, it is helping those who are against us in this argument. That is wrong.
