speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in the debate on Motion 81 presented by the hon. member for MacKenzie which recommends the introduction of income averaging measures to the Income Tax Act. This, it is argued, would reduce the tax paid by individuals whose incomes fluctuate considerably from one year to the next.

October 3, 1991
Private Members' Business
Although the motion talks of the introduction of such provisions, it would be more appropriate to speak of reintroducing them, as they were part of the Income Tax Act provisions until 1987. Indeed, two methods of income averaging were eliminated with the tax reform of 1988. These were general forward averaging and block averaging which was designed to assist farmers and fishermen. To ensure a smooth transition, taxpayers who deducted averaging amounts prior to 1988 have until 1997 to bring such amounts back into their income. This allows taxpayers to obtain a federal tax credit at the highest marginal rate during the year in question. The system of block averaging for farmers and fishermen comtinues to apply to the five-year periods that began prior to 1988.
Madam Speaker, in considering the possibility of reintroducing income averaging provisions to the personal tax system, it is important to review the reasons why these provisions were eliminated in 1988.
The methods of income averaging were eliminated with the tax reform of 1988. The reform was based on five broad principles.
The tax system should be fair and should respect Canadian views of social justice. It should be consistently progressive, imposing little or no burden on those least able to pay. There should be less variation in the tax position of individuals in similar economic circumstances.
The tax system should have a broader base and lower rates. It should minimize preferences that allow high-income individuals and profitable corporations to pay little or no tax. Rates should be lowered to encourage initiative and risk-taking. The tax system should recognize Canadian realities and priorities. It should support Canada's capital requirements for growth and development and contribute to Canada's ability to compete in world markets. It should support regional development.
The tax system should be more understandable and less complex.
The tax system should provide a stable revenue base, to assure reliable and predictable revenues to finance public programs.
Madam Speaker, the application of these principles centred around three major areas of change: First, the reduction of the ten income tax brackets, ranging from a tax rate of 6 per cent to 34 per cent, to three tax brackets with rates of 17 per cent, 26 per cent and 29 per cent; secondly, the conversion of personal exemptions and certain deductions into tax credits. Unlike deductions and exemptions which reduce the tax to be paid by an amount that reflects the level of income, tax credits reduce the tax to paid by a set amount, regardless of the level of income. Thirdly, the reduction or elimination of several tax concessions which primarly benefitted high-income taxpayers.
The elimination of income averaging provisions was part of the latter category of measures which, in broadening the tax base, made it possible to reduce tax rates. The reduction of the number of tax brackets and the lower tax rates meant there was less need for income averaging. In short, smaller differences between the minimum and maximum marginal rates, that is 28 per cent prior to tax reform and 13 per cent after, reduced the tax consequences associated with fluctuations in income from year to year. Moreover, with the broader tax brackets, there is a much lower probability that fluctuations in income from one year to another will give rise to an increase in an individual's tax burden.
Therefore, income averaging provisions were eliminated because of a reduced need for such provisions and in part to finance the lower tax rates.
Tax reform involved a series of interrelated changes and so it is not appropriate to assess the fairness and relevance of specific measures without considering the whole package. The financial statistics for the 1988 taxation year, which were released last year, provided the first opportunity to determine the impact of the reform as a whole.
These statistics clearly show that tax reform achieved its intended objectives: overall, personal income taxes were reduced by more than $2,5 billion; some 905,000 Canadians with incomes under $15,000 no longer had to pay income taxes; the number of taxpayers aged 65 years or older paying tax fell by approximately 300,000.
October 3, 1991

One of the surest ways to threaten these gains would be to gradually reintroduce the provisions in place before the reform. The reintroduction of measures such as income averaging would narrow the tax base and would require an increase in tax rates in order to preserve the government's tax revenue.
Madam Speaker, the elimination of income averaging in 1988 was part of a broader initiative designed to make the tax system simpler and fairer. Given the positive impact of that reform, it would be counter-productive to take a step back and amend some of the elements that have contributed to its success.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise tonight to speak on this bill put forward by hon. colleague, the member for Mackenzie.
The government opposite has been stating, as one of its objectives, a more fair and simpler tax system. I think that an average Canadian today would agree that this objective has not been realized.
There are a number of examples of the fact that taxation in this country is simply not fair. We can look at, for example, the fact that 58 per cent of married people pay more tax living as a married couple than they would if they lived as a common law couple according to Stats Canada. We have the example of corporations in this country with incomes in the neighbourhood of $30 billion on which no tax is paid, not even a penny. Compare this to the United States where Ronald Reagan introduced a minimum corporate tax. At least U.S corporations pay some income tax.
We have, along with that, the absurdity of people in this country, living below the poverty line, paying income tax. We have corporations, on the one hand, which can afford to hire expensive tax consultants, accountants and tax lawyers to look for loopholes in the tax law, many of which they lobbied to have put in place themselves, and on the other hand we have many families in this country which are barely able to make ends meet, can barely afford go to H&R Block to have their income tax done, are paying income tax and are below the poverty line.
Private Members' Business
Only one government in this country has said that it will do away with income tax below the poverty line and that is the Ontario government of Bob Rae. The New Democratic government in that province has said that although it cannot affect federal income tax, the people in Ontario living below the poverty line will not be paying any provincial income tax. That is a move towards tax fairness.
The government has also indicated that it had planned to make a simpler tax system. Again I think an average Canadian looking at his or her tax forms when they do their taxes would simply say that the income tax system in this country is neither simple nor is it fair.
This bill the member for Mackenzie has brought forward is an attempt, in a small way, to make the tax system in this country somewhat fairer. This bill would allow for five-year block averaging. It is not something new, in fact it is something that was initially brought into effect in the late 1940s. It is fairer for professions where income comes about in an unequal manner; people such as artists, sales people, real estate agents, ranchers, farmers, fishermen, writers, small business people, people who may have a number of years of low or mediocre income then suddenly have a year where things go very well for them and they have a very high income. Unfortunately, these people are now forced to pay tax on a very good year when in actual fact their over-all income over a longer period of time is much lower. That, I would suggest, is not fair, and I do not think the people who are into those situations would find it fair.
In the past, people had been able to average their income over a five-year period to allow them to pay a more equitable tax on their income. To me, that sounds fair. I think many Canadians find it fair. Certainly many accountants have found it fair. With respect to farm groups in western Canada, most farm organizations including the Western Canadian Wheat Growers, which tends to be a group that supports many of the government's measures, have said that this is a measure that is fair and equitable and should be maintained.
I believe it was removed by Order in Council in 1987 by this government. I have been following the debate on this quite closely. I have been reading the debates that I have not heard, and the government puts forward three arguments as to why this five-year block averaging

October 3, 1991
Private Members' Business
should be removed and should not be reinstated in the tax system.
I am paraphrasing from the parliamentary secretary, the lead speaker for the government who spoke on this bill, and he said that the fundamental principle is that ability to pay is measured on the basis of income earned and received in a single year. In other words, he is saying that a fundamental principle is that we pay income tax based on each year, regardless of over-all income.
I do not think that is a fundamental principle. That is why the five-year block averaging was put in in the first place, to take out the peaks and valleys. I think a much more accurate statement of the fundamental principle would be that people should be paying taxes on income earned, not being restricted to one single year. By the parliamentary secretary restricting it to one year, I do not think is a fundamental principle that most Canadians would agree with.
He and other members on the government side have indicated that the tax brackets have now been narrowed, that you have a minimum of 17 per cent to 29 per cent tax payable, and that is true. But what they have forgotten is that there is still a large gap, particularly when you take into account provincial income tax, which can mean an 18 per cent difference in tax payable.
If a farmer or a small business person has been having three or four or five bad years and suddenly has a good year and is faced with paying that extra 18 per cent, you tell them that that is not very much money and they are going to tell you something else. If a business or a farmer has been suffering for a number of years and suddenly has a good year, they need that money to help them keep their operation going, pay off bills and so on. So the idea of 18 per cent, I would suggest and many Canadians would suggest, is in fact significant.
The other fact is that the government likes to say that retirement is the most frequent and significant cause for income fluctuation. I think that perhaps that is true, in the sense that at some time in our lives all Canadians will suffer a radical drop in income, and often that occurs at the time of retirement. But this bill is not meant to deal with that. The fact is, we have a small percentage of Canadians which suffer from fluctuating incomes from year, to year, to year, to year. Although the government
can say that it has put in tax reforms to help retirement, that really is not the issue. That is not the purpose of this bill. That was not the purpose of a five-year block averaging. The fact that when people retire they can take advantage of RRSPs does not help a farmer or a businessman or a fisherman or anyone with a fluctuating income. It does not help them in that particular year.
I think the bill that the hon. member has put forward is a bill that will help those entrepreneurs, those Canadians who are into more open market situations. These are people who often run the risks of the marketplace, small business people, artists, people on commission sales, farmers, people who are subject to the disciplines of the open market. This is a government that likes to pretend it represents small business and farmers but in fact this is something it is doing that will hurt small business and farmers.
The argument that we cannot afford to bring in block averaging because it is going to cost the government too much money is again, I would suggest, not accurate in that the actual amount of money lost by the government would be very small and certainly could be made up quite easily. If the government would bring in a minimum tax for corporations, for example, it would more than offset any income loss that Revenue Canada suffered as a result of five-year block averaging.
I believe my time is almost up. In conclusion, I would like to say that if the government wants to have a prosperous nation it is essential that it provide opportunities for Canadians to make an income, and provide for themselves. This in a small way would help a particular group of Canadians to maintain themselves at a time when the Canadian economy is suffering very badly. I would simply conclude by saying that I do wish the government would reconsider its position on this bill and vote for it when the time comes.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to speak today to Motion No. 81 which has been put forward by the hon. member for Mackenzie. It is designed to consider the advisability of introducing amendments to the Income Tax Act to allow some form of income averaging for the benefit of individuals whose incomes fluctuate significantly from year to year.

I am sure that members of the House would agree that the hon. member for Mackenzie is committed, and has been for many years, to the welfare of farmers in Canada. We have to agree also that before the Income Tax Act was reformed in 1988 it contained two provisions for averaging income over a number of years; block averaging and forward averaging, which colleagues have already alluded to this afternoon. These procedures allow taxpayers with large fluctuations in their incomes to spread the burden of tax over a number of years. Both forms of averaging involved complex calculations.
Consider first the block averaging. This was available to individuals whose chief source of income was farming or fishing and it allowed them to average their income from all sources over a five-year period. This provision involved a calculation whereby the taxpayer recalculated the tax liability as if one-fifth of his or her total income over the period had been earned in each of the five years.
An election to block average was made in the last year of the five-year period and resulted in a reduction in tax in that year or in the refund of taxes paid in the earlier years of the period.
The other income averaging technique was known as forward averaging. Unlike block averaging, forward averaging was not restricted to those involved in farming and fishing. It allowed all individuals whose income in a year exceeded 110 per cent of their average adjusted income in the preceding three years to spread out the excess over future years in order to reduce its impact on tax payable.
The excess income which was averaged in this fashion was deductible in computing taxable income for the year in question but gave rise to a special tax in that year at the highest marginal rate.
In future years the average amounts could be brought back and taxed as regular income with a refundable credit provided at the top marginal tax rate.
This was how the system operated before 1988 but as hon. members know the government reformed the corporate and personal income tax systems in 1988 and among the objectives of this reform was the creation of a tax system that contributed to fairness, competitiveness, growth, and job creation. To achieve these objectives, tax reform was guided by two major principles, lower tax rates and a broader tax base. It is readily apparent that
Private Members' Business
lower rates provide an incentive to work and invest, thereby contributing to the goals of competitiveness, growth and job creation. The pre-1988 system had 10 rates ranging from 6 per cent to 34 per cent. This structure was replaced with one comprised of only three rates: 17 per cent, 26 per cent and 29 per cent.
A related element was a conversion of personal exemptions into tax credits. Exemptions provide the greatest benefit to higher income earners, whereas credits are fairer because they provide the same degree of tax relief to all taxpayers.
The rate reduction combined with the conversion of exemptions into tax credits resulted in a fairer and more progressive tax system. I shall return to how these changes reduce the need for income averaging procedures in the tax system in a moment.
The other guiding principle of tax reform, namely broadening the tax base by removing special tax preferences, was equally important. A broader base makes the tax system simpler and fairer. It reduces the opportunities for tax planning, opportunities that were most often used by high income Canadians. Many tax preferences were eliminated or restricted. For example, the deductibility of business expenses for meals and entertainment was significantly reduced.
The hon. member for Mackenzie has proposed a reintroduction of income averaging procedures into our tax system. In order to assess this proposal properly, it is helpful to review the goals and methods of tax reform as we have just done. The lower and fewer tax rates which came with tax reform reduced the need for averaging provisions, a point on which I shall elaborate in a moment.
Since the need for averaging provisions was reduced, such measures were eliminated as part of tax reform. Forward averaging was eliminated for 1988 and subsequent years and the block averaging provisions for farmers and fishermen ceased to apply for any five year block commencing after 1987.
These changes were introduced gradually in such a way as to ease the transition. Forward averaging amounts deducted in prior years can still be brought back into income until 1997 and will entitle a taxpayer to a federal tax credit at the top marginal rate in that year. Block averaging arrangements that were already under way were allowed to run their normal course.

Private Members' Business
Let me now explain why the new tax rates and the reduction in the number of tax brackets brought about by tax reform reduced the need for averaging. Prior to the reform the spread between the lowest marginal tax rates, namely 6 per cent, and the highest, 34 per cent, was 28 percentage points. Such a wide spread of course had severe tax consequences for those whose income fluctuated substantially from year to year.
After tax reform the spread between the lowest, namely 17 per cent and the highest at 29 per cent with marginal tax rates was reduced to 12 percentage points. Furthermore, tax brackets became much broader and the lowest tax bracket now accounts for two-thirds of tax filers.
Therefore, year to year fluctuations in income are now less likely to move a taxpayer from one bracket to another. Even if such a shift does occur, it will not cause a significant fluctuation in tax burdens.
The reforms to the tax system made possible the elimination of averaging provisions and the elimination of the averaging provisions in turn contributed to making the tax system simpler and helped finance the reduction in marginal tax rates.
The most significant income averaging activity that typical Canadians undertake is that of putting away money during their working years to finance their retirement. This type of income averaging now receives more favourable tax treatment. Recent pension reforms provide substantial opportunity to defer income and tax. This tax assistance is based on the principle that money set aside for retirement should be taxed when it is received, not when it is saved.
Accordingly, amounts contributed to registered retirement savings plans, namely RRSPs, registered pension plans and deferred profit sharing plans are deductible in the year contributions are made and the investment income in these plans is not taxed when it is earned. Instead the savings are subject to tax only when benefits are paid out of the registered plans.
For the vast majority of taxpayers who have lower incomes and higher tax credits in retirement years and who therefore face lower marginal tax rates, the tax assistance provided for retirement saving includes an important income averaging advantage in addition to its tax deferral benefits.
As I noted, the system of tax assistance through retirement saving was recently improved. The new contribution limits which come into effect this year eliminate many shortcomings of the previous system and ensure that Canadians have fair access to tax assistance for retirement savings.
For example, taxpayers without an employer sponsored pension plan did not previously enjoy the same opportunities to build adequate pensions on a tax assisted basis. Those with relatively poor pension plans face the same RRSP limits as those with very generous pension plans.
The limits were also vulnerable to a growing number of tax planning arrangements. In short, some taxpayers did not have access to adequate levels of tax assistance, while others were able to obtain excessive tax assistance.
The new single comprehensive limit on contributions, namely 18 per cent of earnings, will apply to all tax assisted savings in all plans. The new system will better integrate RRSP and registered pension plan contributions. It will be more flexible and will enable taxpayers to tailor the pattern of their retirement savings more closely to their financial needs.
In conclusion, we should indeed address the needs of Canadians with incomes which fluctuate from one year to another, but tax reforms combined with the substantial income deferral possibilities provided by the new system of tax assistance for retirement saving does indeed address these very needs.
It does so indeed more fully and more fairly than would the reintroduction of complex averaging measures.
Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Madam Speaker, I would just like to say a few words on this motion on behalf of my party.
Really, they are more in the nature of personal reflection on the concept of income averaging and the taxation of income averaging. I must confess to not having had a great deal of time to think about this matter today, although it is an interesting subject and an interesting motion which the hon. member for Mackenzie has put before the House.
October 3, 1991

It is one on which I would have preferred to have a little more time to give some careful reflection to. However, I would just like to say a few things from the perspective of two of the income groups that are prominent in my riding and for whom this system of income averaging would be relevant, that is to say, the fishermen and the farmers.
Certainly, in the case of fishermen, their income fluctuates every year with the catch and the success of their catch. In the case of the farmers, it is the same story with their incomes dependent on the weather conditions, on the price of their product and on all sorts of factors over which they have no control. Certainly a form of averaging of income which would allow them to plan further ahead would be advantageous to both those income groups.
It is really a form of social insurance in the sense of allowing them to be compensated in the bad years by the income that they earned in the good years.
The questions that this system raises are many, particularly when they are thought about in relation to our system of progressive income taxation. In our system of retirement income, Canadians are given tax advantages for putting money away into RRSP and other forms of deferred income plans. In that sense, they are able to lower their taxable income in current years and only have to pay taxes on that income when they have lower income. In that sense, they are subject to a lower marginal tax rate.
This subject of income averaging has to be considered in the context of measures in the income tax system, particularly in terms of deferred income plans and the RRSP plans which allow people to defer their income to a future date. The five-year block averaging mentioned in the member's motion and his remarks in support of his motion lead me to ask the question: What is so special about five years? I could see, if we were to conduct some genuine tax reform, a system in which all income would be equally considered and one might be able to defer one's income indefinitely. Our tax rate might be something approaching what one of my colleagues has called a single tax, that is to say, a flat tax rate on income. The individual taxpayer would simply be able to choose how much income he would reserve for a particular year or
Private Members' Business
put the extra income in a plan of some sort for future years for future purposes. He would only pay taxes on it when that income was withdrawn in the form of annuity like an RRSP.
I could see a system extended beyond that to allow, for example, individual taxpayers to plan for future education and retraining possibilities down the road. They would be allowed to take income from a good year and put it aside into an education plan or some form of savings account that would not be subject to tax in that year. Later on perhaps, if there is a change of career or need for retraining, that income would be there to be drawn upon. They would not pay high tax rates on it in the year they earned the income.
The idea of averaging income over a longer period than a year certainly has merit, provided it is part of a more comprehensive set of tax reform proposals. I would include in that a movement toward something I would call a single tax. For people in many income categories it also has to be related to some minimum level of income and perhaps, some form of guaranteed annual income, minimum tax or some level of minimum income which people could have without having to pay taxes. We have something similar in the current system, which is often subject to many inequities because of the complicated nature of our income tax system.
I would have preferred to have more time to give this matter some structured thought. I believe the principle of the motion has merit. It is the kind of thing one wants to examine in the context of many other facets of the income tax system which is very, very complex. I would submit that it is far too complex and a source of great frustration for many Canadians.
The government's tax reform proposals which involve the closure of some of the brackets in our progressive income tax system go part way to simplifying the tax system. There are still many loopholes, tax expenditures and kinks in the tax system which favour the well-to-do and which favour those Canadians who have a persistently high income. They can employ the services of accountants to take advantage of these loopholes and thereby escape taxation and impose a higher burden of taxes on the rest of the population including those very individuals the member for Mackenzie would like to help with his block averaging proposal.

I would submit that the way to true tax reform would involve a form of averaging over a longer period of time than a year, but it would also involve many other components including a movement toward a far simpler system of tax rates and a more comprehensive base. It would be an income tax system which would eliminate many of the loopholes that still exist in our income tax system. It makes that system far too complicated and ends up creating many inequities for Canadians. It creates distortions and disincentives for all sorts of things and that in the end weakens our economy. It also creates all sorts of problems of fiscal management for the government.
It is an interesting idea. It certainly benefits income groups like the farmers and the fishermen, but it would need to be studied more carefully and would need to be incorporated with other sorts of tax measures such as those that I have described.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity for a few moments this evening to comment on the hon. member for Mackenzie's proposition before the House:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should
consider the advisability of introducing amendments to the Income
Tax Act so that taxpayers whose income may fluctuate from one year
to the next would be able to average their income over five years.
I have been most interested in the comments that various members have made this evening with respect to our tax system and with respect to this specific proposition. I think two comments stand out especially in my mind: first, that the tax system should be a fair one and, second, that the tax system should be a simple one, as simple as it possibly can be.
You and I are well aware, Madam Speaker, that the tax system we have in place today, in spite of all of the efforts to simplify, improve and reform it, is anything but simple. You and I just have to pick up our income tax return form as we are required to do each year, take a look at it, see what if anything we can make of it and how long it is going to take to fill out, to know that it is a very complex system indeed.
Many of my constituents come to me regularly and tell me that when they started paying income tax the return was one simple page. Not only have I seen those forms, but I am just old enough to have filled in a few of those myself years and years and years ago when the income tax return was one simple page.
We have made it more complex every year and every year in this House, sometimes several times a year, we debate further income tax measures, we pass further income tax legislation, and each year it becomes more and more complex.
I recall many people over the years advocating a simpler system, the single tax system.
We recall the campaign of one Mr. Peter Pocklington across this country in 1982-83 leading up to the leadership convention that took place in this city which chose the now Prime Minister of our country to be leader of the Progressive Conservative Party. One of the candidates in that campaign was Mr. Peter Pocklington, who campaigned virtually on a single issue, the issue of a simple income tax form, a one-page tax form, a flat tax form. It was a very popular issue and Mr. Pocklington, at least for a while, became a very popular figure in the country, at least until he decided to trade away Wayne Gretzky to the United States. He became a very popular figure in this country on the theory that we should make the system more simple than it is now.
One of the members of this House says I think he has written a book on it now. The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood, one of my neighbouring ridings in the city of Toronto, has another proposal out on simplifying the system, on a flat tax, getting back to the basics.
All of those proposals, it seems to me, make a good deal of sense but they do conflict with concepts like the one that has been put forward by the hon. member for Mackenzie and so many other concepts in our Income Tax Act. What the hon. member is proposing is not really something that will make the system more simple and straightforward but will bring back a complexity to the system that we had previously.
I am not sure if I am correct, and my mind may be a little foggy on this, but it seems to me that income averaging in the income tax system probably came about back in the 1970s following something called the Carter commission on taxation. My hon. friends say it was 1948. In any event, I remember that in 1970 there were further attempts to reform the income tax system as a result of the Carter commission and the so-called Benson budget, if you will recall, that of then Minister of Finance Edgar Benson. He did a lot of things at that time to try to make the system a fairer one. He brought in things like capital gains tax. He eliminated things like the estate tax. Now we hear that maybe the estate tax would be a fairer way to tax and maybe we should bring it back, rather than leave it in the junkyard con the scrap heap.
October 3, 1991

There have been other attempts, as I have indicated, at tax reform in the past. The latest attempt back in 1987-88 did away with income averaging in the income tax system. Now we have another suggestion for bringing it back. I do not think it meets the criterion of simplicity, even though it may be helpful with respect to the criterion for fairness. It certainly does not help to make our tax system any more simple than it is now. In my view, by bringing it back it would only make it more complex. In the days when we had income averaging in the Income Tax Act we either had to rely on a chartered accountant to figure that out for us or maybe even the tax department itself. We were often at its mercy in making out what was quite a complex calculation and one that if we did try it ourselves usually was wrong.
We are left then, it seems to me, with the other criterion when examining this proposition, and that is the criterion of fairness. Certainly it would seem anything but fair to people who have income that goes in peaks and valleys to have a tax which impacts on them at different tax rates, one sometimes at a higher tax rate when their income is a way up, sometimes at a lower tax rate or perhaps even nil when their income is a way down.
The possibility that their income may be so low that there is no tax payable at all was another issue of concern raised in this House for some period of time by our colleagues in the NDP, and to some extent I suppose with respect to corporations they are still raising that concern. They did raise the concern that at the low end of the scale, at least, all people should pay tax and there should be no way of getting out of it.
As a result of the concerns they brought forth and as a result of reflection and study on the part of the government, the minimum tax was put in place and is in place today to eliminate that concern and to make it fair.
I am sure the hon. members who are murmuring and nodding their heads in approval on the other side of the House will agree that the present government has made very substantial strides to tiy to make the tax system a
Private Members' Business
fairer one by eliminating an awful lot of those tax loopholes that have been referred to and by trying to make it fair.
Just one complex loophole that I can recall, having had a good deal to do with it, was the scientific tax credit which opened up a gigantic sieve in the system and fortunately that has been eliminated.
Who introduced that?

My colleague asks who introduced that. He knows and I know that it was the former Liberal government that introduced that. Virtually every one of the tax loopholes that are in the Income Tax Act and other tax loopholes were introduced by previous Liberal governments over many, many years.
They did it to try to provide some incentives for people to get into scientific investment and research and all of the rest. They did it in good faith and I certainly do not quarrel with the motives. It did not help to create a fair system. Certainly what we should be doing is trying to create a fair system, but at the same time balancing it off with the basic need of the tax system which is to try to make sure that we have enough money to pay the bills that all of us want to pay.
I have listened to our colleagues on the other side this afternoon talking about helping our farmers in this country, a very noble proposition and something that I wholly agree with. They know and I know that somehow or other, if we are going to do that, we need to raise the money to do that and that is raised through the tax system.
While the tax system has to be fair, it also has to make sure that we raise the money not only to look after people like our farmers and our fishermen and all of the other people we need to look after in this country, but to look after something called our deficit and our national debt which they keep reminding us are enormous.
Certainly we are all searching for a system that is simple. We are all searching for a system that is fair. I think the debate this afternoon on this proposition has helped that process. I applaud the hon. member for bringing forward the bill for our consideration.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member who just made a reference to the scientific research tax credit. Something like $2 billion went down the drain in that program. Imagine if we had that kind of money today to help our farmers! I remember one project in particular, the Dream Street Holstein. An enormous amount of money was spent on research on black and white Holsteins and brown and white Holsteins. It cost a fortune. If we had that money today to help farmers in Western Canada, it would be fantastic.
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to motion M-81 introduced by the hon. member for Mackenzie. The hon. member asks the government to consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act so that taxpayers whose income may fluctuate considerably from one year to the next would be able to average their income over five years.
The payment procedure proposed in this motion is almost identical to the provision for averaging the income of farmers and fishermen over a period of five years, a provision that became part of the Income Tax Act in 1946 and was dropped in 1988 as part of our tax reform.
This provision, Madam Speaker, allowed individuals whose chief source of income was farming or fishing to average their income over a five year period. When their income fluctuated substantially from year to year, this procedure made it possible to reduce the total income tax payable over the five year period in question. Averaging was intended to lessen the fiscal impact of substantial fluctuations in the income of farmers and fishermen, more likely to be affected by such fluctuations as a result of drought, disease or price swings.
Today, this is a very common concept, and I think the hon. member for Mackenzie realized that when he introduced his motion, which is entirely appropriate, considering what is happening toda-at GATT they are discussing article XI, and the subject is very much in the news.
However, Madam Speaker, this particular provision of the 1946 Income Tax Act was used by a mere 4 per cent of farmers and fishermen. Only 4 per cent took advantage of this provision. It was a difficult mechanism to comply with and administratively very complex.
With fewer tax brackets and lower tax rates, incomeaveraging measures became less necessary and were abolished in 1988. This also helped simplify the tax
system, which was obviously one of the main objectives of that reform, Madam Speaker.
Averaging was supposed to give some protection to farmers and fishermen whose income is particularly prone to large variations from year to year. Even though this measure was intended to lessen the impact of such fluctuations, it had mixed success, witness the low participation rate I mentioned earlier.
The government still continues to take account of farmers' vulnerability to fluctuating income. That is why, in early 1991, it announced new measures to help them: the Gross Revenue Insurance Program and the Net Income Stabilization Account.
GRIP, the Gross Revenue Insurance Program, is meant to protect farmers' income. It is based on the existing crop insurance plan and adds income protection to it. Farmers can thus count on an assured gross revenue that will not be affected by natural risks or market forces beyond their control. GRIP also enables farmers to calculate the guaranteed return of each crop in the early spring and obtain operating funds as required.
Under the Net Income Stabilization Account, commonly called NISA, farmers and the federal and provincial governments make equivalent payments into individual accounts. Farmers draw on these accounts when their income is low. The interest earned is only taxed when it is withdrawn from the account.
The close cooperation, Madam Speaker, between farmers, the provinces and the federal government that led to these mechanisms is a very important feature of them. When he revealed the terms and conditions of these plans, the Minister of Agriculture declared that this program was designed from scratch by the farmers themselves, the provinces and the federal government as part of a policy review. This is a unique case in public policy development. Together the interested parties set up a whole new program to reduce the need for special assistance every time. The new support measures provide assistance to farmers in all regions of the country equitably and encourage the adoption of sound management practices based on long-term market trends.
I think it is imperative that we collectively recognize this is the type of partnership we must look for, not only in the agricultural sector but in other sectors as well. Governments cannot go it alone any more; they need the input of the various stakeholders.
Members of this House know that Quebec maple syrup producers have come to us asking for $22 million in special assistance. Based on the number of maple syrup producers in Eastern Ontario and in Quebec, for the

Ozmost part, I figure this would represent around $17,000 or $18,000 for each of them. That is a lot of money in times of economic restraint, and I think these new programs will help them pull through.
Madam Speaker, we can see better the level of cooperation between the various stakeholders if we take
a look at what went before the implementation of these measures because extensive consultations have been necessary to formulate such policies.
I can see that my time has run out. Thank you for having recognized me again.
